title: Anyone can read a table you didn't make public
what: Your database answers anonymous visitors with rows from a table that gaugeline.access.json doesn't list as public.
why: The project's public key is in your site's code by design, so anyone can use it to download every row of that table: orders, emails, whatever it holds.
fix: Turn on row level security for the table and add a policy that allows only what visitors need, or mark the table public in gaugeline.access.json if it really is.
tech: Supabase: the exposed tables from PostgREST's OpenAPI description (GET /rest/v1/), then one HEAD /rest/v1/<table>?select=* per table with the anon key and Prefer: count=exact (at most 20); the count comes from Content-Range and no row is downloaded. Readable and empty is not a finding
done: Every table the site does not mean to publish has row level security on, and a request with no login gets no rows from it.
estimateChanges: More tables than the evidence lists, or policies that depend on how people sign in, add time. A table that really is public takes one line in gaugeline.access.json.

title: A signed-in user can read other people's rows
what: Signed in as a test user, Gaugeline can read rows of a table that belong to someone else, by the owner column set in gaugeline.access.json.
why: Any customer who signs up can read every other customer's records, and nobody sees it from the site.
fix: Change the table's read policy so a user sees only rows where the owner column is their own id (auth.uid()).
tech: Supabase: per configured test user and per table with an owner column, one HEAD /rest/v1/<table>?select=*&<owner>=neq.<user id> with that user's token and Prefer: count=exact; a count above 0 is a finding. Tokens come from the environment and are only ever sent in the Authorization header
done: A signed-in user asking for the table gets only their own rows, checked with two test accounts.
estimateChanges: Time grows with the number of tables that share the pattern, and with whether an owner column exists yet: adding one to old rows is a data migration.

title: An AI route on your site answers anyone or shows the provider's error text
what: A route you listed as a model endpoint answered a plain GET with no login: it listed its models, replied as a model would, or showed the provider's own error text (a provider error type, a fragment of the key, a stack trace or a server path). Gaugeline names the route and what it saw, never the text.
why: A model route that answers anyone lets strangers run your model account up, read what the model was told to do, or use your site as a free relay. An error that passes the provider's message through tells them which provider and model you use, and sometimes part of your key.
fix: Put a login, a signed session or a rate limit in front of the route, and answer an error with a short message of your own: catch the provider's error on the server, log it there, and send back a plain status.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent and a modelEndpoints entry in gaugeline.ai.json: one GET each of the routes you list (at most 8, each a path starting with /), once per run, to the site's own origin with no cookie, no Authorization header and no query, at most 16384 bytes of each answer read and never kept; Gaugeline never picks a route itself and never sends a POST, so a route that needs a POST and answers 405 is shown as closed, which says nothing about a POST. A JSON list of models (an OpenAI-style data list of models, or a models list with names) or a model's reply (choices, candidates, a text content block, or a response with a model) answered with 2xx is a high finding that gives the route and a count, never a model name; a provider error type, a provider message, a masked key fragment, a stack trace, a server file path or an SDK error class in the body of any answer is a medium finding that names the signs and none of the text; 401, 403 and 405 and plain answers pass; 404, 429, a 5xx with no such text and no answer are could-not-check. The shapes are from memory (uncited)
done: Every route you listed answers a GET with 401, 403 or 405 and a plain message, and none shows a provider's error text.
estimateChanges: Putting a login or a rate limit on the route is the work; a route built on a framework's AI helper usually has one place to do it. Stopping the raw error text is one catch block.

title: An AI provider's key is in your site's JavaScript
what: A key for an AI service (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Groq, Hugging Face and others) is in JavaScript the site sends to every visitor. Gaugeline names the provider and the file, never the key.
why: Anyone can copy it from their browser and run models on your account. You pay for what they use, and some providers let a key read the files and conversations stored under your account.
fix: Revoke the key in the provider's dashboard now, make a new one, and keep it on the server: call the model from a server route or a server action, and never put the key in code the browser loads or in a variable the framework exposes to the browser (a NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_ name).
tech: Inline scripts of any type (JSON data blocks included) and up to 15 same-site script files (GET, first 5 MB each, the files secret-in-js reads) matched against the shapes in checks/ai-keys/detectors.ts: a prefixed key (OpenAI sk-proj-, sk-svcacct-, sk-admin- and the older sk- with T3BlbkFJ; Anthropic sk-ant-; Hugging Face hf_; Replicate r8_; Groq gsk_; OpenRouter sk-or-v1-; Perplexity pplx-; xAI xai-; ElevenLabs sk_ and 48 hex) with a length floor and no placeholder or run of one character; a Google key (AIza) only when the Gemini API, its host or its SDK is named within 400 characters, because the same shape is the public browser key of Maps and Firebase; a provider whose keys have no prefix (Cohere, Mistral, Together AI and others) only when the name of the value says the provider and key, token or secret, and the value mixes letters and digits at 3.5 bits per character or more. One finding per provider and file, with a byte offset; no character of the value is kept, so none can be printed. Third-party script files are not read. A key shape is from memory, not from a provider's page (uncited), so a new provider's shape is added by a branch that names its source
done: The old key is revoked at the provider, a new one lives on the server only, and the site's JavaScript holds no AI key.
estimateChanges: The code that called the model from the browser has to move to a server route, and the provider's usage log has to be read for what the key was used for. A key exposed for long means more to read.

title: Analytics are loaded twice on this page
what: The page installs the same Tag Manager container twice, loads or configures the same Google Analytics 4 id twice, or sends a Google Analytics 4 id both from its own gtag code and from its Tag Manager container.
why: Every visit, lead and sale is counted twice, so conversion numbers and the ad bidding that learns from them are wrong, and a before-and-after comparison of a new menu measures the doubling, not the menu.
fix: Keep one install: delete the second snippet, or take the Google Analytics 4 tag out of the page's code (or out of the container) so the id is sent from one place.
tech: The page's script tags (addresses and inline code), no request: a Tag Manager container id (GTM-...) found in 2 or more of them (the noscript iframe is the other half of one install and is not counted); a GA4 measurement id (G-...) named by 2 or more gtag.js addresses, or by 2 or more gtag('config', id) calls. With --trackers and a hard-coded GA4 id on a page that also loads a container, the container's public file (one GET each of www.googletagmanager.com/gtm.js?id=..., at most 3, the file every visitor receives, read as text and never run) is searched for the same measurement id; a container that cannot be read, or is longer than the size cap, is could-not-check. A tag a script adds after the page loads is not seen, and the finding says "can" be counted twice: a tag that is paused or has a trigger that does not fire here is not visible
done: Each Tag Manager container is installed once, and each Google Analytics 4 id is sent from one place.
estimateChanges: Usually deleting one snippet. Which copy is the real one has to be decided by whoever owns the Tag Manager and Analytics accounts.

title: The live Angular site is serving its development tools
what: A page of this Angular or Analog site loads the Vite dev client or the dev server's component update address. Those exist only when the site runs from `ng serve` or `analog dev`.
why: A development server is slow, serves unminified source and modules, and shows error overlays a built site never does. Visitors see an unfinished site and anyone can read how it is put together.
fix: Deploy the output of `ng build` (or `analog build`) instead of running the dev server on the host.
tech: Angular sites only, no extra request: the page's own HTML is searched for src=/@vite/client, /@ng/component (Angular's dev-server component updates) and /@analogjs/ module addresses
done: The live pages come from a production build, with no dev client in their HTML.
estimateChanges: If the host runs ng serve or analog dev as its start command, the deploy settings change too.

title: The live Angular site points search engines at a preview deployment
what: A production page of this Angular site gives a preview domain as its canonical address, its og:url or og:image, or in its sitemap.
why: Search engines and social cards follow those addresses to the preview, which can show old content or vanish when the preview is cleaned up.
fix: Build the canonical link and the share tags from the production domain (a setting per environment, not the address a deployment host gives each build), and rebuild.
tech: Angular sites served from a non-temporary host: the canonical, og:url, og:image and sitemap entries whose host ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev
done: The live site builds its canonical and share addresses from the production domain.
estimateChanges: A base address set wrong only in some deployments means checking each environment, then rebuilding.

title: A page hands private-looking fields to the browser in its transfer state
what: The server-rendered state Angular embeds in this page (the ng-state script) has a field named like a secret, token, password, internal note or admin value.
why: Angular writes everything stored in TransferState, and every cached HttpClient response, into the page as readable JSON. Anyone can view source and read it, whatever the page shows.
fix: Store only what the page displays: map an API response to the fields the template uses before it reaches TransferState, or turn off the HttpClient transfer cache for that request. Read the private value on the server and leave it out.
tech: Angular sites only, no extra request: each application/json script whose id ends in -state (ng-state, serverApp-state) in the HTML is parsed (at most 5 scripts, 500,000 characters each) and its field names, not values, matched against secret, token, passw, api key, private, internal, credential, authorization, admin, wholesale and margin; a state that cannot be parsed is reported as unread
done: The page's transfer state carries no field named like a secret or an internal note.
estimateChanges: Each flagged field is a value to drop; a whole API response stored as is means mapping it to the fields the page shows.

title: The app this page links to isn't in the store
what: An App Store or Google Play link on the page names an app the store no longer has.
why: Visitors who tap "Get the app" land on an error page. Apps disappear when they are renamed, moved to a new developer account or pulled.
fix: Link to the app's current store page, or remove the link if the app is gone.
tech: the iTunes Lookup API returns no result for the id (in the link's storefront and in the US), or the Google Play listing answers 404. A 429 or a regional-only app is could-not-check, not dead
done: The link goes to the app's current store page, or is gone, and the store page loads.
estimateChanges: The same link in the header, the footer and old posts is one edit each.

title: The live Astro site is serving its development tools
what: A page of this Astro site loads the Vite dev client or the Astro dev toolbar, or carries data-astro-source-file attributes. Those exist only when the site runs from `astro dev`.
why: A development server is slow, exposes source file paths, and serves modules and errors that a built site never does. Visitors see an unfinished site and anyone can read how it is put together.
fix: Deploy the output of `astro build` (a static folder, or the server adapter's output) instead of running `astro dev` on the host.
tech: Astro sites only, no extra request: the page's own HTML is searched for src=/@vite/client, the dev-toolbar entrypoint under /@id/astro/runtime/client/dev-toolbar/, an astro-dev-toolbar element, or data-astro-source-file attributes
done: The live pages come from astro build, with no dev client or dev toolbar in their HTML.
estimateChanges: If the host runs astro dev as its start command, the deploy settings change too.

title: The live Astro site points search engines at a preview deployment
what: A production page of this Astro site gives a preview domain as its canonical address, its og:url or og:image, or in its sitemap.
why: Search engines and social cards follow those addresses to the preview, which can show old content or vanish when the preview is cleaned up.
fix: Set `site` in astro.config.mjs to the production domain (not the preview address a deployment host gives each build), and rebuild.
tech: Astro sites served from a non-temporary host: the canonical, og:url, og:image and sitemap entries whose host ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev
done: The live site builds its canonical and share addresses from the production domain.
estimateChanges: A site address set wrong only in some deployments means checking each environment, then rebuilding.

title: A page hands private-looking fields to the browser in an island's props
what: An Astro island (a component with a client: directive) on this page has props with a field named like a secret, token, password, internal note or admin value.
why: Everything passed to a client island is written into the page as readable JSON. Anyone can view source and read it, whatever the component shows.
fix: Pass the island only the fields it displays. Read the private value on the server (in the frontmatter or an Action) and leave it out of the props.
tech: Astro sites only, no extra request: each astro-island's props attribute in the HTML is decoded and its field names (not values) matched against secret, token, passw, api key, private, internal, credential, authorization, admin, wholesale and margin; at most 100 islands, 200,000 characters of props each; the evidence lists names, never values
done: No island's props carry a field named like a secret or an internal note.
estimateChanges: Each flagged field is a prop to drop; one passed whole from a database row means picking the fields the component needs.

title: Links on this page go nowhere
what: Links to other pages on the site return an error (404, 410 or 5xx).
why: Visitors who click hit a dead end, and search engines take broken links as a sign the site is neglected.
fix: Point each link at the page's current address, or remove it. When a page moved, add a 301 redirect from the old address.
tech: a sampled same-site a[href] ends in 4xx or 5xx. 401, 403, 429 and 503 with Retry-After are refusals: listed as could not check, never broken. A 200 page that says "not found" (a soft 404) is out of scope
done: Every link on the page loads or has been removed, and a moved page answers with a 301 from its old address.
estimateChanges: One cause (a renamed folder) is a single redirect rule. Links typed into CMS content are edited one by one.

title: This page tells Google to show a different page
what: The page's canonical tag names a different address as the real one.
why: Search engines treat the page as a copy, so it may never appear in results.
fix: Give each page a canonical tag that points at its own address. Shared SEO components are the usual cause.
tech: <link rel="canonical"> on the page points at another URL
done: Each page's canonical tag names its own address.
estimateChanges: A canonical that comes from one shared SEO component is a single edit. Ones set by hand in the CMS are one edit per page.

title: Nothing is left, but the page still looks open for orders
what: Your remaining capacity (dishes for tonight, seats, tickets) is zero, and the order page does not say it is sold out.
why: Customers keep ordering or paying for something you cannot make. Each one is a refund, an apology and a bad review.
fix: Show the sold-out message from the same number that counts what is left, and remove the order button when it reaches zero. If the evidence says a cache served the page, purge it after the count changes.
tech: for each capacity rule in gaugeline.switches.json, the remaining count is read from its source (a published Sanity field or a one-row query through the read-only database source); when it is zero or below, each whenZero.pageSays page must say its phrase (case-insensitive, accents and spacing ignored, per language where given) in the page as sent without JavaScript; the evidence says whether the page still has a form; a page that answers 404, a source or a page that cannot be read is could not check (the link checks report dead pages); the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page
done: When the count reaches zero the page shows the sold-out message and no order button, in the visible page and in its structured data.
estimateChanges: A cache or a static build between the count and the page adds work. Two systems that each keep a count need one chosen as the source.

title: The site's certificate expires soon
what: The https certificate the site presented expires in under 21 days (fix soon) or under 7 (fix first), or has expired.
why: When it lapses, every browser shows a full-page security warning instead of the site, and most visitors leave.
fix: Renew it, or find why automatic renewal stopped (a DNS change at cutover often breaks the renewal check). Domain registration expiry is a separate date: check it at your registrar.
tech: Read from the TLS connection of the page's own GET: no extra request. Days left = whole days until notAfter, by the run's clock. Plain http, or a certificate that failed verification, gives nothing here. With --renewals the certificates of the bare domain and www are read too (one HEAD each, from the connection), and one with a different expiry is reported as well. Domain registration expiry is a separate check (domain-expires-soon)
done: The certificate is renewed with a date well ahead, and automatic renewal is working again.
estimateChanges: If renewal stopped after a DNS or host change, finding the cause can take an afternoon. A certificate installed by hand takes minutes.

title: A form sends details over an insecure connection
what: A form, its iframe, its embed script or its tracking script loads over plain http on an https page.
why: Browsers may block it on a secure page, and what people type isn't encrypted.
fix: Use https for the form, the tracker domain and the tracking script (pd.js for Pardot).
tech: http:// in a form action, a recognised iframe src, an embed script src or a tracking script src on an https page; the code inside an inline script is not read
done: The form, the tracker domain and the tracking script all load over https.
estimateChanges: Several forms, or an old embed code pasted into many pages, raise the count.

title: Leads from this form arrive without where they came from
what: A form from Pardot, HubSpot or Marketo is on the page, but that service's tracking code is not.
why: The service can't connect a new lead to the ad, email or search that brought them.
fix: Add the service's tracking code to every page that has its form (for Pardot: Account Engagement Settings, Domain Management, Tracking Code Generator).
tech: A form or iframe of Pardot, HubSpot or Marketo in the HTML, and no script of that service's tracking code anywhere in it (pi.pardot.com/pd.js or piAId, js.hs-scripts.com or _hsq, munchkin.js or Munchkin.init); Web-to-Lead, Formstack and Typeform have no tracking script and are skipped; a form drawn by JavaScript is could-not-check; code a tag manager adds at run time is not seen
done: The tracking code is on every page that has the form, and a test lead shows where it came from in the CRM.
estimateChanges: Pages built from several templates each need the snippet. A cookie banner that blocks the script adds setup.

title: Leads have stopped arriving
what: The CRM was getting new leads every few days, and none has been created for several days, while the form is still on the page.
why: A form can load, accept the visitor's details and thank them while the lead goes nowhere: a changed field, an expired integration user, a full queue. Nobody sees it until the phone stays quiet.
fix: Submit the form yourself with a test lead (your own, in a sandbox if you have one), see whether it reaches the CRM, and check the form's connection to Salesforce and the integration user's access.
tech: Through Salesforce's read-only MCP server (soqlQuery on Lead: COUNT and MAX(CreatedDate) since 14 days ago, or four times quietDays if longer): no lead created for quietDays whole days (default 3) after at least 5 in the lookback, on a page that has a form or embed from Pardot, Web-to-Lead, HubSpot, Formstack, Marketo or Typeform; a page with no recognised form, or too few leads to call it quiet, is could-not-check
done: A test lead sent through the form reaches the CRM, and real leads arrive again.
estimateChanges: The break may be in the form, the connection or a rule inside the CRM, and finding which is most of the work.

title: The Content-Security-Policy allows more than it did
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, the Content-Security-Policy header is gone, a directive is gone, or a directive lists a source it did not before (for example 'unsafe-inline').
why: The policy decides which scripts and frames the browser will run. A looser one lets more code in, and a deploy can loosen it without anyone deciding to.
fix: Find the deploy or the setting that changed it. If the change was meant, keep it; if not, restore the line. A new source is better as a nonce or a host than as 'unsafe-inline'.
tech: With --since last only. The header of the page's final response, split into directives. A source added, a directive removed or the header removed is reported; a source removed or a directive added is not. Nonces and hashes are one word, so a new nonce per request is not a change. A risky source ('unsafe-inline', 'unsafe-eval', *, data:, https:) added to default-src or a script directive is high. Meta-tag policies and Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only are not read. On a first run: could not check
done: The policy allows what it did before, or the change was meant and the policy is saved as the new baseline.
estimateChanges: Tightening a policy again takes testing on every page that loads something new. A tag manager or a payment widget often needs the looser setting.

title: A data assertion found rows that should not exist
what: A query you wrote in gaugeline.sources.json to return nothing returned rows: two bookings in one slot, a paid order with no matching payment, a product with no price id.
why: These are the problems a customer finds before you do. No page looks wrong yet, so a check of the page cannot see them, but the next person to book, pay or order runs into one.
fix: Read the rows in the evidence and correct them in the database, or fix the code that wrote them, then run again. If the rule itself is wrong, change the assertion's query.
tech: each assertion is one SELECT that should return no rows, run through the read-only database connector (a statement classifier, BEGIN READ ONLY with a statement timeout and a 5,000 row cap, and the database role); any row is a finding with the assertion's own severity and title, and the evidence is its id, the row count and the allow-listed evidence columns of the first 20 rows; a query that could not run (database down, timeout, wrong evidence column) is could not check, never a pass
done: The assertion returns no rows when it is run again.
estimateChanges: A few bad rows are minutes. Rows created by a bug mean fixing the code as well as the rows.

title: The numbers on this page are older than they should be
what: The page says when its data was last updated, and that time is older than the limit you set for it while the data is expected to move.
why: A sync that stopped fails quietly: the page keeps showing last week's numbers, and nobody notices until a visitor or a customer does.
fix: Find out why the sync stopped (the evidence says whether the source is just as old), or why the page is not rebuilt after it runs. Then check the stamp itself is generated from the data, not typed or built once.
tech: for each rule with a stamp in gaugeline.freshness.json, the stamp is read from the page as sent, without JavaScript (the selector's datetime, content or named attribute, else its text; else the structured data property) in the stamp's own time zone, else the file's timeZone; it is older than maxAge only when it is older at every instant the stamp could mean (a date alone is a whole day, a time with no zone and no timeZone could be any zone, 3 hours ago is a span of an hour); the rule is checked only in the months of activeWhen, in the site's time zone, and a rule that is not active is listed as could not check, not passed; when the rule also has a source and the page is behind it by more than maxLag, data-behind-source reports that cause instead, so each cause has one finding; a stamp that cannot be read or is undecided is could not check; the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page
done: The numbers on the page match their source and the stamp shows a recent time.
estimateChanges: A stopped sync, a missing rebuild and a cache each have a different fix. The evidence says whether the source is just as old.

title: Private-looking content is in a public Sanity dataset
what: The Sanity dataset your images come from answers without a token, and it has document types that sound like people's details: orders, inquiries, customers, bookings.
why: Anyone can download those documents with one request: names, emails and whatever else the forms collect.
fix: Make the dataset private in sanity.io/manage today and give the site a read token, or move those types to a private dataset.
tech: As dataset-public, and a type name whose last word is in checks/leaks/private-types.ts (order, inquiry, submission, customer and others); only the type names are read, never the documents. dataset-public is not also reported
done: The dataset is private, the site reads it with a token, and those types cannot be read without one.
estimateChanges: A site that reads the dataset from the browser needs those queries moved to the server, which can take a day.

title: Development tools are live on your site
what: A page or script this site serves to everyone carries a sign that it came from a development server or a development build: Vite, webpack, Next.js or React tooling, NODE_ENV set to development, or an address on the visitor's own computer.
why: A development build can expose original code and file paths, accepts hot reload connections, and runs slowly. An address such as 127.0.0.1:3000 in a script means the live site is asking each visitor's own machine for its data, so it breaks for everyone and can leak what the developer was working on.
fix: Deploy a production build (npm run build, then serve its output) and set the API address variable on the host for production. If only a stray address remains, search the code and the host's environment variables for it.
tech: No request of its own: the page's HTML and up to 15 same-site script files already read are searched for /@vite/client, /@react-refresh, /__webpack_hmr, webpack-dev-server/client, webpack-internal://, /_next/static/development/ or a development buildId, the React DevTools development notice, NODE_ENV assigned the value development, and a development build of a library named by a script address (.development.js); a loopback address (localhost, 127.0.0.1, 0.0.0.0 or [::1]) is reported only with a port, as host and port with nothing after them, and never the page's own address; a script cut at the cap is could not check; an Angular, Astro, SvelteKit, Hydrogen, Gatsby, Remix, Qwik, SolidStart or static-generator page on which that framework's own dev-server check reports is left to it; dev-only paths the page does not name are never asked for (that would be a probing check)
done: No page or file the site serves names a development server, a development build or an address on a developer's own machine.
estimateChanges: Usually a deploy of a real production build. An API address that was meant to change per environment needs its environment variable set on the host.

title: A PDF shows different opening hours than the site or a listing
what: A PDF linked from your site states opening hours that differ from the hours on your site or on a business listing.
why: People plan the evening from the printed menu. Hours that are an hour off in the PDF send them to a closed door, or turn them away from a kitchen that is still open.
fix: Decide which hours are right, then fix the others: re-export the PDF, or update the site and the listings.
tech: the PDF's opening hours are read by the same parser the listing checks use (per-day intervals in the venue's local time; a close after midnight belongs to the day it opens; a day given two answers is not compared); only days the PDF states are compared, against the hours fact in gaugeline.facts.json or LocalBusiness structured data, and against each configured listing that has hours; a PDF that states hours when the site states none is could-not-check, never a pass
done: The opening hours in the PDF are the hours on the site and its listings.
estimateChanges: Update the hours in the PDF, or on the site and listings, after deciding which are right.

title: A PDF menu or price list shows a different price than the site
what: A PDF linked from your site (a menu, price list or brochure) gives an item a different price than the site does.
why: People screenshot the PDF. A burger that is $16 on the page and $14 in the printable menu is a price you either honour at a loss or argue about at the counter.
fix: Decide which price is right, then change the other. If the PDF is last season's, re-export it from the current menu, or remove the link until you can.
tech: GET of each linked PDF (HEAD first for size, type and Last-Modified; redirects followed, the final address reported; files over 10 MB skipped with the reason), text read by the optional @gaugeline/documents package, item-and-price lines parsed (name, price in cents, optional size) and compared by normalised name and size with the first source that names the item: the content system and Stripe, then the facts in gaugeline.facts.json, then the words of the pages; both values are quoted; an item that appears twice in the PDF with two prices is not compared; without the package the check says it could not check
done: The prices in the PDF menu or price list are the prices on the site.
estimateChanges: Re-export the PDF from the updated menu (or price list), or take it down. Decide which price is right first.

title: Unpublished work is in the live page
what: The published HTML carries Sanity draft document ids (drafts.…) or a preview-mode banner.
why: Drafts are work nobody approved: prices, announcements or pages that weren't meant to be public yet, readable by anyone who opens the page source.
fix: Build the live site with the published perspective (no drafts), turn preview mode off for public requests, and rebuild.
tech: Ids matching drafts.<id> in attribute values or as string values inside JSON script blocks (application/json, ld+json, __NEXT_DATA__), not in prose; or visible text such as Preview mode or Exit preview. Only the count and the first id are reported, never document content
done: The live page shows published content only, and a request without a preview cookie gets no drafts.
estimateChanges: Preview mode wired into several routes, or the same query repeated in many files, each need the change.

title: This page has two titles
what: The HTML has more than one title element (titles inside SVG images do not count).
why: Search engines pick one, not always the one you meant, so the result shows the wrong title. It usually means two SEO components both render one.
fix: Keep one <title> in the head. Remove the one a theme, plugin or layout adds on top of your SEO component.
tech: more than one <title> element outside <svg>
done: The page's head holds one title tag.
estimateChanges: The extra title often comes from a plugin or a theme, and removing a plugin can change other pages.

title: Your domain doesn't say who may send its email
what: The domain receives email but publishes no SPF record listing the services allowed to send mail as it.
why: Mail you send (receipts, booking confirmations) is more likely to land in spam, and anyone can send mail that claims to be from you.
fix: Add one TXT record at the domain starting v=spf1 that includes each service that sends your mail (your email host, your newsletter tool), ending -all or ~all.
tech: Public DNS only (node:dns/promises, TXT and MX): MX records exist and are not a null MX, and no TXT record at the host (without www.) starts with v=spf1. No mail server is contacted
done: One TXT record starting v=spf1 lists every service that sends the domain's email.
estimateChanges: Each sending service (newsletter tool, shop, booking system) has to be found and listed. Slow DNS changes add waiting, not work.

title: A page that is an error says everything is fine
what: A page this run read answers 200 (success), but what it shows is an error: a framework's error page, or a title or heading such as "Page not found" or "Something went wrong".
why: Google and other crawlers believe the status code. A broken page that says 200 can stay in search results, be treated as a soft 404, and wastes visits: a customer lands on the error and your monitoring, which looks at status codes, stays green.
fix: Make the page answer the status it shows: 404 (or 410) for a page that is gone, 500 for a failure, or fix the page so it shows its content. In Next.js call notFound() and let the not-found page set 404; in Nuxt, SvelteKit and Remix throw an error with the status instead of rendering a page with an error message.
tech: no request of its own: it reads the checked page and the run's shared sample of other same-site pages (up to 4, fetched once for every check that reads them), 2xx HTML only; pages outside the sample are not read, and the run says how many were. Reads the first 200,000 characters of each body. A finding is a framework error page (Next.js html id __next_error__ or its client-side exception text, the Nuxt error page, the SvelteKit error template, the React Router and Remix default error boundary) or a title or first heading that is wholly an error phrase (English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch) on a page with under 150 visible words. The finding shows the address and the kind of marker, never page text. A body cut at the size cap with no marker is could not check. A page with no marker passes only for these markers
done: Every page that shows an error answers 404, 410 or 500, and a page that answers 200 shows its content.
estimateChanges: One shared layout that renders an error for every missing record is one fix. Pages that each catch their own errors and render a message are one fix each.

title: The page and the calendar disagree about an event
what: An event in the page's structured data has a different start time, name or place than the .ics calendar entry on the same day.
why: Search results, the page and guests' phone calendars each show one of the two versions, so some guests turn up at the wrong time.
fix: Correct whichever is wrong, then generate both from one source so they cannot drift.
tech: Event JSON-LD and an .ics occurrence on the same local date: matched by normalised name, then start time and location compared; a lone occurrence that day with another name is reported as renamed
done: The page and the calendar show the same date, time and place for every event.
estimateChanges: Events kept by hand in two places are one edit each. One source for both removes the drift but needs a template change.

title: The page still promotes an event that already happened
what: An event in the page's structured data, or a card marked as the next or upcoming event, is dated before now.
why: Guests plan around the date on the page. A night that already happened, still shown as next, sends people to a closed room or to a different night.
fix: Update the card and the structured data when an event ends. Generating both from the calendar keeps them current.
tech: an Event's endDate (or startDate when there is none) is before the run time, or a next/upcoming element's time[datetime] is; dates are read in the venue's time zone
done: Finished events no longer appear as upcoming, in the page or in its structured data.
estimateChanges: Events entered by hand are removed one at a time. A list built from the calendar fixes it for good but needs a code change.

title: A fact about your business differs between pages
what: A phone number, opening hours, payment handle or price you declared shows a different value somewhere on the site, in the text, a link or the structured data.
why: Customers call the old number, turn up at the old time or send money to a mistyped handle. Search engines show whichever version they read.
fix: Correct each place the evidence names. Better, render the fact from one source so the pages cannot drift.
tech: every occurrence (visible text by pattern or selector, links, JSON-LD; not image descriptions) equals the declared value in gaugeline.facts.json. "$5" = "$5.00", "5pm" = "5:00 PM", handle case ignored; a value that doesn't parse is unchecked
done: The fact reads the same on every page the evidence names.
estimateChanges: The number of pages that repeat the fact. A fact stored once and rendered everywhere takes a template change instead.

title: A payment link goes nowhere
what: A Cash App or Venmo link on the site answers with an error: the profile it names doesn't exist.
why: Customers who tap Pay land on an error, or worse, find a look-alike profile and pay a stranger.
fix: Correct the handle in the link, and check it by opening the link on a phone.
tech: cash.app/$handle and venmo.com/(u/)handle links on the pages checked are requested (HEAD, then GET on 405/501) and answer 4xx or 5xx; at most 5, and only the address the page names is sent (ADR-0004)
done: The payment link opens the right payment page on a phone.
estimateChanges: One link used in many places is one edit. Links typed into content are one edit each.

title: The feed this page advertises is broken
what: The page links to an RSS or Atom feed that returns an error (4xx or 5xx).
why: Feed readers, podcast apps and newsletter tools that follow the site stop getting new posts, usually without anyone noticing.
fix: Restore the feed at that address, or update the link rel="alternate" tag to where the feed lives now.
tech: an advertised feed returns 4xx or 5xx
done: The feed address loads and the page's feed link points at it.
estimateChanges: A feed made by a plugin or route that was removed takes longer than correcting a link.

title: A form now sends to a different service
what: A form that sent its entries to one service (HubSpot, say) now posts to another.
why: Leads go somewhere nobody is watching, or to an account you don't control, from the moment it changed.
fix: Check who changed the form's action; point it back at your service, or update your follow-up to the new one.
tech: With --since last only: the same form key (id, else name, else position) now posts to a host in a different provider row of the frozen table; position keys can swap and read as a change
done: The form posts to the service you use, confirmed with whoever changed it.
estimateChanges: An unnoticed plugin update takes longer to trace. A move that was meant needs your follow-up changed to match.

title: A download meant for customers is handed to anyone
what: A download route returns its file to a request with no session and no purchase.
why: A route that protects a paid file should refuse, or send the visitor to sign in. If it returns the file, everyone who has the address gets it for free, and the address is easy to find in the page, in a search engine or in a customer's email.
fix: Check the purchase inside the route before it answers, then hand back a short-lived signed link instead of the file itself. A route with no session should answer 401, 403 or a redirect to sign in.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: one anonymous GET per route (no cookie, no Authorization, no Referer, no compression), the status and headers, then at most 1,024 bytes of the body and the connection is closed; the route is a same-site link whose path contains download, file, deliver or export or sits under /api/, or a route file given with --routes (app/**/route.ts, pages/api/**) whose path says the same; a dynamic segment is asked only for an address seen in a link and ids are never guessed; at most 10 routes, in sorted order, the rest named; a finding is status 200 with a file content type or Content-Disposition attachment and first bytes that are not HTML (%PDF, PK, ID3 and a few other signatures are read); 401, 403, 404, a redirect to a sign-in address and a 200 HTML page pass; a redirect elsewhere is followed one hop; the body and the query string are never stored, logged or printed
done: A request with no session to the download route gets 401 or 403, and a paying customer gets a short-lived link.
estimateChanges: Several download routes, no purchase record to check, or files in public folders mean building the check and moving files.

title: A page address returns Gatsby data, not a page
what: A page of this Gatsby site answers with the framework's page data (application/json starting with componentChunkName), or the sitemap lists page-data addresses.
why: Search engines and visitors get a JSON file instead of a page, or index the data files: the page can drop out of search while a browser that navigates inside the site looks fine.
fix: Serve HTML at page addresses (look for a proxy, CDN or redirect rule that rewrites to page-data.json), and list only pages in the sitemap.
tech: Gatsby sites only, from responses already read: the page's own answer with a JSON content type whose body starts {"componentChunkName"; sitemap entries under /page-data/ ending /page-data.json, /app-data.json or /sq/d/<hash>.json. No extra request
done: The page address returns HTML, and the sitemap lists pages only.
estimateChanges: A proxy or CDN rule that rewrites page addresses to the data file is one change; a sitemap built from every file under public may need its own filter.

title: The live Gatsby site is a development server
what: This page was served by `gatsby develop`: its scripts include /socket.io/socket.io.js, /commons.js or /framework.js, the unhashed files only the development server writes.
why: The development server exposes a GraphQL explorer over all your content, hot-reload endpoints and error overlays with file paths. It is not meant to face visitors.
fix: Build the site (`gatsby build`) and serve the public folder (a static host, or `gatsby serve` for a quick check), not `gatsby develop`. Check the host's start command.
tech: Gatsby sites only, read from the page already fetched, no extra request: a script address ending /socket.io/socket.io.js, /commons.js or /framework.js (a production build names its files with a content hash, as in framework-<hash>.js). Dev-only paths are not asked for
done: The live address serves the built site (public/ from gatsby build), not gatsby develop.
estimateChanges: A host that runs the develop command as its start command needs the build and serve commands set.

title: The GraphQL explorer is reachable on the live site
what: The address /___graphql of this Gatsby site answers with the GraphiQL page (titled Gatsby - GraphiQL), which only `gatsby develop` serves.
why: That explorer can read every node in your content layer, drafts and private fields included, from any browser.
fix: Serve the built site (`gatsby build`) on the live address and keep `gatsby develop` on your own machine. If a proxy forwards /___graphql, remove the rule.
tech: Probing check: off unless --owner-consent or gaugeline.consent.json; run only on sites you own or have permission to test. Gatsby sites only: one GET of /___graphql per run, no query sent and no POST ever; a 2xx HTML answer whose title contains GraphiQL is a finding. A production build does not serve this address
done: /___graphql answers 404 on the live address.
estimateChanges: A host that runs gatsby develop needs to be moved to the built site; a proxy rule that forwards /___graphql needs removing.

title: The live Gatsby site points search engines at a preview deployment
what: A production page of this Gatsby site gives a preview domain as its canonical address, its og:url or og:image, or in its sitemap.
why: Search engines and social cards follow those addresses to the preview, which can show old content or vanish when the preview is cleaned up.
fix: Set siteMetadata.siteUrl (and the sitemap plugin's site URL) from the production domain in every build, and rebuild.
tech: Gatsby sites served from a non-temporary host: the canonical, og:url, og:image and sitemap entries whose host ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app, .pages.dev, .gatsbyjs.io or .gtsb.io. The two Gatsby hosts are from memory of the hosted product (uncited)
done: The live site builds its canonical and share addresses from the production domain.
estimateChanges: A siteUrl set wrong only in some deployments means checking each environment, then rebuilding.

title: The data sent with a Gatsby page has fields that look private
what: The page-data file of this Gatsby page, a static query it lists, or the page data embedded in its HTML has fields named like something private (password, token, secret, apiKey, private notes).
why: Everything a page query returns is written to a public JSON file, whether or not the page shows it. A field used only at build time still travels to every visitor if the query selects it.
fix: Select only the fields the page shows in its query. Keep secrets in environment variables read in gatsby-node or a Function, never in a query result.
tech: Gatsby sites only. Names only, never values: the property names in the page's own /page-data/<path>/page-data.json (one GET, the file the framework's client fetches on every visit), in the /page-data/sq/d/<hash>.json files it lists (at most ten) and in an inline window.pageData literal, walked to depth 8 and capped, matched by word against password, passwd, secret, token, private, credential, ssn, salt, bearer, authorization, cvv, iban, apiKey, accessKey, secretKey, privateKey, internalNotes. A file that cannot be read in full is could not check. The word list is a guess (uncited)
done: The page's data holds only what the page shows: no field named for a password, token, secret or private note.
estimateChanges: Each field is dropped from the GraphQL query that returns it; a field several pages query needs each of them checked.

title: The live site points search engines at a WordPress preview link
what: A production page of this headless WordPress site gives a WordPress preview link (a query with preview=true, preview_id or previewId) as its canonical, its og:url or og:image, or in its sitemap.
why: Search engines and social cards follow that address to a draft, which asks for a login or shows content nobody approved. A preview deployment (vercel.app, netlify.app) used as the canonical is reported by the framework's own check (next-preview-canonical on Next.js).
fix: Build canonical and share addresses from the production domain and the post's permalink, never from the request that rendered the preview; rebuild.
tech: Headless WordPress sites: the canonical, og:url, og:image and sitemap entries whose query has preview=true, preview_id or previewId (WordPress's preview link, and Faust.js's, read from the @faustwp/core source: preview=true; preview_id and previewId are uncited). Preview deployment hosts are left to the framework's own check. From responses already read; no extra request
done: The live site's canonical and share addresses are the production page's own address.
estimateChanges: The address usually comes from one setting (the WordPress site URL or the front end's base address); each environment needs it checked.

title: A preview link shows an unpublished page without a login
what: A preview address this headless WordPress site links to answers a visitor who is not logged in with a page that looks like an unpublished draft, not a login page.
why: Anyone with the address sees posts, prices or announcements nobody approved yet, as if they were live.
fix: Serve previews only to a logged-in editor: check the session on the server before the draft is fetched or rendered, and redirect everyone else to the login page. In Faust.js, keep the draft query behind the authenticated client.
tech: Probing check: off unless --owner-consent or gaugeline.consent.json; run only on sites you own or have permission to test. Headless WordPress sites only. One GET, with no cookie or secret, of each preview address the checked page itself links to on its own origin (a query with preview=true, preview_id or previewId; at most 3). A finding needs an answer of 200 HTML that is not a login address or form and carries a draft marker: a status of draft, auto-draft, pending, private or future in its embedded data, isPreview set, or a draft title. An answer with no marker is could not check, because an unpublished page cannot be told from a published one without a marker. Only the path and the query parameter names are shown, never their values. Faust.js checks the login in the browser and fetches the draft with an authenticated client (read from the @faustwp/core source, 4.1.1: preview=true, previewPathname and p); the markers other than that are conventions (uncited)
done: A preview address answers a visitor who is not logged in with the login page, not the draft.
estimateChanges: The preview route needs an authenticated check on the server; a front end that checks only in the browser (Faust's default) needs the data request authenticated too.

title: The data sent with a page has private fields or unpublished posts
what: The state this headless WordPress page embeds (__NEXT_DATA__ with WPGraphQL data) has fields named like something private, a user's email or roles, or posts that are not published.
why: Everything a page's queries return is sent to every visitor, whether or not the page shows it. A fragment that asks for the whole user, or a query that includes drafts, puts them in the page source.
fix: Ask only for the fields the page shows (not the whole User or Post type), and keep draft and private posts behind an authenticated request.
tech: Headless WordPress sites only, from the page already read, no extra request. The __NEXT_DATA__ script is read as JSON (up to 1 MB, 100,000 nodes, 12 levels deep; a larger or cut one is could not check) and walked once. Names only, never values: field names matched by word against password, passwd, secret, token, credential, ssn, salt, bearer, authorization, cvv, iban, private, apiKey, accessKey, secretKey, privateKey, authKey, internalNote (is.../has... flags are left out); email, username, capabilities, roles and registeredDate on a node whose __typename is User; and a count of nodes whose status is draft, auto-draft, pending, private or future. The names are matched by their words, which is a guess (uncited)
done: The state embedded in the page holds only what the page shows: no user's email, no secret, no unpublished post.
estimateChanges: Each field is dropped from the GraphQL query that asks for it; a fragment shared by many pages needs each of them checked.

title: Hidden text on the page talks to AI agents
what: Text that visitors can't see, or a comment in the page's code, speaks to AI agents or assistants (for example 'If you are an AI agent, ...'), and may ask them to recommend, buy, click or send something.
why: AI agents that browse and act for a person read text that the person never sees. Whoever planted it can try to steer what the agent says or does for your visitors, and it is one of the commonest signs a site has been tampered with or left with a rogue SEO script.
fix: Find where the text comes from (a plugin, a theme file, a content field, an injected script or an SEO template) and remove it. Then find out how it got there, and change the passwords and keys that could have put it there.
tech: text under hidden, aria-hidden, display:none, visibility:hidden, font-size:0, opacity:0, an off-screen left or top, text coloured as its own background, noscript, or an HTML comment (the scan hidden-ai-directive uses), that contains an opening addressed to AI agents (if you are an AI or LLM or chatbot, attention or note to or for AI agents, and similar) or an AI noun with a must, should or please and an act (recommend, buy, click, send, visit); bare agent, assistant and bot do not count on their own. Text that already contains a phrase from data/ai-directives.json is left to hidden-ai-directive. An address is medium and an instruction to act is high; text is escaped and cut at 120 characters; at most 10 findings per page. Styles from a stylesheet or class are not read. The wording is from memory (uncited)
done: The hidden text is gone, the source that put it there is found and closed, and the passwords that could reach it are changed.
estimateChanges: Finding how it got in (a plugin, a content field, an injected script, an SEO agency's template) is the unknown. More than one way in multiplies the work.

title: Hidden text on the page gives orders to AI assistants
what: Text that visitors can't see, or a comment in the page's code, speaks to an AI assistant (for example 'ignore previous instructions').
why: It is one of the commonest signs a site has been tampered with. Assistants and crawlers read text that visitors never see, so whoever planted it can steer what they say about your business.
fix: Find where the text comes from (a plugin, a theme file, a content field or an injected script) and remove it. Then find out how it got there, and change the passwords and keys that could have put it there.
tech: text under hidden, aria-hidden, display:none, visibility:hidden, font-size:0, opacity:0, an off-screen left or top, text coloured as its own background, noscript, or an HTML comment, containing a phrase from data/ai-directives.json
done: The hidden text is gone, the source that put it there is found and closed, and the passwords that could reach it are changed.
estimateChanges: Finding how it got in (a plugin, a content field, an injected script) is the unknown. More than one way in multiplies the work.

title: Unlaunched pages are in your sitemap
what: The sitemap lists addresses in a section gaugeline.hidden.json says is hidden until launch.
why: The sitemap is the list you hand to search engines: they will crawl and index the section before anyone meant it to be public.
fix: Leave the hidden section out of the sitemap until launch, usually a filter on the same flag that hides the pages.
tech: Every address listed by the sitemaps read (robots.txt's, /sitemap.xml, one level of sitemap index), matched against the hidden path globs
done: The sitemap no longer lists the pages of the hidden section.
estimateChanges: A sitemap built by a plugin may need a filter on the same flag that hides the pages.

title: An unlaunched page can be indexed
what: An address in a hidden section, found in the sitemap or through a link, answers 200 with no noindex and no login.
why: Anyone who finds it can read it, and search engines can list it before launch.
fix: Send noindex (X-Robots-Tag or a robots meta tag) on the hidden section until launch, or put it behind a login.
tech: Hidden addresses from the sitemaps and from hiddenLinks, at most 5, fetched once with GET for the status, X-Robots-Tag and meta robots only (nothing else of the page is read); 401, 403, 404 or a redirect out of the section is a pass
done: The hidden pages send noindex or sit behind a login.
estimateChanges: One shared layout is one edit. Hidden pages built separately need it each.

title: A public page links to an unlaunched section
what: A public page links to an address in a hidden section, directly or through a redirect.
why: Visitors and search engines follow the link into pages nobody meant to show yet, usually from a shared menu, footer or related-posts block.
fix: Hide the link behind the same flag as the section, or remove it until launch.
tech: Links on the checked page and the run's other public pages whose address matches a hidden path glob, and sampled same-site links whose redirects end in one
done: No public page links to the unlaunched section.
estimateChanges: Links in the menu, the footer and body content are separate edits.

title: Your whole site exists at two addresses
what: Both www and the bare domain load the site, instead of one redirecting to the other.
why: Search engines can split your ranking between two copies of every page.
fix: Pick one address and 301-redirect the other to it at your host or DNS provider.
tech: the alternate host returns 200 instead of 301
done: One address answers and the other redirects to it with a 301.
estimateChanges: Mail on the second address, or a host that needs a support request to change this, add time.

title: A preview of the site can be found by search engines
what: A Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages or Amplify preview or deploy address that the live site names answers with a page and does not ask search engines to stay away.
why: Search engines can index the preview next to the real site, with old prices, test content or a duplicate of every page competing with yours.
fix: Turn on the host's deployment protection for previews (Vercel Authentication, Netlify password protection, Cloudflare Access, Amplify access control) or send X-Robots-Tag: noindex on every preview page, and stop the live site naming the address.
tech: One GET of each preview address (at most 3 per page) that the page, the sitemap or a feed names, no address guessed (the canonical, og:url and sitemap entries on a .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev host of a Next.js, Astro, SvelteKit, Angular, Gatsby, Hydrogen, Remix, Qwik, SolidStart or static-generator page are left to that framework's own preview-canonical check): a final 200 on a preview host with no noindex or none in meta robots or X-Robots-Tag and a canonical that is missing or its own. A 401 or 403 is protected, a canonical elsewhere is consolidated and a redirect away is fine; no answer or a cut-off body is reported as could not check
done: Every preview address the live site names answers with a login, noindex, or nothing at all.
estimateChanges: A host setting is quick; a preview that is already indexed also needs removal requests in Search Console.

title: The live site names a preview address
what: A page, the sitemap or a feed of the live site gives a Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages or Amplify preview or deploy address as its canonical, og:url, a language version, a script or an entry.
why: Search engines and feed readers follow those addresses to a copy of the site that can show old content, can be indexed next to the real one, and disappears when the host cleans up the preview.
fix: Build absolute addresses from the live domain, not from the host's per-deploy variable (VERCEL_URL, DEPLOY_PRIME_URL, CF_PAGES_URL, AWS_BRANCH) and rebuild; then search the CMS content for the old name.
tech: On a page not served from a .vercel.app, .netlify.app, .pages.dev or .amplifyapp.com host: canonical, og:url, hreflang, script src, feed links, the sitemap's entries and alternates and the feed items whose host has the shape of a preview address (deploy-preview-<n>--site, <branch>--site, <hash>.project.pages.dev, pr-<n>.<app id>.amplifyapp.com, project-git-<branch>-team and project-<hash>-team .vercel.app). Nothing is requested; links are left to temp-host-links, and the canonical, og:url and sitemap entries on a .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev host of a Next.js, Astro, SvelteKit, Angular, Gatsby, Hydrogen, Remix, Qwik, SolidStart or static-generator site to that framework's own preview-canonical check
done: No page, sitemap or feed of the live site names a preview or deploy address any more.
estimateChanges: An address built from a host-provided variable is one setting; one pasted into content or a CMS is a search through both.

title: This page's HTML is enormous
what: The HTML of the page alone is over 2 MB, before any image, script or stylesheet.
why: Phones on slow connections wait seconds before anything shows, and search engines may stop reading the page before the end.
fix: Find what fills the HTML: usually a framework data payload, inlined SVG or CSS, or a long list rendered in full. Load it on demand or paginate it.
tech: the UTF-8 HTML body is over 2 MB (2,097,152 bytes); html-heavy is not reported for the same page
done: The page's HTML is back under the size limit, with the bulky part loaded when needed.
estimateChanges: A long list, a framework data payload and inlined SVG each need different work. A page filled by one big CMS field is quick.

title: The live Hydrogen store is a development server
what: This page was served by the Hydrogen dev server: it loads /@vite/client, /@react-refresh, the inject-hmr-runtime module or the Vite preamble.
why: The dev server serves source files, can expose files from the project folder and is slow and unsupervised. It is not meant to face shoppers.
fix: Deploy the storefront to Oxygen (`shopify hydrogen deploy`) and point the domain at the deployment, not at a machine running `shopify hydrogen dev`.
tech: Hydrogen storefronts only (the powered-by: Shopify, Hydrogen header, or React Router's context beside Shopify's CDN; a React Router page with neither is a Remix site and remix-dev-tools-live reports it), read from the page already fetched, no extra request: the HTML or a script address names /@vite/client, /@react-refresh, inject-hmr-runtime, __vite_plugin_react_preamble_installed__ or /node_modules/.vite/. Dev-only paths are not asked for. The dev server is Vite, as run by @shopify/cli-hydrogen 13.0.6
done: The live address serves the built storefront on Oxygen, not the dev server.
estimateChanges: A tunnel or host that runs shopify hydrogen dev as its start command needs a deployment.

title: The live Hydrogen store points search engines at a preview deployment
what: A production page of this Hydrogen storefront gives an Oxygen preview or other temporary address as its canonical, its og:url or og:image, or in its sitemap.
why: Search engines and social cards follow those addresses to the preview, which can show old products and prices or vanish when the preview is deleted.
fix: Build the storefront's base address from the production domain (an environment variable set per Oxygen environment, or the request's own origin), and redeploy.
tech: Hydrogen storefronts (the powered-by: Shopify, Hydrogen header) served from a non-preview host: the canonical, og:url, og:image and sitemap entries whose host ends in myshopify.dev, o2.myshopify.dev, vercel.app, netlify.app or pages.dev. The two myshopify.dev suffixes are the owner's note, not confirmed in Shopify's documentation (uncited)
done: The live storefront builds its canonical and share addresses from the production domain.
estimateChanges: A variable that is wrong only in some Oxygen environments means checking each one, then redeploying.

title: A Hydrogen preview deployment can be found by search engines
what: A preview deployment of this Hydrogen storefront (an Oxygen preview address, or another temporary host) answers with a public page that carries no noindex, in a header or a robots meta tag.
why: A preview shows work in progress, old prices and products that are not for sale. Once a search engine finds its address (from a link on the live site, a sitemap or a share) it can list it beside, or instead of, the real store.
fix: Send `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` from every non-production deployment (check the environment in the server entry), serve a disallow-all robots.txt there, take the preview's address out of the live site's links and sitemap, and turn off the deployment's shared link when it is not needed.
tech: Hydrogen storefronts. Only addresses the site itself reveals are asked for, with one GET each and at most the run's hiddenPages budget: the page's own address when it is on a preview host, and links and sitemap entries (the canonical and og:url are reported by hydrogen-preview-canonical and not asked for) of a production page whose host ends in myshopify.dev, o2.myshopify.dev, vercel.app, netlify.app or pages.dev. A 200 HTML answer without noindex is a finding; a sign-in redirect, 401, 403 or 404 is not (Shopify documents that only signed-in staff can open a deployment until a shared link is made). No other path is asked for. The two myshopify.dev suffixes are the owner's note and not confirmed in Shopify's documentation (uncited)
done: Every preview deployment answers with noindex (X-Robots-Tag or a robots meta tag) or asks for a sign-in.
estimateChanges: Previews on several Oxygen environments or on another host each need the header; a shared link can be turned off in the deployment's Share settings.

title: This Hydrogen product's prices disagree
what: On a product page of this Hydrogen storefront, the price shown to the shopper, the price in the page's structured data (JSON-LD offer, product:price:amount or og:price:amount) and the variant price in the page's embedded state are not all the same, or are in different currencies.
why: Shoppers see one price and the cart can start from another, and Google shows the structured data's price in results: a mismatch costs trust and can get listings pulled.
fix: Build the JSON-LD and meta tags from the same selected variant the page shows (selectedOrFirstAvailableVariant, after the ?option= choices are applied) rather than the product's first variant or a cached copy.
tech: Hydrogen storefronts, no extra request. Amounts are integers in minor units with the currency's own exponent (JPY 0, USD 2, BHD 3), read digit by digit, never as floats; currencies are compared, never converted. Shown: the text of the .product-price element (or aria-label Price), compare-at (s, del) left out. Structured: the JSON-LD Product offer for ?variant= or the first, product:price:amount with product:price:currency, og:price:amount with og:price:currency. Embedded: product.selectedOrFirstAvailableVariant.price (MoneyV2) in the streamed state. What a cart or checkout would charge is not compared: it needs a cart, which Gaugeline never creates, and the Storefront API is POST only; the check says so under could not run. The product and price fields are those of the @shopify/cli-hydrogen 13.0.6 starter; JSON-LD and the meta names are schema.org and Open Graph conventions (uncited for Hydrogen)
done: The price shown, the product data search engines read and the price in the page's state are the same for the variant on offer.
estimateChanges: Product data written by hand in the route needs to read the same variant field the page shows; a theme with several price components needs each one checked.

title: The data sent with a Hydrogen page has fields that look private
what: The state this Hydrogen page embeds for the browser (window.__reactRouterContext, with the storefront data its loaders return) has fields named like something private (password, private token, secret, apiKey, private notes).
why: Everything a loader returns is sent to every shopper, whether or not the page shows it. A server-only value such as the private Storefront API token or the session secret travels with the page.
fix: Return only the fields the page shows from the loader, and keep PRIVATE_STOREFRONT_API_TOKEN, SESSION_SECRET and other secrets in server-only code (context.env in a loader or action) that never returns them.
tech: Hydrogen storefronts. Names only, never values: the property names in the page's own embedded context and in its first streamed turbo-stream chunk (a flat JSON array, each index decoded once, capped), matched by word against password, passwd, secret, token, private, credential, ssn, salt, bearer, authorization, cvv, iban, apiKey, accessKey, secretKey, privateKey, internalNotes. The public Storefront token (storefrontAccessToken, which the starter's root loader sends for the consent banner) and checkoutDomain are public by design and are not flagged. No extra request. A state that cannot be read in full, or deferred chunks after the first, are could not check. The header, globals and starter fields are read from @shopify/hydrogen 2026.10.3 and @shopify/cli-hydrogen 13.0.6 on npm; matching names by their words is a guess (uncited)
done: The page's embedded state holds only what the page shows: no field named for a password, private token, secret or private note.
estimateChanges: Each field is dropped in the loader that returns it; a field several routes read needs each of them checked.

title: Your calendar shows the wrong hour on some phones
what: Events in your .ics calendar have a start time with no time zone (no TZID and no Z).
why: Phones read such a time in the guest's own zone, so anyone in another zone, or travelling, sees the event at the wrong hour.
fix: Give each DTSTART a time zone, for example DTSTART;TZID=America/Los_Angeles:20261112T190000. Most calendar exports have a time zone setting.
tech: a VEVENT's DTSTART has neither TZID nor a trailing Z (a floating time, RFC 5545 §3.3.5); all-day VALUE=DATE events are not reported
done: Every DTSTART in the calendar names a time zone.
estimateChanges: A calendar made by software with no time zone setting needs its export changed.

title: Your image settings let the image address fetch from any website
what: The image settings you gave (next.config, nuxt.config, astro.config or netlify.toml) allow a wildcard host, a pattern with no host, or a match-everything expression, so the site's image address will fetch, resize and serve a picture from any address a visitor puts in it.
why: Anyone can then use your site to resize and serve images from any address. You pay for the bandwidth and the optimization, your cache fills with other people's pictures, and your site's name sits on an open relay.
fix: List the exact hosts your pictures come from (and a path prefix where you can) in remotePatterns, domains or remote_images, and remove the wildcard.
tech: Not a probing check: no request is made. Reads the files named in settingsFiles of gaugeline.images.json as text (never run) and reports a hostname that is only wildcards or a wildcard and a top-level name, a remotePatterns entry with no hostname (an https-only pattern), a domains list holding a wildcard, and a Netlify remote_images expression that matches every address. A page that uses /_next/image, /_vercel/image, /_ipx/, /_image or /.netlify/images with no settings given is could not check. A statement about the file, not about the running site
done: The image settings list the exact hosts the site fetches pictures from, with no wildcard that matches every host.
estimateChanges: Replacing a wildcard with the real image hosts is one settings change. If pictures come from many hosts, finding that list is the work.

title: Your image address fetched a picture from a website you did not list
what: The site's image address (/_next/image, /_vercel/image, /_ipx/, /_image or /.netlify/images) fetched an image from the address you chose for the test, on a host that is not one of your image hosts, and sent it back.
why: Anyone can then use your site to resize and serve images from any address. You pay for the bandwidth and the optimization, your cache fills with other people's pictures, and your site's name sits on an open relay.
fix: Allow only the hosts your pictures come from: remotePatterns or domains in next.config, nuxt.config or astro.config, images in the Vercel project settings, remote_images in netlify.toml. Then rebuild and run the check again.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: needs imageOptimizerProbeUrl in gaugeline.images.json, an https address on a public host you control that is not your own host, not a host your image addresses already use and not a host in the settings files given, never an IP address or a private name; one GET per optimizer the page uses (at most 5 a run), to the site's own origin, with the width and quality the page itself used, no cookie, no redirect followed, 1,024 bytes of the answer read to see whether it is an image and then dropped; 200 with an image content type and image bytes is a finding, 400, 403 and 404 pass, anything else is could not check; the query string and the body are never stored, logged or printed
done: The image address answers 400, 403 or 404 for a picture on a host that is not in your image list.
estimateChanges: Closing the allowlist is one settings change, then a rebuild. If pictures come from many hosts, finding that list is the work.

title: Some images on this page don't load
what: An image on the site (or the original behind a Next.js /_next/image address) returns an error.
why: Visitors see an empty box or a broken-image icon where a product photo or a diagram should be.
fix: Upload the image again, or point the img at its current address. For /_next/image, check the file named by url= exists.
tech: a sampled same-site img src answers 4xx or 5xx (images on other hosts are not requested); a refusal (401, 403, 429, 503 with Retry-After) is listed as could not check
done: Every image on the page loads.
estimateChanges: Many images lost in a migration are re-uploaded one by one. One wrong folder is a single path change.

title: The page carries text in invisible characters
what: Characters from the Unicode tag block are in the page's text. They show nothing on screen but each one stands for a letter.
why: They have no ordinary use on a web page, and AI assistants can read the message they spell. Seeing them is a sign of tampering or of text pasted in from somewhere untrusted.
fix: Delete them from the field or file they came from, then check who and what can edit that content.
tech: code points U+E0000 to U+E007F in a text node or comment, other than the England, Scotland and Wales flag emoji (U+1F3F4, tag letters, U+E007F)
done: The invisible characters are gone from their source and the content's history shows who or what put them there.
estimateChanges: How they got in (a paste, a script, a compromise) matters more than removing them. Several fields multiply the cleanup.

title: An item that is sold out or off the menu is still listed
what: An item your database or CMS marks as unavailable (86'd, sold out, off the menu) is still on a page that lists items, or in the page's Menu structured data.
why: Customers order or plan around something you cannot serve, and search results and assistants repeat it from the structured data long after the page is fixed.
fix: Build the menu pages and the Menu structured data from the same list that holds the availability, so an item that is off cannot be rendered. If the evidence says a cache served the page, purge it.
tech: for each availability rule in gaugeline.switches.json, the unavailable item names are read from the source (a Sanity list of names or one column of a query through the read-only database source) and looked for in the text of each mustNotAppearOn page, as sent without JavaScript and with hidden elements left out: an item is found when its words stand on their own in a row, ignoring case, accents and plural endings, at the start of a line or after punctuation (so Tamal is not found in Tamal de rajas); with alsoIn menu-jsonld the names of MenuItem nodes in the structured data of those pages and of the page checked are compared the same way; the evidence gives both spellings when they differ and adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page; an unreadable source or page is could not check (one that answers 404 lists nothing)
done: An item marked off or sold out no longer appears on the menu pages or in the Menu structured data.
estimateChanges: A cache between the data and the page adds work. Menus kept as separate hand-edited pages are edited one by one.

title: Structured data points at pages that don't exist
what: Addresses on the site named in the page's structured data (a product URL, an image, a logo) return an error.
why: Search engines use these addresses for rich results. A dead product or image address can drop the rich result entirely.
fix: Update the structured data to the current addresses. Generated structured data usually means a stale CMS field or a renamed route.
tech: same-site http(s) strings inside JSON-LD answer 4xx or 5xx; at most 12 are requested, the first 12 in document order
done: Every address in the page's structured data loads.
estimateChanges: A stale CMS field is one fix. Addresses written into templates are edited one by one.

title: This page's structured data is broken
what: A structured data block (script type="application/ld+json") is not valid JSON.
why: Search engines ignore the whole block, so prices, reviews, FAQs or opening hours in it never reach the results.
fix: Fix the JSON in that block: usually a trailing comma, an unescaped quote or a template that printed nothing. Paste it into a JSON validator to find the line.
tech: JSON.parse fails on a script type="application/ld+json" block (one finding per block)
done: The structured data parses as valid JSON and a rich results test can read it.
estimateChanges: A template that prints nothing for an empty field needs a guard, and several templates each need it.

title: Prices differ between language versions
what: The same item (matched by its structured data sku, or name) shows a different price on another language version of the page.
why: Customers see one price and pay another, or compare the two versions and stop trusting either.
fix: Update the price on every version, ideally from one product record. A version that was copied and translated keeps last month's price.
tech: Product or Offer price in JSON-LD (then the configured priceSelector; never free text) differs for one sku across versions; "$12", "12 USD" and "$12.00" are equal
done: Every language version shows the same price.
estimateChanges: Versions kept as separate pages are edited one by one. One product record feeding all of them needs a template change.

title: A listing shows different opening hours
