what: On at least one day, the hours on your Google, Yelp or Apple listing are not the hours on your site.
why: People decide where to go from the hours in the search result. A listing that says you close at 10 when you stay open until 2 loses the late crowd, and one that says you open early sends people to a locked door.
fix: Make the hours the same in the listing's own dashboard and on the site. Decide which one is right first, then fix the other.
tech: both sides become seven lists of intervals in the venue's local time (a close after midnight belongs to the day it opens, split shifts stay split) and each day the site states is compared; a day the site does not mention is not; a day missing from a listing that gave hours is closed; the site's hours are the hours fact in gaugeline.facts.json, else LocalBusiness openingHours or openingHoursSpecification
done: The listing and the site show the same opening hours.
estimateChanges: Each listing (Google, Yelp, Apple) is edited in its own dashboard. Deciding which hours are right comes first.

title: A listing still uses your old business name
what: The name on your Google, Yelp or Apple listing is not the name your site uses.
why: Most people find a bar or a clinic through the listing, not the website. If it still shows a name you retired, they search for the wrong thing and doubt that the place is the one they want.
fix: Change the name in the listing's own dashboard (Google Business Profile, Yelp for Business, Apple Business Connect) to the one on your site, or fix the site if the listing is right.
tech: the listing's name, normalised (case, accents, punctuation and a leading or trailing "The" ignored), is neither equal to the site's name nor the site's name with words around it; the site's name is the text fact "name" in gaugeline.facts.json, else the LocalBusiness name in structured data; permanently closed listings are not compared
done: The listing and the site use the same business name.
estimateChanges: Each listing is its own login, and a name change that needs verification can take days.

title: A listing shows a different phone number
what: The phone number on your Google, Yelp or Apple listing is not the one on your site.
why: The phone number on the listing is the one people tap from the search result. A wrong one sends bookings and orders to a dead line or a stranger.
fix: Update the phone number in the listing's own dashboard, or on the site if the listing is the right one.
tech: the digits of the listing's phone number (a leading +1 or 1 on a North American number ignored) differ from the digits of the site's: the phone fact in gaugeline.facts.json, else the LocalBusiness telephone in structured data; numbers that are not 7 to 15 digits are not compared
done: The listing and the site show the same phone number.
estimateChanges: Each listing is edited separately, and a number repeated in many pages of the site adds edits.

title: A listing links to the wrong place
what: The website link on a listing, or in a social bio, leads to an old domain, to a page that no longer works, or through a long chain of redirects.
why: The website button on the listing is how a guest reaches the menu and the booking form. When it points at an old domain that lapses, or a page you deleted, every one of those visits ends in an error.
fix: Set the listing's website to your site's current address, in the listing's own dashboard or in the bio.
tech: the link is opened with GET (at most 8 distinct links, one request each): it is wrong when it cannot be opened, answers 400 or above, is on a different host from the checked site (www ignored) even if it redirects there, or takes 3 redirects or more; a link-in-bio page is right when it lands on the site or links to it; Yelp does not return a website, so it is not compared
done: The listing's website is the site's current address.
estimateChanges: Each listing is edited in its own dashboard or bio.

title: Test content is on the live site
what: The page's main content shows test or sample content: a test product, a sample post, John Doe, an example.com email address or a 555 phone number.
why: Unlike placeholder copy, a visitor can act on it: buy the test product, email the example address or call the fake number.
fix: Delete or unpublish the test entries in the CMS or shop, and replace sample contact details with real ones.
tech: main content (code and pre ignored) contains "test product", "sample product", "sample post", "sample page", "test post", "hello world!", "john doe", "jane doe", "john smith example", "your name here", "product name here", an @example.com/.org/.net address, or a 555 phone number (English lists)
done: The test entries are deleted or unpublished and sample contact details are replaced with real ones.
estimateChanges: Test content spread across many entries or shop products is one edit each.

title: A listing shows fewer entries than are published
what: A listing page you mapped to a document type shows fewer entries, across all its pages of results, than there are published documents of that type (less the ones you said it leaves out).
why: A query that drops documents (a filter on a field older documents lack, a reference that does not resolve) leaves the page looking complete: 31 cards instead of 48 is not an error, and nobody counts.
fix: Open the entries named in the evidence in the Studio and compare them with the listing's query. If the listing leaves some out on purpose, say so with filter in gaugeline.model.json.
tech: For each listing in gaugeline.model.json: the page is read with GET and its next link (rel=next, or the next selector) is followed, up to 10 pages; entries are the item selector's matches, counted once per address. The published count is count(*[_type == T && (filter)]) over published documents (GET). When fewer are shown, the ids of the published documents whose slug is not on the page come back (up to ten, in id order); titles are never requested. A page that cannot be read, or a listing longer than 10 pages, is could not check
done: The listing shows every published entry named in the evidence, or the filter that leaves entries out is written down on purpose.
estimateChanges: A query shared by several listings, or a count limit in a template, adds work.

title: Published documents are missing a field the schema now requires
what: The schema says every document of a type must have a field, and published documents of that type do not have it: the ones written before the field was required.
why: Older documents never got the new field, so a page or a query that depends on it shows an empty section, or drops those documents, on pages nobody opened since the change.
fix: Fix first when the document's page is live. Open the documents named in the evidence in the Studio and fill the field in, or run a one-off migration that sets it; then, if a few are meant to be empty, make the field optional in the schema.
tech: From the schema file named in gaugeline.model.json (sanity schema extract): each document type's fields, required unless the extract says optional. For each required field one GROQ query over published documents only (perspective=published, GET) returns two numbers and ids: count(*[_type == T && !defined(field)]) and the first three ids in id order. Grouped by type and field. No field value is requested or shown; a field required only on some types is judged on those types. Without a schema file the check is could not check
done: The documents named in the evidence have the field filled in and the schema check passes.
estimateChanges: Many documents need a one-off migration. A few are filled in by hand in the Studio.

title: A page shows a raw reference where content should be
what: A live page shows a Sanity reference id, a type name or "[object Object]" instead of the content it points to, in its text, in an address, or in the data it embeds.
why: A query that stopped following a reference (a missing ->) or a template that prints an object instead of a field still returns 200, so the page looks loaded and nobody opens it.
fix: Follow the reference in the query (author->{name}) or print the field you meant, not the object. A page that shows an id on purpose goes under idsShownOn in gaugeline.model.json.
tech: Read from the HTML as sent, without JavaScript, on the checked page and the few it links to: visible text (scripts, styles and templates removed) with [object Object], a _ref key with its id or a quoted _type key; links and images whose address holds [object Object]; and JSON the page embeds (__NEXT_DATA__ and application/json scripts) holding an object with _type "reference" and a _ref. An asset reference (image-…, file-…) is how Sanity stores a picture, so it is not reported. At most five places per page; pages under idsShownOn are skipped. The evidence is the page, the piece of it and the id. Nothing is asked of Sanity
done: The page prints the field's value, not a raw reference object.
estimateChanges: The same query pattern repeated in several templates is one edit each.

title: Menu links don't answer 200 at once
what: A link in the header or footer menu takes two or more redirects, ends in a redirect loop, answers 4xx or 5xx, or answers a 2xx that is not 200 (204, for one).
why: The menu is the part of the site every visitor and every crawler follows first. Each extra hop is a round trip and a place for tracking and rankings to be lost, and a menu link that does not land on a page is a dead end on every page of the site.
fix: Point the menu link at the address it ends at, so it needs no redirect, and fix or remove one that errors. Where an old address must keep working, redirect it once, straight to the final page.
tech: header and footer a[href] of the checked page on the same site, each once (at most 40, header first; a longer menu is listed under could not check); one HEAD each (GET if HEAD answers 405 or 501), every hop kept, with an address the link sample already asked reused and not asked again. Two or more 3xx hops is a chain (the count and each hop's status and address are the evidence); a loop or more than 10 hops is reported as such; a final status that is not 200 is reported (a 4xx or 5xx that the link sample found is broken-links's and is left to it); 401, 403 and 429 are could-not-check. A single redirect is links-via-redirect's, and a link into a hidden section or a draft is hidden-linked's and drafts-live's: nothing is added for them
done: Every menu link answers 200 at once, or through a single redirect.
estimateChanges: A moved page with a rule for the old address and another for the slash is one rule each; a menu link edited to point at the final address needs no rule.

title: Anyone can switch on draft mode
what: A draft or preview route on this Next.js site turns draft mode on for a request that carries no secret.
why: Anyone who visits that address sees unpublished content (prices, announcements, pages nobody approved) as if it were live.
fix: Make the route check a secret (compare a token from the request with one from your environment) before it enables draft mode, and return 401 otherwise.
tech: Next.js sites only: one GET per conventional route (/api/draft, /api/preview, /api/draft-mode/enable, /api/enable-draft), no secret sent or guessed; a Set-Cookie of __prerender_bypass or __next_preview_data on any hop is a finding
done: The draft mode route checks a secret and answers 401 without it.
estimateChanges: Several draft routes, or preview tools that call the route, need the secret as well.

title: The live site points search engines at a preview deployment
what: A production page of this Next.js site gives a preview domain as its canonical address, its og:url or og:image, or in its sitemap.
why: Search engines and social cards follow those addresses to the preview, which can show old content or vanish when the preview is cleaned up.
fix: Build the site's base address from the production domain (often NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL set only for preview builds), and rebuild.
tech: Next.js sites served from a non-temporary host: the canonical, og:url, og:image and sitemap entries whose host ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev
done: The live site builds its canonical and share addresses from the production domain.
estimateChanges: A variable set wrong only in some deployments means checking each environment, then rebuilding.

title: This page asks search engines not to list it
what: The page has a robots meta tag containing noindex.
why: If that isn't on purpose, the page is invisible in search.
fix: Remove noindex from pages you want found.
tech: <meta name="robots" content="noindex">
done: The page no longer asks search engines to skip it.
estimateChanges: A noindex set in a plugin, a header and a meta tag all have to be found.

title: A route the page metadata does not reach has no noindex header
what: The site is set to stay out of search, and an address its pages' metadata does not reach (the made-up not-found address, and each route you listed) answers without noindex in the X-Robots-Tag header or in the page.
why: A robots meta tag only covers HTML pages that set it. A not-found page, the studio, an API route or a file can only be kept out of search by a header; without it a hidden site can still be found through them.
fix: Send X-Robots-Tag: noindex for those routes while the site is hidden: a headers() entry in next.config for each, or one proxy rule for every response. Remove it at launch.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent and a gaugeline.hidden.json section that hides the whole site ("match": "/*"): one GET each of /gaugeline-not-found-3f9c2a71 and of the routes in noindexRoutes there (at most 8), no cookie or Authorization, at most 16384 bytes of each answer read and never kept, once per run; Gaugeline never picks a route such as /studio itself. A 2xx answer with no noindex in X-Robots-Tag or in a robots meta tag is a finding; 401, 403, 404 and 410 on the made-up address are not; a listed route that answers 404, 429, a 5xx or nothing is could-not-check
done: Every route you listed, and the not-found page, answers with noindex in the X-Robots-Tag header while the site is hidden.
estimateChanges: One headers() entry in the framework's config per route, or one rule in the proxy that covers them all. A studio served from another host is set in that host's settings.

title: This Nuxt site is running its development server
what: A page of this Nuxt site loads Vite's dev server client (/_nuxt/@vite/client) or other dev-only files, or its payload carries the Nuxt DevTools state.
why: A development server is slow, ships source code and debug information, and exposes tools (the DevTools, error overlays with source) that were never meant for visitors.
fix: Deploy the output of nuxt build (or nuxt generate), not the dev server, and check the host's start command. The Nuxt DevTools module only runs under nuxt dev.
tech: Nuxt sites only, read from the page already fetched: a script whose address has /@vite/client, /_nuxt/@id/, /_nuxt/@fs/ or /__nuxt_devtools__/, or a __nuxt_devtools__ useState key in the payload (added by the DevTools server plugin, which exists only in a dev build). The payload is the inline __NUXT_DATA__ script, and the page's own _payload.json when the page points at one. No separate dev-tools address is asked here (see nuxt-devtools-public)
done: The live site is a production build: its pages load /_nuxt/ files built by nuxt build, with no dev server client.
estimateChanges: Usually a deploy that ran nuxt dev (or a start command that did) is replaced with nuxt build and its output. Allow longer if the host's build settings need changing.

title: The Nuxt DevTools are reachable
what: This Nuxt site answers at /__nuxt_devtools__/client/ with the Nuxt DevTools page.
why: The DevTools show the app's files, routes, runtime config, server routes and modules to whoever opens the address.
fix: Run the live site from a production build (nuxt build, then the server output or the static files), never nuxt dev, and keep the @nuxt/devtools module to development.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: Nuxt sites only; one GET of /__nuxt_devtools__/client/ on the site's origin (the route the Nuxt DevTools module registers; a site under a base URL prefix is not asked at its prefix), once per address in a run, at most 6 Nuxt addresses; a finding needs a 200 HTML answer whose text includes "Nuxt DevTools" (that title is uncited: it comes from the module's own branding, not from the documentation). Any other answer, including a 200 page that is the site's own, is not reported; no answer is could-not-check
done: /__nuxt_devtools__/client/ answers 404 on the live site.
estimateChanges: Normally the same fix as nuxt-dev-build-live: deploy the output of nuxt build instead of the dev server.

title: The live Nuxt site points search engines at a preview or local address
what: A production page of this Nuxt site gives a preview deployment or a local address as its canonical address, its og:url or og:image, one of its hreflang alternates, or in its sitemap.
why: Search engines and social cards follow those addresses to the preview, which can show old content or vanish when the preview is cleaned up, and the language versions of the page are tied to the wrong site.
fix: Build the site's base address from the production domain (site config, runtimeConfig.public, or the language module's baseUrl, often set only for preview builds), and rebuild.
tech: Nuxt sites served from a host that is not a temporary one: the canonical, og:url, og:image, hreflang alternates and sitemap entries whose host ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev, or is localhost or 127.0.0.1
done: The live site builds its canonical, share and language addresses from the production domain.
estimateChanges: A site address set wrong only in some deployments means checking each environment, then rebuilding. A language module that builds its alternates from its own base address (baseUrl in @nuxtjs/i18n) is one setting.

title: Anyone can switch on Nuxt preview mode
what: This Nuxt page, asked with ?preview=true and no secret, is rendered on the server with preview mode switched on (the page's own state says enabled: true).
why: Pages that show unpublished content in preview mode (prices before an announcement, drafts nobody approved) show it to anyone who adds the query to the address.
fix: Give usePreviewMode a shouldEnable that checks a secret (compare a token from the request with one from runtimeConfig, server side) and returns false otherwise, and fetch draft content only from server routes that check the same secret.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: Nuxt sites only; one GET of the page's own address with ?preview=true&token=gaugeline-probe (the documented default query of usePreviewMode; the token is a fixed word, not a secret), at most 6 Nuxt addresses per run, no cookie and no header added; the answer's __NUXT_DATA__ is read as a flat JSON array and its $s_preview-state useState value is looked at for enabled being true. A page that never sends that state, a cached copy that ignores the query, a payload held in a separate file or one that is cut or not JSON is could-not-check, never a pass. The preview state's contents are never shown
done: A request with ?preview=true and no secret is rendered as an ordinary page: usePreviewMode only turns on after the app checks a secret.
estimateChanges: Often one shouldEnable function that compares a token from the request with one in runtimeConfig. Allow longer if preview links are shared with editors who then need the token.

title: A Nuxt page sends fields that look private to every visitor
what: The page's embedded state (the __NUXT_DATA__ payload, or its _payload.json) or its public runtime config (window.__NUXT__) has a field whose name says it is a secret, password, private key, service role key, access token or API key, with a value in it.
why: Everything in that state is in the page's source for anyone to read. A field named like a secret usually is one: a key someone put under runtimeConfig.public, or a whole server record returned to the page.
fix: Keep the value in the private runtimeConfig (outside public) and use it only in server routes, return only the fields the page shows from useAsyncData and useFetch (pick or transform them), and rotate any key that has been public.
tech: Nuxt sites only: the __NUXT_DATA__ script (a flat JSON array, read as the page was sent), the page's own /_payload.json when the data script points at one (one GET, same site only), and the window.__NUXT__ config literal, each read up to 2 MB or 256 KB by a single linear scan, never evaluated. Every object key is split into words (camelCase and snake_case alike) and matched against service role, secret, password, private key, access/auth/bearer/refresh/session token and API key; a field with an empty, null or true/false value is not reported. A name containing only API key is medium, the rest high. Only field names and the kind of place are shown, never a value; names are held in a Map keyed by name so a repeated field counts once, and a __proto__ key is an ordinary name. A payload that is cut, too large or not JSON is could-not-check, not a pass
done: The page's embedded state and public runtime config hold only what a visitor may see.
estimateChanges: Moving a value from runtimeConfig.public to the private runtimeConfig is one line, but the key it names may also need rotating, and any server code that used it from the browser needs a server route.

title: A page from the last run is gone
what: An address the last run read (saved with --since last) now answers 404 or 410, or redirects to a different page; the evidence says where it now leads.
why: Links from other sites, bookmarks and search results still point at the old address: a page that went missing loses them all, and one redirected to the wrong place loses them more slowly.
fix: Put the page back, or redirect it with a 301 to the page that replaces it. A page removed on purpose goes under expectedChanges in gaugeline.pages.json.
tech: With --since last only. Each saved address is taken from this run's pages when it was read anyway, else requested once with GET. A redirect that ends on the same path (a trailing slash, https) is not gone. A server error or refusal is could not check. On a first run: could not check
done: The page is back, or it redirects with a 301 to the page that replaces it.
estimateChanges: A whole deleted section is one redirect rule. Pages removed on purpose are listed in gaugeline.pages.json.

title: A page lost content since the last run
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, a page's main content fell by more than 40%, or a whole section (a heading and everything under it) is gone.
why: The page still loads, so nothing else notices: a template change, a failed import or an editor's mistake can empty a page that visitors and search engines relied on.
fix: Restore what went missing, or list the page under expectedChanges in gaugeline.pages.json with the reason when the loss was meant.
tech: With --since last only. Words are counted in the main content (main, else body) with the header, footer, navigation and asides left out, so a menu change doesn't count. A section is an h2 or h3; a heading gone is a section gone. Exactly 40% fewer words is not a loss. On a first run: could not check
done: The missing content is back on the page, or the page is listed under expectedChanges with a reason.
estimateChanges: A template change, a renamed CMS field and a deleted entry each need a different repair.

title: Page 2 of this list shows page 1 again
what: A later page of the list answers, and its main text is identical to the first page's.
why: The page parameter is ignored, so every older item is unreachable for visitors and search engines, and the copies count as duplicate pages.
fix: Make the list read the page number (often a query parameter the framework drops, or a cache that ignores the query string).
tech: At most 2 later pages (from findPagination), fetched with GET inside the links budget; the main text (no header, nav, footer, script or style), whitespace collapsed, hashed with SHA-256, equals page 1's. A later page that answers 4xx/5xx is broken-links' to report
done: Page 2 of the list shows different items from page 1.
estimateChanges: A cache that ignores the query string and a framework that drops the parameter have different fixes.

title: Page 2 of this list has no address
what: The page shows page numbers or a next or load-more control, and the HTML has no address for page 2: the control only works with JavaScript.
why: Search engines don't click buttons, so everything after the first page of the list is never found, and nobody can link to it.
fix: Give the control a real link (<a href="/blog?page=2">) and add <link rel="next">, keeping the JavaScript on top if you like.
tech: Read from the HTML as sent: no link rel=next, no a[rel=next], and no same-site link differing from this address only by ?page=N or /page/N, while a button, [role=button] or href-less a says Next or Load more, or a pagination element shows 2. Infinite scroll with no control at all can't be seen and isn't reported
done: The page 2 control is a real link and a rel next link is in the head.
estimateChanges: A custom pagination component fixed once covers every list that uses it.

title: A file people pay for is on a public address
what: A page that shows a price links straight to a file (pdf, zip, epub, mp3, mp4, docx or xlsx) on a public asset store.
why: Asset stores are world-readable by design. Anyone who has the address, or finds it in the page's source or a search engine, can download the file without paying.
fix: Check the purchase in your own download route, then hand back a short-lived signed link. Never put the asset address in the page or in an email.
tech: a[href] to a file with a sold file type (pdf, zip, epub, mp3, mp4, docx, xlsx) on a public asset store host (Sanity file CDN, S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure blob, R2, Supabase public, Cloudinary and similar) on a page with a price (a currency next to a number in the visible text, or an Offer price in the structured data); the file is never requested; the query string is not printed; a signed address with an expiry is a pass; a link whose text is terms, privacy or policy is asset-file-public instead
done: The paid file is no longer on a public address, and only a purchase check hands out a short-lived link.
estimateChanges: A file already shared or indexed stays copied somewhere. Moving the files and building the download route is the bulk of it.

title: A payment handle differs from yours
what: A page shows a Zelle, Cash App, Venmo or PayPal handle that is not the one you set for that service.
why: Customers who copy it send their money to someone else, and nobody finds out until you ask where the money went.
fix: Correct the handle where it is written (usually one shared footer or CMS field), then open it on a phone to check it is yours.
tech: Handles read from links, visible text, image descriptions and aria-labels (text handles only within 40 characters of the provider's name, in the same sentence) on the pages checked, compared case-insensitively with gaugeline.payments.json; Zelle phone numbers by their digits
done: The handle is correct everywhere and opens your payment page on a phone.
estimateChanges: One shared footer or CMS field is one edit. Handles typed into many pages are one edit each.

title: A payment detail you didn't set is on the site
what: A page shows a payment handle for a service you didn't set up, or a Square or Stripe payment link that isn't one of yours.
why: An old account, a copied template or a stranger's handle takes customers' money where you can't see it.
fix: Remove it, or add it to gaugeline.payments.json if it really is yours.
tech: Handles for a service with no entry in gaugeline.payments.json, and square.link, checkout.square.site and buy.stripe.com links not listed there, on the pages checked
done: The payment detail is removed from the site, or listed in gaugeline.payments.json as yours.
estimateChanges: If someone else's handle was added, finding who added it comes first.

title: A payment link no longer works
what: A Square or Stripe payment link on the site answers 404, or shows the provider's page for a link that has been turned off.
why: Customers who are ready to pay hit a dead end, and most of them don't come back to try another way.
fix: Make a new payment link in Square or Stripe and replace the old one everywhere it appears.
tech: square.link, checkout.square.site and buy.stripe.com links on the pages checked, requested once each with GET (nothing is submitted), at most 5: dead on 404 or 410, or a 2xx page with the provider's inactive-link wording
done: The new payment link works on a phone and the old one appears nowhere on the site.
estimateChanges: One link used in many places is one edit. Links in emails and printed material are out of reach from here.

title: Assistants find two different names for your business
what: The business name in the page's structured data and the title of /llms.txt are not the same name.
why: Assistants match a question to a business by name. Two names can make them treat one business as two, or quote the wrong one.
fix: Use the same business name in the LocalBusiness structured data and as the first heading of llms.txt.
tech: LocalBusiness JSON-LD name and the llms.txt H1 disagree (case, punctuation and a leading "The" ignored)
done: The business name in the LocalBusiness data matches the first heading of llms.txt.
estimateChanges: A name kept in several places is one edit each.

title: A page address returns Qwik City data, not a page
what: A page of this Qwik or SolidStart site answers with the framework's route data (Qwik City's q-data.json payload), or the sitemap lists q-data.json or /_server addresses.
why: Search engines and visitors get a JSON payload instead of a page, or index the payloads: the page can drop out of search while a browser that navigates inside the app looks fine.
fix: Serve HTML at page addresses (look for a proxy, CDN or adapter rule that rewrites to q-data.json), and list only pages in the sitemap.
tech: Qwik and SolidStart sites, from responses already read: the page's own answer with a JSON content type whose body starts {"_entry":"..","_objs": (Qwik City's q-data format); sitemap entries ending /q-data.json or starting /_server. No extra request
done: The page address returns HTML, and the sitemap lists pages only.
estimateChanges: A proxy or CDN rule that rewrites page addresses to the data address is one change; a sitemap built from the route files may need its own filter.

title: The live Qwik or SolidStart site is a development server
what: This page was served by the Vite development server of a Qwik or SolidStart site: it loads /@vite/client, /@qwik-city-plan or /_build/@fs/ files, or its Qwik container says it was rendered in dev mode.
why: The dev server serves source files, can expose files from the project folder and is slow and unsupervised. It is not meant to face visitors.
fix: Build the site and serve the build's output with the adapter or start command of your host, not the dev command. Check the host's start command.
tech: Read from the page already fetched, no extra request: q:render ending -dev or a q:manifest-hash starting dev on the Qwik container, or a script or the HTML naming /@vite/client, /@qwik-city-plan (Qwik) or /_build/@fs/ (SolidStart). Paths such as /__inspect are not asked for
done: The live address serves the built site, not the development server.
estimateChanges: A host that runs the dev command as its start command needs the build and start commands set.

title: Anyone can switch on preview mode on a Qwik or SolidStart site
what: A preview or draft route on this Qwik or SolidStart site sets a preview or draft cookie for a request that carries no secret.
why: Anyone who visits that address sees unpublished content (prices, announcements, pages nobody approved) as if it were live.
fix: Make the route check a secret (compare a token from the request with one from your environment) before it sets the cookie, and answer 401 otherwise.
tech: Probing check: off unless --owner-consent or gaugeline.consent.json; run only on sites you own or have permission to test. Qwik and SolidStart sites only: one GET per conventional route (/api/preview, /api/draft, /preview, /draft), no secret sent or guessed; a Set-Cookie whose name contains preview or draft on any hop is a finding, and only its name is shown. The routes and the cookie rule are conventions, not the frameworks' own (uncited)
done: The preview route checks a secret and answers 401 without it.
estimateChanges: Several preview routes, or preview tools in the CMS that call the route, need the secret as well.

title: The live Qwik or SolidStart site points search engines at a preview deployment
what: A production page of this Qwik or SolidStart site gives a preview domain as its canonical address, its og:url or og:image, or in its sitemap.
why: Search engines and social cards follow those addresses to the preview, which can show old content or vanish when the preview is cleaned up.
fix: Build the site's base address from the production domain (often an environment variable that is set only for preview builds, or an origin taken from the request behind a proxy), and rebuild.
tech: Qwik and SolidStart sites served from a non-temporary host: the canonical, og:url, og:image and sitemap entries whose host ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev
done: The live site builds its canonical and share addresses from the production domain.
estimateChanges: A setting that is wrong only in some deployments means checking each environment, then rebuilding.

title: The data a Qwik or SolidStart page sends has fields that look private
what: The state Qwik or SolidStart embeds in this page (Qwik's qwik/json script, SolidStart's _$HY hydration data), or this Qwik page's q-data.json, has fields named like something private (password, token, secret, apiKey, private notes).
why: Everything a loader or a hydrated component holds is sent to every visitor, whether or not the page shows it. A field that is only used on the server still travels with the page.
fix: Return only the fields the page shows from the routeLoader$ or the server function. Keep secrets in server-only environment variables and read them only in server code.
tech: Qwik and SolidStart sites only. Names only, never values: the property names of the objects in the embedded state (Qwik: the objs list of <script type="qwik/json">; SolidStart: the literals of the inline scripts that write to _$HY.r, read as text, strings skipped) and, for Qwik, in the page's own q-data.json (one GET of <page>/q-data.json, _objs list, capped), matched by word against password, passwd, secret, token, private, credential, ssn, salt, bearer, authorization, cvv, iban, apiKey, accessKey, secretKey, privateKey, internalNotes. A state that cannot be read (including Qwik 2's format, uncited) is could not check. The names are matched by their words, which is a guess (uncited)
done: The page's data holds only what the page shows: no field named for a password, token, secret or private note.
estimateChanges: Each field is dropped in the loader or server function that returns it; a field several pages read needs each of them checked.

title: One Qwik or SolidStart address serves a page and JSON, and caches aren't told
what: The same address of this Qwik or SolidStart site returns HTML to a browser and JSON to a request with Accept: application/json (an endpoint and a page sharing a route), and neither response lists Accept in its Vary header.
why: A shared cache (a CDN, a proxy) then keys both on the address alone and can hand the JSON to a visitor or a search engine: an outage that returns 200.
fix: Send Vary: Accept on both answers (in the middleware or endpoint that negotiates), keep Vary in the CDN's cache key, or give the endpoint its own address.
tech: Qwik and SolidStart pages only. One extra GET of the same address with Accept: application/json, the only header added, sent on same-origin hops only. Vary tokens from both answers, lower case; Vary: * counts as covering Accept. A 429 or 5xx answer is could not check. Neither framework negotiates a successful page on Accept by itself (Qwik City only answers an error as application/qwik-json when Accept lacks text/html, from the package source), so this catches custom endpoints and middleware: the check itself is uncited
done: Both responses send Vary: Accept and the CDN keeps it in its cache key.
estimateChanges: A CDN setting that is not editable on your plan adds a support request.

title: A page address returns Remix data, not a page
what: A page of this Remix or React Router site answers with the framework's route data (a single-fetch .data payload or a ?_data= answer), or the sitemap or the canonical names a .data or ?_data= address.
why: Search engines and visitors get a data payload instead of a page, or index the payloads: the page can drop out of search while a browser that navigates inside the app looks fine.
fix: Serve HTML at page addresses (look for a proxy, CDN or server rule that rewrites to .data or keeps the ?_data= query), and list only pages in the sitemap and canonical.
tech: Remix and React Router sites. From responses already read, no extra request: the page's own answer with content type text/x-script or the header X-Remix-Response (the framework sets both on every data answer), sitemap entries ending .data or carrying a _data query, and a canonical that does. The markers are in react-router 7.18.5 (lib/server-runtime/single-fetch.ts) and @remix-run/server-runtime 2.17.5 (server.ts), read from npm
done: The page address returns HTML, and the sitemap and canonical name pages only.
estimateChanges: A proxy or CDN rule that rewrites page addresses to the data address is one change; a sitemap built from the route list may need its own filter.

title: The live Remix site is a development server
what: This page was served by the Remix or React Router dev server: it loads /@vite/client, /@react-refresh, the inject-hmr-runtime module or the live-reload script.
why: The dev server serves source files, can expose files from the project folder and is slow and unsupervised. It is not meant to face visitors.
fix: Build the site (`react-router build` or `remix vite:build`) and serve the build with `react-router-serve` or your host's adapter, not `vite dev`. Check the host's start command.
tech: Read from the page already fetched, no extra request: the HTML or a script address names /@vite/client, /@react-refresh, inject-hmr-runtime (virtual:react-router/ or virtual:remix/), remixLiveReloadConnect, __vite_plugin_react_preamble_installed__ or /node_modules/.vite/. Vite's paths count only on a page that is Remix or React Router by its own context, header or dev module, so another Vite framework's dev server is not named here. Dev-only paths are not asked for. Names read from @react-router/dev 7.18.5 and @remix-run/dev 2.17.5 on npm
done: The live address serves the built site (react-router-serve or your host's server build), not the dev server.
estimateChanges: A host that runs the dev command as its start command needs the build and start commands set.

title: Anyone can switch on Remix preview mode
what: A preview or draft route on this Remix or React Router site sets a preview or draft cookie for a request that carries no secret.
why: Anyone who visits that address sees unpublished content (prices, announcements, pages nobody approved) as if it were live.
fix: Make the loader check a secret (compare a token from the request with one from your environment) before it sets the cookie, and answer 401 otherwise.
tech: Probing check: off unless --owner-consent or gaugeline.consent.json; run only on sites you own or have permission to test. Remix and React Router sites only: one GET per conventional route (/api/preview, /api/draft, /preview, /draft), no secret sent or guessed, never a POST (actions are not called); a Set-Cookie whose name contains preview or draft on any hop is a finding, and only its name is shown. The routes and the cookie rule are conventions, not the frameworks' own (uncited)
done: The preview route checks a secret and answers 401 without it.
estimateChanges: Several preview routes, or preview tools in the CMS that call the route, need the secret as well.

title: The live Remix site points search engines at a preview deployment
what: A production page of this Remix or React Router site gives a preview domain as its canonical address, its og:url or og:image, or in its sitemap.
why: Search engines and social cards follow those addresses to the preview, which can show old content or vanish when the preview is cleaned up.
fix: Build the site's base address from the production domain (often an environment variable that is set only for preview builds, or an address taken from request.url behind a proxy), and redeploy.
tech: Remix and React Router sites served from a non-temporary host: the canonical, og:url, og:image and sitemap entries whose host ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev
done: The live site builds its canonical and share addresses from the production domain.
estimateChanges: A variable that is wrong only in some deployments means checking each environment, then rebuilding.

title: The data sent with a Remix page has fields that look private
what: The state this Remix or React Router page embeds for the browser (window.__remixContext, window.__reactRouterContext or window.__staticRouterHydrationData) has fields named like something private (password, token, secret, apiKey, private notes).
why: Everything a loader returns is sent to every visitor, whether or not the page shows it. A field that is only used on the server still travels with the page.
fix: Return only the fields the page shows from the loader, and keep secrets in server-only code (process.env in a loader or action, or a .server module) that never returns them.
tech: Remix and React Router sites. Names only, never values: the property names in the page's own embedded context (JSON, read as text) and in its first streamed turbo-stream chunk (a flat JSON array, walked from index 0 once per index, capped), matched by word against password, passwd, secret, token, private, credential, ssn, salt, bearer, authorization, cvv, iban, apiKey, accessKey, secretKey, privateKey, internalNotes. No extra request. A state that cannot be read in full, or deferred chunks after the first, are could not check. The embedded globals and the turbo-stream layout are read from react-router 7.18.5 and @remix-run/react 2.17.5 on npm; matching names by their words is a guess (uncited)
done: The page's embedded state holds only what the page shows: no field named for a password, token, secret or private note.
estimateChanges: Each field is dropped in the loader that returns it; a field several routes read needs each of them checked.

title: Your robots.txt tells every search engine to stay away
what: robots.txt has a group for every crawler (User-agent: *) that disallows the whole site.
why: Search engines stop crawling the site, so new pages never appear and old ones fade out of results.
fix: Remove the Disallow: / line from the User-agent: * group, or replace it with the paths you mean to hide. This line is often left over from a staging site.
tech: robots.txt: User-agent: * with Disallow: / and no Allow that overrides it
done: robots.txt no longer disallows everything for every search engine.
estimateChanges: A block set by the host or a plugin setting rather than the file means finding that setting.

title: The page address returns app data, not a page
what: A normal request to the page returns the framework's data format (text/x-component), or HTML with no readable words while the prefetch request returns the page's data.
why: Search engines and visitors without JavaScript get nothing to read: the page can drop out of search while every check that loads it in a browser looks fine.
fix: Serve HTML to requests without the RSC header. On Next.js this is usually a custom server, middleware or CDN rule that answers every request with the RSC response, or a page that renders only on the client.
tech: React framework pages only (Next.js signals in the response). One extra GET of the same address with RSC: 1, the only header added, sent on same-origin hops only. 401, 403, 404, 429 and 5xx are could not check
done: A request without the RSC header returns HTML, and one with it returns app data.
estimateChanges: A custom server, middleware and a CDN rule each fix differently, and finding the one that answers is the work.

title: One address serves a page and app data, and caches aren't told
what: The same address returns HTML to a normal request and text/x-component to a request with RSC: 1, and neither response lists RSC in its Vary header.
why: A shared cache (a CDN, a proxy) then keys both on the address alone and can hand the data format to a visitor or a search engine: an outage that returns 200.
fix: Send Vary: RSC (Next.js sends RSC, Next-Router-State-Tree, Next-Router-Prefetch) on both responses, and make sure the CDN keeps it in its cache key. If the origin already sends it, look at the CDN's header and cache-key settings.
tech: React framework pages only. Vary tokens from both responses, compared in lower case; Vary: * counts as covering RSC. A CDN header in either response adds a note that the CDN may be stripping Vary
done: Both responses send Vary: RSC and the CDN keeps it in its cache key.
estimateChanges: A CDN setting that is not editable on your plan adds a support request.

title: Your organization has more than one identity in structured data
what: The Organization or WebSite @id differs from the one in your schema guide, or differs from page to page.
why: Search engines join structured data across pages by @id. Two ids make two organizations, splitting what is known about yours.
fix: Use one fixed @id for the Organization and one for the WebSite on every page, for example https://example.com/#organization.
tech: an Organization or WebSite @id (compared after resolving and trimming a trailing slash) differs from organizationId/websiteId, or, with no guide, differs between the sampled pages
done: One fixed @id for the Organization and one for the WebSite appear on every page.
estimateChanges: Templates that build the id from the page's address each need the change. Structured data written by a plugin may not allow it.

title: A script comes from a host on the known-bad list
what: The page loads a script from a host that a published report says served injected or malicious code.
why: A script runs with the page's full access, including a checkout form. Whoever controls the host controls what it does to your visitors.
fix: Remove the script tag, or point it at a copy you host or at a service you trust. Then ask whoever added it why it was there.
tech: a script src whose host, or a parent domain of it, is in data/known-bad-script-hosts.json. The list names its source for every host. Nothing is requested: the address is read from the page
done: The page loads no script from that host, and the script it replaced works.
estimateChanges: The same address in the theme, a plugin and a tag manager is three edits. A library that needs the script may need a replacement.

title: A private key is in your site's JavaScript
what: A secret key (a Stripe secret or restricted key, a Sanity token, a Contentful, Contentstack or Storyblok preview token, or a long random value named like a secret) is in JavaScript the site sends to every visitor.
why: Anyone can read it in their browser and use it as you: take payments, read customer data or change your content.
fix: Revoke the key in the provider's dashboard now, make a new one, and keep it on the server: never in code the browser loads.
tech: Inline scripts and up to 15 same-site script files (GET, first 5 MB each) matched against the detectors in checks/leaks/detectors.ts; publishable keys (pk_) are ignored; a Contentful preview token is a 43-character value named like a token or key next to the preview.contentful.com host, and a finding for it names the kind and the place only, with no character of the token; a Contentstack preview token is a value of "cs" and hex named like a token or key, and either "preview" is in its name in a file that names Contentstack or the Live Preview host (preview.contentstack.com) is in the same object; it is reported the same way, with no character of it; a Contentstack delivery token is public by design and is never reported; a Storyblok preview token is 20 to 32 letters and digits named like a token or key, and either "preview" is in its name in a file that names Storyblok or a draft version (version: "draft") is asked for in the same object; it is reported the same way, with no character of it; a Storyblok public token looks the same and is public by design, so it is never reported; a 43-character Contentful delivery token (a value in a place that names Contentful or createClient, and not the Preview API) is public by design and is never reported; a value that ai-key-in-js reports as an AI provider key is left to that check; the other values are redacted to their first 6 and last 2 characters before a finding exists; names are capped at 40 characters each side of the word token or key, so a hostile file is scanned in linear time
done: The old key is revoked, a new one lives on the server only, and the site's JavaScript holds no key.
estimateChanges: Code that used the key in the browser has to move to a server route. A key exposed for long also means reading the provider's logs.

title: Your sitemap lists pages that don't exist
what: Pages listed in the sitemap return an error (4xx or 5xx).
why: The sitemap is where you tell search engines which pages matter. Dead entries waste their visits and make them trust the sitemap less.
fix: Remove the dead addresses from the sitemap, or restore the pages. A generated sitemap usually means a deleted page is still in the CMS or the route list.
tech: sampled sitemap entries return 4xx or 5xx; a refusal (401, 403, 429, 503 with Retry-After) is listed as could not check
done: Every address in the sitemap loads.
estimateChanges: A generated sitemap fed by deleted CMS entries is fixed at the source. A hand-edited one is edited by hand.

title: Your staging site can be found by search engines
what: staging.<your domain> answers with a page and doesn't ask search engines to stay away.
why: Search engines can index the unfinished copy alongside the real site, with old prices, test content or duplicate pages competing with yours.
fix: Put the staging site behind a password, or send X-Robots-Tag: noindex (or <meta name="robots" content="noindex">) on every staging page.
tech: One GET of <scheme>://staging.<host without www.>/: a final 200 on the staging host with no noindex or none in meta robots or X-Robots-Tag. A staging host that doesn't resolve, asks for a login or redirects away is a pass
done: The staging site sits behind a password or sends noindex on every page.
estimateChanges: Several staging or preview hosts each need the setting, and pages already indexed need removal requests.

title: The live static site generator is a development server
what: This page loads a live-reload or development script of a static site generator (Hugo, Jekyll, Eleventy, Docusaurus or VitePress).
why: A development server shows drafts and future posts, rebuilds on every request and was never meant for visitors: it is slow, and it keeps a connection open for every one of them.
fix: Build the site (hugo, jekyll build, eleventy, docusaurus build, vitepress build) and serve the output folder from a static host.
tech: The page's own script addresses only: /livereload.js (Hugo and Jekyll servers: uncited), /.11ty/reload-client.js (eleventy-dev-server 2.1.2), /@vite/client beside a vitepress script (VitePress dev), or a Docusaurus generator tag with no version (the development template, @docusaurus/core 3.10.2). Names of the markers only
done: The live address serves the built files, not the generator's development server.
estimateChanges: A host that runs a start command needs it changed to serve the build folder.

title: A page that says it is a draft is live
what: This page, built with a static site generator, shows a draft marker and is open to search engines or listed in the sitemap.
why: Drafts are work nobody approved. A draft in the sitemap is handed to search engines to list, and a visitor can read it.
fix: Build the live site without drafts (Hugo: drop --buildDrafts; Jekyll: drop --drafts; Docusaurus and VitePress: set the page's draft or unlisted option and rebuild), or finish the page and remove the marker.
tech: Sites with a Hugo, Jekyll, Eleventy, Docusaurus or VitePress generator tag only: a class name "draft", "is-draft", "post-draft", "draft-badge", "badge-draft", the Docusaurus theme-draft-banner or theme-unlisted-banner on the page (class names only, never text), and no noindex, or an address the sitemaps list. The badge class names are theme conventions (uncited); the Docusaurus banners are from @docusaurus/theme-common 3.10.2
done: Draft pages are left out of the live build, so no page that says it is a draft is public.
estimateChanges: Drafts built by a deploy preview and by the main build are two settings to change.

title: A post dated in the future is already live
what: This page, built with a static site generator, gives a publish date more than a day after today.
why: A post dated for later (a sale, a menu, an announcement) is public now: anyone with the address, a search engine or a feed reader can read it before you meant them to.
fix: Build the live site without future posts (Hugo: drop --buildFuture; Jekyll: drop --future; Eleventy: skip pages whose date is ahead) and rebuild, or correct the date.
tech: Sites with a Hugo, Jekyll, Eleventy, Docusaurus or VitePress generator tag only: the page's article:published_time and JSON-LD datePublished, compared with the run's clock plus one day (a date with no zone is UTC, and the day absorbs any time zone). Only the date is shown, never the title or text. The Hugo and Jekyll flags are from memory of their docs, which could not be reached: uncited
done: The live site is built without future-dated posts, and the post's date is the day it should appear.
estimateChanges: A build that runs on a schedule needs the date filter in every build command, not only this one.

title: The site was built with a placeholder or preview address
what: A page built with a static site generator gives a placeholder (example.org, localhost) or preview domain as its canonical address, its og:url, or in its sitemap.
why: Search engines and social cards follow those addresses away from your site, to a domain that is not yours or a preview that disappears.
fix: Set the site's base address to the production domain (Hugo: baseURL; Jekyll: url; Eleventy: a site url in the data; Docusaurus: url; VitePress: sitemap hostname) and rebuild.
tech: Sites with a Hugo, Jekyll, Eleventy, Docusaurus or VitePress generator tag, served from a non-temporary host: the canonical, og:url and sitemap entries whose host is example.org, example.com, example.net, localhost or 127.0.0.1, or ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev (the same list as next-preview-canonical). Hugo's example.org default is uncited
done: The built site's canonical and share addresses use the production domain.
estimateChanges: A base address that is right in one build and wrong in another means checking every build setting.

title: The site's search lists pages that are meant to be hidden
what: The search index a static site generator built lists pages that the sitemap leaves out and that are marked noindex or draft.
why: Anyone who types a word into your site search, or who downloads the index file, is shown those pages, even though you told search engines to skip them.
fix: Leave drafts, unlisted and noindex pages out of the search index at build time (the same filter as the sitemap's), and rebuild.
tech: Probing check: off unless --owner-consent or gaugeline.consent.json; run only on sites you own or have permission to test. Sites with a Hugo, Jekyll, Eleventy, Docusaurus or VitePress generator tag only. The index is the file the page's own markup names (a JSON alternate link, or VitePress's @localSearchIndex chunk named in its modules: read without consent, it is what every visitor's browser loads), else /index.json, /search.json, /search-index.json (conventions: uncited). Read up to 5 MB and 50,000 addresses; a larger, cut or unrecognised index is could not check. Addresses the sitemaps do not list are asked once each with GET (up to 4); a finding needs one that says noindex or shows a draft marker. Paths and counts only; reads use the run's script and page allowances
done: The site's search index lists only pages the sitemap lists and search engines may index.
estimateChanges: The index and the sitemap are built by different plugins, and each needs the same filter on drafts and noindex pages.

title: Hidden editing characters leaked onto the live site
what: The title, a meta tag or the structured data contains invisible characters: Unicode tag characters or long runs of zero-width characters, the kind a CMS preview (such as Sanity's stega) adds.
why: They are invisible to you but not to everyone else: search results, share previews and copied text carry them, and they can break string comparisons and structured data.
fix: Turn stega encoding off for production builds (in Sanity, set stega: false outside preview) and strip it from fields that end up in metadata.
tech: a code point in U+E0000 to U+E007F, or 4 or more zero-width characters in a row, in the title, meta content or JSON-LD strings
done: Production builds have stega turned off and no field in the page's metadata carries the characters.
estimateChanges: Fields copied into metadata by several templates each need stripping.

title: This live site is using Stripe's test key
what: The page, or a script on the same site, carries a Stripe test publishable key (it starts pk_test_) and the page is not on a hosting provider's preview address.
why: A checkout built on a test key looks like it works and takes no real money: every order a customer places goes nowhere, and no card is charged.
fix: In Stripe, switch to live mode, copy the live publishable key (pk_live_) and put it where the site reads its key, then redeploy and place one small real order to be sure.
tech: The page's HTML and the same-site scripts already read by the leak check are searched for pk_test_ followed by at least 16 letters or digits, not inside a longer word; no new request is sent; pages on vercel.app, netlify.app and pages.dev are skipped
done: The site uses the live key and one small real order went through.
estimateChanges: Checkout code in several places, a webhook secret and product ids that differ between test and live add work.

title: A page address returns SvelteKit data, not a page
what: A page of this SvelteKit site answers with the framework's route data (application/json or text/sveltekit-data holding {"type":"data","nodes":...}), or the sitemap lists __data.json addresses.
why: Search engines and visitors get a JSON payload instead of a page, or index the payloads: the page can drop out of search while a browser that navigates inside the app looks fine.
fix: Serve HTML at page addresses (look for a proxy, CDN or adapter rule that rewrites to __data.json), and list only pages in the sitemap.
tech: SvelteKit sites only, from responses already read: the page's own answer with a JSON or text/sveltekit-data content type whose body starts with {"type":"data","nodes"; sitemap entries ending /__data.json or .html__data.json. No extra request
done: The page address returns HTML, and the sitemap lists pages only.
estimateChanges: A proxy or CDN rule that rewrites page addresses to the data address is one change; a sitemap built from the route files may need its own filter.

title: The live site is a development server
what: This page was served by `vite dev`: its bootstrap script is __sveltekit_dev, or it loads /@vite/client, /.svelte-kit/ or /node_modules/.vite/ files.
why: The dev server serves source files, can expose files from the project folder and is slow and unsupervised. It is not meant to face visitors.
fix: Build the site (`vite build`) and serve the adapter's output (or `vite preview` for a quick check), not `vite dev`. Check the host's start command.
tech: Read from the page already fetched, no extra request: the inline script assigns __sveltekit_dev (the name SvelteKit gives its global only under vite dev), or a script or the HTML names /@vite/client, /.svelte-kit/ or /node_modules/.vite/. Paths such as /__inspect are not asked for
done: The live address serves the built site (adapter output or vite preview), not vite dev.
estimateChanges: A host that runs the dev command as its start command needs the build and start commands set.

title: Anyone can switch on preview mode
what: A preview or draft route on this SvelteKit site sets a preview or draft cookie for a request that carries no secret.
why: Anyone who visits that address sees unpublished content (prices, announcements, pages nobody approved) as if it were live.
fix: Make the route check a secret (compare a token from the request with one from your environment) before it sets the cookie, and answer 401 otherwise.
tech: Probing check: off unless --owner-consent or gaugeline.consent.json; run only on sites you own or have permission to test. SvelteKit sites only: one GET per conventional route (/api/preview, /api/draft, /preview, /draft), no secret sent or guessed; a Set-Cookie whose name contains preview or draft on any hop is a finding, and only its name is shown. The routes and the cookie rule are conventions, not SvelteKit's own (uncited)
done: The preview route checks a secret and answers 401 without it.
estimateChanges: Several preview routes, or preview tools in the CMS that call the route, need the secret as well.

title: The live SvelteKit site points search engines at a preview deployment
what: A production page of this SvelteKit site gives a preview domain as its canonical address, its og:url or og:image, or in its sitemap.
why: Search engines and social cards follow those addresses to the preview, which can show old content or vanish when the preview is cleaned up.
fix: Build the site's base address from the production domain (often a PUBLIC_ variable that is set only for preview builds, or a canonical written from event.url.origin behind a proxy), and rebuild.
tech: SvelteKit sites served from a non-temporary host: the canonical, og:url, og:image and sitemap entries whose host ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev
done: The live site builds its canonical and share addresses from the production domain.
estimateChanges: A setting that is wrong only in some deployments means checking each environment, then rebuilding.

title: The data sent with a page has fields that look private
what: The state SvelteKit embeds in this page, or its __data.json, has fields named like something private (password, token, secret, apiKey, private notes).
why: Everything a load function returns is sent to every visitor, whether or not the page shows it. A field that is only used on the server still travels with the page.
fix: Return only the fields the page shows from load. Keep secrets in $env/static/private or $env/dynamic/private, and read them only in server code.
tech: SvelteKit sites only. Names only, never values: the property names in the embedded state (the data literal of the inline __sveltekit_ script, read as text, strings skipped) and in the page's own __data.json (one GET of <page>/__data.json, devalue payload walked to depth 6, capped), matched by word against password, passwd, secret, token, private, credential, ssn, salt, bearer, authorization, cvv, iban, apiKey, accessKey, secretKey, privateKey, internalNotes. A payload that cannot be read is could not check. The names are matched by their words, which is a guess (uncited)
done: The page's data holds only what the page shows: no field named for a password, token, secret or private note.
estimateChanges: Each field is dropped in the load function that returns it; a field several pages read needs each of them checked.

title: One address serves a page and JSON, and caches aren't told
what: The same address of this SvelteKit site returns HTML to a browser and JSON to a request with Accept: application/json (a +page and a +server in one route), and neither response lists Accept in its Vary header.
why: A shared cache (a CDN, a proxy) then keys both on the address alone and can hand the JSON to a visitor or a search engine: an outage that returns 200.
fix: SvelteKit adds Vary: Accept to GET responses of a route that has both a +page and a +server. If it is missing, a CDN or proxy is stripping it: keep Vary in its cache key and header settings, or give the endpoint its own address.
tech: SvelteKit pages only. One extra GET of the same address with Accept: application/json, the only header added, sent on same-origin hops only. Vary tokens from both answers, lower case; Vary: * counts as covering Accept. A 429 or 5xx answer is could not check. The routing rule and the Vary header are in SvelteKit's routing docs (Content negotiation) and runtime/server/respond.js
done: Both responses send Vary: Accept and the CDN keeps it in its cache key.
estimateChanges: A CDN setting that is not editable on your plan adds a support request.

title: A switch is off but the site still links to what it controls
what: You turned a feature off (pre-orders, online ordering, bookings), and a page still has a link to the page that feature runs on.
why: Visitors click the link, land on a page that no longer works or takes orders you cannot fill, and call or leave. A cached or hard-coded link is the usual cause: the menu and the header were built before the switch was flipped.
fix: Make every link to the controlled page depend on the same switch (in Sanity or the database), or remove the link. If the evidence says the answer came from a cache, purge the cache after the switch changes.
tech: for each switch in gaugeline.switches.json whose state is off, the checked page, the other pages the run read and every page named in the file are searched for same-site links whose path is a whenOff.noLinksTo path or sits under it (/order covers /order/checkout, not /order-history); the state comes from its source (a published Sanity field or a one-row query through the read-only database source); a source that cannot be read, or gives a value that is not on or off, is could not check, and so is a page that cannot be read (one that answers 404 has no links); the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page
done: Every link to the controlled page follows the same switch.
estimateChanges: Links in many templates are one edit each, and a cache needs purging.

title: Links still point at a temporary address
what: The page, on your own domain, links to a hosting provider's temporary address (vercel.app, netlify.app or pages.dev).
why: Those addresses are previews: they can show old content, ask for a login, or vanish when the preview is cleaned up, and search engines split your site between two names.
fix: Change each link to the same path on your domain. Search the code and the CMS for the temporary name: it is often in a menu, a button or an environment variable.
tech: a[href] whose host ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev (checks/launch/hosts.ts), on a page that is not itself served from one
done: No link points at the temporary address any more.
estimateChanges: Links in the menu, in buttons, in CMS content and in an environment variable are separate places.

title: Google sees an almost empty page
what: Fewer than 60 words exist in the page before JavaScript runs, outside the header, nav and footer.
why: Many crawlers and AI tools read the page without running JavaScript, so they see almost nothing.
fix: Render the main content on the server. In Next.js, keep it out of client-only components and Suspense boundaries that wait for the browser.
tech: word count of server-rendered HTML
done: The main content is in the HTML the server sends, not built in the browser.
estimateChanges: One client-only component is an afternoon. A page built entirely in the browser means restructuring its components.

title: A planned page doesn't exist on the preview
what: A page the plan lists returns 404 (or 410) on the preview given with --base.
why: A planned page that doesn't exist at cutover loses every visitor and link meant for it.
fix: Build the page, or take the row out of the plan if it was dropped.
tech: Each planned path on --base fetched once with GET; 404 or 410 on the final hop. One finding per path, with every row on it
done: Each planned page loads on the preview, or its row is taken out of the plan.
estimateChanges: A dropped page is a plan edit. A page that was never built is the full cost of building it.

title: A canonical points somewhere other than the planned page
what: The page's canonical names another address, often the legacy one, instead of the planned page.
why: Search engines index the canonical: the new page won't be listed, the old address will.
fix: Point the canonical at the page's own planned address on production.
tech: The canonical's path (lower case, no trailing slash) against the row's path, on the preview's host or the plan's production host, with or without www
done: Each page's canonical is its own planned address on production.
estimateChanges: A canonical that comes from one template is a single edit.

title: A moved page is set not to be indexed
what: A page that replaces an old address (a row with a Legacy URL) is set not to be indexed: a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag header says noindex.
why: The old address now redirects to a page that search engines are told to leave out, so the ranking the redirect was meant to move has nowhere to go and the page drops out of results.
fix: Remove the noindex from the moved pages when the site goes live. A staging setting is usually the cause.
tech: Plan rows with a Legacy URL whose path differs from the row's. The page already fetched on --base: robots meta content and X-Robots-Tag containing noindex or none (a bot-named directive such as googlebot: noindex counts); no request beyond the one each planned page already gets (robots.txt is not read: the plan check asks one request per planned path and legacy address). When every page read, two or more, is set that way it is the preview's own switch: those rows are could-not-check, never a finding. The canonical of a moved page is judged by plan-canonical-elsewhere
done: Each moved page can be indexed: no noindex in the page or its headers.
estimateChanges: A noindex left from the staging site is usually one setting or one header rule.

title: An old address doesn't redirect
what: An old address in the plan's Legacy URL column still answers 200 or 404 on the preview instead of redirecting.
why: The old address's rankings and links go nowhere: a 404 loses them, a page left in place competes with the new one.
fix: Add a 301 from the old address to the row's new one. A meta refresh or JavaScript redirect isn't one.
tech: The legacy address (its path and query, moved onto --base) fetched with GET; the first hop isn't a 3xx. A 200 with a meta refresh or a location assignment is reported with that hint
done: Each old address answers with a 301 to the page its plan row names.
estimateChanges: Many legacy addresses are one redirect file or rule, within the host's limits. The count of addresses matters less than the host.

title: An old address redirects with a temporary status
what: An old address redirects with 302, 303 or 307, or with 308 to the wrong place.
why: A temporary redirect tells search engines the old address is coming back, so its rankings may not move to the new page.
fix: Make it a 301. A 308 is permanent too and is accepted when it goes to the right place.
tech: The status of the first hop. 308 to the planned page is accepted, with a note on stderr
done: Each old address redirects with a 301, or a 308 to the right place.
estimateChanges: A host setting that defaults to a temporary redirect fixes all of them at once.

title: An old address redirects somewhere the plan doesn't say
what: An old address redirects, but not to the page the plan says it should.
why: The old address's visitors and rankings land on the wrong page, and the planned page starts from nothing.
fix: Point the redirect at the row's URL. Right path on www instead of the bare host (or the reverse) costs another hop.
tech: The trail's final address (or where the last hop points, when it leaves the preview): its path against the row's, on the preview's host or exactly the plan's
done: Each old address lands on the page its plan row names.
estimateChanges: Overlapping rules mean testing each address after the change.

title: One old address is claimed by two rows
what: One old address is the Legacy URL of two rows that plan different pages.
why: An address can redirect to one place only: one of the two rows won't get its traffic, and no crawl will show it.
fix: Decide which page the old address goes to and remove it from the other row.
tech: Legacy URL cells split on line breaks and commas, keyed by path and query (lower case, no trailing slash); two rows with different addresses on one key. Needs no --base
done: Each old address appears in one plan row only.
estimateChanges: Someone who owns the plan has to decide which page wins.

title: A page that exists today has no row in the plan
what: An address in the --live export (a crawl, a sitemap, a Search Console export or a list) has no row in the plan and no Legacy URL pointing at it.
why: A page that ranks today and has nowhere to go at launch loses its traffic and links: the most expensive thing on a migration.
fix: Add a row for the page, or put its address in the Legacy URL of the row that replaces it.
tech: Live paths (lower case, no trailing slash, no query) against a Set of every row path and legacy path; assets, feeds, ?page= and --ignore globs left out. Sorted by clicks, impressions or position when the export has them. Three or more that differ from planned rows only by a leading prefix are one finding
done: Every live page has a row in the plan, or is named as the legacy address of its replacement.
estimateChanges: Many pages are a spreadsheet job. Deciding what replaces each page is the real work.

title: A menu item has no page in the plan
what: An item in a menu tab of the plan workbook has no page row in the page plan, and no page shares a distinctive word with it (or several do).
why: The menu will link to a page nobody planned: it gets built late, without a title or keyword, or the link goes nowhere.
fix: Add a row for the page, or rename the menu item to the page it means. A menu heading with no page of its own can have a row with no URL.
tech: Menu labels against Page and H1 cells by labelKey (G16's textKey, & as and, a trailing note such as (anchor) dropped). Headings (the first column) may match a row with no URL and are reported at medium. With several candidates, up to three are named
done: Every menu item has a row in the plan, or has been renamed to match one.
estimateChanges: Several items from one restructure share one decision.

title: Two rows in the plan share one address
what: Two or more rows of the plan give the same address (path and #section), so only one of those pages can exist.
why: The pages compete for one address: one gets built, the other is lost, and whichever wins gets the wrong title, heading and redirects.
fix: Give each planned page its own address, or merge the rows into one page.
tech: Rows grouped by host without www. and path in lower case, no trailing slash or query, plus #fragment when there is one; an anchor row and its page row differ by the fragment. One finding per group, with every line
done: Each planned page has its own address.
estimateChanges: Deciding which of two competing rows is the real page.

title: A printed address doesn't land on a page
what: A printed address (a QR code, a flyer, a short link) ends in a 4xx or 5xx, or no longer answers on the http:// that was printed.
why: A printed code can't be reprinted when a page moves: everyone who scans it gets an error.
fix: Add a redirect from the printed address to the page it was for, and answer on http if http was printed.
tech: The printed URL fetched as printed with GET; the trail's last hop is 400 or above. A printed http:// that refuses the connection while https:// answers is reported here
done: Each printed address lands on a live page, on the scheme that was printed.
estimateChanges: One redirect per address. Printed material cannot be changed, so each address has to be covered.

title: A printed address lands somewhere it shouldn't
what: A printed address lands somewhere other than its expectedDestination, or stops on an interstitial page that sends people on.
why: People scanned a code for one thing and got another, or a page they have to wait through.
fix: Point the printed address's redirect at the expected page, and make a short link redirect with a 301 rather than show its own page.
tech: The trail's final address against expectedDestination (host without www, path without trailing slash). A 200 with a meta refresh or a location assignment and no redirect is an interstitial
done: Each printed address lands on its expected page with no stop on the way.
estimateChanges: A short link made by a third party may need its own settings changed.

title: Campaign tags are lost
what: A redirect between the ad and its landing page drops utm_source, utm_campaign, gclid or fbclid.
why: The visit arrives with no sign of the ad that paid for it, so the report credits nobody, the campaign looks like it did nothing and the money is spent without a way to learn from it.
fix: Make the redirect pass the query string on, or point the ad straight at the final address.
tech: Per landing page, one GET of the destination with one ad's own campaign keys (utm_*, gclid, fbclid) or, when none of its ads has any, utm_source=gaugeline-check and gclid=test; the keys on the first address against the last, values compared after URL decoding and order ignored; the first redirect whose Location no longer carries a lost key is named with its status; a key moved into the fragment counts as lost; a trail that stopped early without a loss is could-not-check
done: The campaign tags arrive on the final page.
estimateChanges: A redirect set in the host, a CDN and the app each need checking.

title: The page doesn't load
what: An ad sends people to a page that answers 404, 410 or a server error, or that cannot be reached at all.
why: Everyone clicking that ad lands on an error, so every click is paid for and nobody can buy, book or call.
fix: Bring the page back, or redirect its address to the page that replaced it, then check the ad's link. Pause the ad until it works.
