a final 2xx answer is the finding, 404 or 410 is a pass for that entry, a page reached through a redirect to another path, and any other answer, is could-not-check for that page; the finding shows the model, the entry's slug or id, the path and the status, never a field
done: Every Hygraph entry that is not published, in the models you named, has no page on the live site.
estimateChanges: A few minutes when it is one page: unpublish or remove it in the front end, or find the route that builds pages from the DRAFT stage. Allow an hour when the front end reads the DRAFT stage everywhere and needs a PUBLISHED-only token for the live build.

title: A published Umbraco node has no page on the live site
what: Umbraco says a node is published, and the address its page should have answers 404 or 410 on the live site.
why: Links, the sitemap and search results point at a page that is not there, and the client's announcement leads to an error page.
fix: Check the content type has a template (or the front end builds a route for it), that the node's culture and domain settings match the site being checked, and that a headless front end was rebuilt or revalidated after publishing. If the node should not be public, unpublish it in the Umbraco backoffice.
tech: GET /umbraco/delivery/api/v2/content?filter=contentType:{alias} for each content type named in the settings (the published list; skip and take step by the number of nodes that came back, and a list is complete only when the position reaches the total it reports), then one GET of the live address: the settings' `urls` pattern when the type has one, else the route.path the API gave the node (redirects followed). A final 404 or 410 is the finding; any other answer that is not a 2xx is could-not-check for that page. A node with no route and no pattern, and a path that is not a plain path (a host, `..`, an escaped slash), are could-not-check by name and are not asked. Ids and paths only: no property is requested beyond those named in `fingerprint`, and none is used for this. A site with several root nodes and no domains may give paths relative to a start item: set `urls` for those types.
done: Every published node of the content types you named has a page that answers on the live site.
estimateChanges: One node is usually a page that was unpublished in a different language or a route that was renamed. Every node of a content type missing means the template or the front end route for that type. A content type with no pages of its own always shows as could not check, which is expected.

title: The Umbraco Delivery API answers visitors with no key
what: gaugeline.adapters.json says the Content Delivery API is meant to be private (expectPrivate: true), and a plain GET of its list route with no key is answered with the list of published nodes.
why: Anyone who finds the route can read every published node as data, including nodes that are published but not linked from the site, and can page through the whole content tree. If the API was meant to be private, its protection is off.
fix: In appsettings.json set Umbraco:CMS:DeliveryApi:PublicAccess to false and keep an ApiKey, then send the key from the server only (never from the browser). If the API is meant to be public (a public API that also has a key, so that preview works, is a normal setup), remove expectPrivate from gaugeline.adapters.json: the key is not touched.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: this check asks the Delivery API's public route as a visitor with no key, so it runs only with --owner-consent (or gaugeline.consent.json), on sites you own or have permission to test; only when the settings say expectPrivate: true (a key being set says nothing: Umbraco's preview needs the key on a public API too); one GET of /umbraco/delivery/api/v2/content?take=1 with no Api-Key header, no cookie and nothing the fetcher adds per address, fields=properties[] and expand=none; a 200 with a list and a numeric total is the finding (the total is a count, never a node); 401 or 403 is a protected API and 404 is an API that is off or not at that address, both with no finding; a 200 that is not the API's list (a page that answers every path) and any other status are could-not-check; the answer is read as a count and nothing else
done: The Delivery API answers a visitor who sends no key with 401, and nothing else, because gaugeline.adapters.json says it is private (expectPrivate).
estimateChanges: One setting in appsettings.json: Umbraco:CMS:DeliveryApi:PublicAccess to false (and an ApiKey set). Allow longer if the public front end calls the API from the browser and needs to move that call to the server.

title: A route published to Sitecore Experience Edge has no page on the live site
what: Experience Edge says a route is published for a language, and the address its page should have answers 404 or 410 on the live site.
why: Links, the sitemap and search results point at a page that is not there, and the client's announcement leads to an error page. Edge is what the front end reads, so a route that is on Edge and not on the site means the front end did not build it.
fix: Check that the front end has a route for the path (a rebuild or a revalidation may be needed after publishing), that the language's urls prefix in gaugeline.adapters.json matches how the site addresses that language, and that the item is not published by mistake. If the page should not be public, unpublish the item in Sitecore.
tech: POST https://edge.sitecorecloud.io/api/graphql/v1 (a documented read-only query, through the fetcher's query allowlist, ADR-0006) with the Delivery API token in the sc_apikey header: site { siteInfo(site) { routes(language, first, after) { total pageInfo { endCursor hasNext } results { routePath } } } }, every value a variable; pages are followed by the cursor Edge returns, and a repeated cursor or route, a missing hasNext, an empty page before the end and fewer routes than total are could-not-check. Then one GET of each route's address on the live site: the route path for the first language, the settings' urls prefix plus the route path for any language that has one (redirects followed). A final 404 or 410 on the site's own host is the finding, but only after Experience Edge is asked again for that language and still lists the route; a route that is gone by then, a second read that fails, a redirect to another site, a 429 (the pages after it are not asked) and any other answer that is not a 2xx are could-not-check. A language with no prefix that is not the first, an address on another site, and a path that is not a plain path (a host, `..`, an escaped slash) are could-not-check by name and are not asked. Routes only: no field of any item is requested. Routes are kept in a Set per language to catch a repeat.
done: Every route published to Experience Edge for the languages you named has a page that answers on the live site.
estimateChanges: One route is usually a page the front end does not build, or a path that was renamed. Every route under one folder missing means one route or one template in the front end. After a publish, a headless front end often needs a rebuild or a revalidation. A language with no urls prefix in the settings always shows as could not check, which is expected.

title: A published Joomla article has no page on the live site
what: Joomla says an article is published for every visitor, and the address its page should have answers 404 or 410 on the live site.
why: Links, the sitemap and search results point at a page that is not there, and the client's announcement leads to an error page.
fix: Check that a menu item or a category menu item shows the article, that the menu item is published and its access is Public, and that the article's category is published. If the article should not be public, unpublish it in the Joomla administrator. If every article fails, the address pattern in gaugeline.adapters.json (urls, articles) does not match the site's menu.
tech: GET /api/index.php/v1/content/articles?filter[state]=1 (Accept: application/vnd.api+json, X-Joomla-Token) in windows of up to 100, stepped by the number that came back; the count is taken first with a window of one article (meta.total-pages is a page count) and checked with a window of two, and a list is complete only when every counted article was seen; articles at a view level other than Public (access 1), with a start time in the future, with a finish time in the past, or in one language (not All) are counted and not asked; then one GET of the live address, which is the settings' urls pattern filled with the alias or id (Joomla's API gives no address), redirects followed. A final 404 or 410 is the finding; any other answer that is not a 2xx is could-not-check for that page. With no pattern for articles nothing is asked and that is could-not-check. Ids and aliases only: a field is requested only when the settings name it in fingerprint, and none is used for this.
done: Every published article of the Joomla site has a page that answers on the live site.
estimateChanges: One article is usually a menu item that was unpublished or an alias that was renamed. Every article missing means the address pattern in the settings does not match the site menu, so fix the pattern first.

title: The Joomla Web Services API answers visitors with no token
what: gaugeline.adapters.json says the Web Services API is meant to be private (expectPrivate: true), and a plain GET of its article list with no token is answered with a list of articles.
why: Anyone who finds the route can read every article the Public view level can see as data, including articles that are not linked from the site, and can page through all of them. If the API was meant to be private, its protection is off.
fix: In the Joomla administrator open System, Plugins and switch off the Web Services plugins you do not use (Web Services - Content, for articles), or find the extension that registered a public route (Joomla's own routes need a token). Send the token from the server only, never from the browser. If the API is meant to be public, remove expectPrivate from gaugeline.adapters.json: the token is not touched.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: this check asks the Web Services API's article list as a visitor with no token, so it runs only with --owner-consent (or gaugeline.consent.json), on sites you own or have permission to test; only when the settings say expectPrivate: true (a token being set says nothing); one GET of /api/index.php/v1/content/articles?page[limit]=1 with Accept: application/vnd.api+json and no X-Joomla-Token, no cookie and nothing the fetcher adds per address; a 200 with a JSON:API list (data) and a numeric meta.total-pages is the finding (the number is a count, never an article); 401 or 403 is a route that needs a token and 404 is an API that is off or not at that address, both with no finding; a 200 that is not the API's list (a page that answers every path) and any other status are could-not-check; the answer is read as a count and nothing else
done: A visitor who sends no token is refused by the Joomla article list, because you said the API is private.
estimateChanges: Usually one plugin to switch off or one route to make private, then a re-run. Allow longer if a headless front end calls the API from the browser and needs to move that call to the server.

title: A DatoCMS token meant for published content can read drafts
what: gaugeline.adapters.json says the token is meant for published content only (expectPublishedOnly: true), and a request that asks for drafts with it is answered with records that are not published.
why: A token for the live site is often placed in the front end or in a build setting. If it can read drafts, anyone who finds it can read unpublished work: prices not announced yet, a closure notice, a page that was pulled.
fix: In the DatoCMS dashboard, open Settings, API tokens, and edit the token the live site uses: turn off access to the Content Delivery API with draft content (the preview flag), keep the Content Delivery API on for published content, and keep the Content Management API off. Give a preview site its own token. If the token is meant to preview drafts, remove expectPublishedOnly from gaugeline.adapters.json.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: this check asks DatoCMS for draft content with the token you gave Gaugeline, so it runs only with --owner-consent (or gaugeline.consent.json), on sites you own or have permission to test; run only on sites you own or have permission to test; only when the settings say expectPublishedOnly: true for datocms and name the collections, since a token that may preview is a normal setup; per collection, POSTs of one GraphQL query each, through fetcher.query and the registered allowlist entry datocms-cda-query (a document that parses as one query is the only body ever sent): the published list, then the same list with the header X-Include-Drafts: true, each asking for id only, first 100, an explicit orderBy: [id_ASC], skip stepping by the number of records that came back, a page shorter than the page asked for ending the list, and the first page also asking the collection's count (a list that ends with another number of records is could-not-check, and a count over 10000 fails on the first page); the ids of the first list are held in a Set and subtracted from the second, and a non-empty difference is the finding (a count; ids only when the settings say showDraftIds, at most five; never a field); when there is a difference the published list is read once more and a list that changed in between is could-not-check; HTTP 401 or 403 to the first page of the draft request, after the published one was answered, means the token cannot read drafts, which is a pass for that collection, while a refusal on a later page is could-not-check; a draft request that is accepted with no extra record shows no sign of drafts, which is not proof since none may exist, so it is could-not-check; the check judges the token you give Gaugeline, so to test the live site's token give Gaugeline that token; a collection that cannot be read, a list that moves while it is read, one over 10000 records scanned and a rate limit that stays are could-not-check for that part
done: The DatoCMS token you gave Gaugeline cannot read a draft record, as gaugeline.adapters.json says it should not (expectPublishedOnly).
estimateChanges: A few minutes in the DatoCMS dashboard: turn off draft access on the token, or make a new token for the live site and swap it in the hosting settings. Allow longer if the same token also powers a preview site that needs drafts, because that site needs its own token first.

title: A published Prismic document has no page on the live site
what: Prismic says a document is published, and the address its page should have answers 404 or 410 on the live site.
why: Links, the sitemap and search results point at a page that is not there, and the client's announcement leads to an error page.
fix: Check the front end builds a page for the type (a static site may need a rebuild or a revalidation after publishing, which a Prismic webhook can trigger) and that its address matches the pattern in gaugeline.adapters.json. If the document should not be public, unpublish it in Prismic.
tech: GET /api/v2 on the repository's cdn.prismic.io host for the master ref and the document types, then GET /api/v2/documents/search for each type that has an address pattern in the settings (ref, lang=*, page, pageSize, an explicit orderings, q for the type, fetch for the fields the settings fingerprint); each page asks for the number it should, the same total and page count as the first, no document twice, and the list ends only when the count read equals the total, otherwise it is could-not-check; then one GET of the live address from the urls pattern (redirects followed). A final 404 or 410 is the finding; any other answer that is not a 2xx is could-not-check for that page. A document in a language other than the repository's main one, a document with no uid where the pattern needs one, a type with documents and no pattern, a type the repository would not list and a private repository without an access token are could-not-check by name and are not asked. Ids, uids and times only: no field is used for this.
done: Every published document of the types you gave an address pattern for has a page that answers on the live site.
estimateChanges: A page that is gone for every document of a type is one route or one address pattern in the front end. A single document is a uid that was changed or a page the front end does not build. A type with no pages of its own always shows as could not check, which is expected.

title: A published Directus item has no page on the live site
what: Directus says an item is published, and the address its page should have answers 404 or 410 on the live site.
why: Links, the sitemap and search results point at a page that is not there, and the client's announcement leads to an error page.
fix: Check the front end builds a page for the collection (a static site may need a rebuild or a revalidation after publishing) and that its address matches the pattern in gaugeline.adapters.json. If the item should not be public, set its status back to draft in Directus.
tech: GET /items/{collection} for each collection named in the settings (limit, offset and sort=id, fields=id,status,slug and the dates; meta=filter_count for the total), a row whose status is not published is dropped, then one GET of the live address from the `urls` pattern (redirects followed). A final 404 or 410 is the finding; any other answer that is not a 2xx is could-not-check for that page. A collection the token may not read, one with published items and no pattern, and an item whose slug the pattern cannot use are could-not-check by name and are not asked. Ids, slugs and statuses only: no field is used for this.
done: Every published item of the collections you named has a page that answers on the live site.
estimateChanges: A page that is gone for every item of a collection is one route or one address pattern in the front end. A single item is a slug that was changed or a page the front end does not build. A collection with no pages of its own always shows as could not check, which is expected.

title: A Directus collection marked private is readable by visitors with no token
what: gaugeline.adapters.json marks a collection private (privateCollections), and a plain GET of its items with no token is answered with items.
why: Anyone who guesses the route can read the collection as data: bookings, customer notes, prices before they are announced. A search engine or scraper may already have it.
fix: In Directus open Settings, then Access Policies, then the Public policy, and remove read access from the collection (or narrow it with a filter). If the front end needs the data, read it on the server with a token whose role is limited to what the page shows. If the collection is meant to be public, take it out of privateCollections.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: this check asks Directus for collections you marked private, as a visitor with no token, so it runs only with --owner-consent (or gaugeline.consent.json), on sites you own or have permission to test; only for the collections named in the settings' privateCollections; per collection one GET of /items/{collection}?limit=1&fields=id&meta=filter_count with no Authorization header, no cookie and nothing the fetcher adds per address; a 200 with at least one item is the finding (its count is the reported filter_count, or "at least 1" when none is reported); a 200 with no items is could-not-check (the role may read it and there is nothing to count); a 401 or 403 is a closed collection only when its body is Directus's own error envelope (error code FORBIDDEN or INVALID_CREDENTIALS), otherwise it is could-not-check (a firewall or CDN page answers 403 too); a closed collection passes only when the token can read the same collection (a second request with the token, id only), because Directus also answers 403 for a collection that does not exist, and a Public policy that allows some fields but not id also answers 403 for fields=id, so a pass means no public read of id was seen, not that nothing is public; any other answer is could-not-check; the answer is read as a count and nothing else, and a finding is a collection name and a count, never an item
done: A visitor with no token cannot list a single item of any collection you marked private.
estimateChanges: Usually one change in Directus: open Settings, then Access Policies, then the Public policy, and remove read access from the collection. Allow longer if the front end reads that collection with no token and needs a server-side token instead.

title: A Drupal node that is not published can be opened by a visitor
what: A node is saved in Drupal and not published, and its own page at /node/ID answers a visitor with a page instead of Drupal's access denied.
why: Unpublished work is meant to be private: a staff change not announced yet, a price list for next year, a notice that was pulled. If a visitor can open it, so can anyone who guesses the number, and a search engine may already have it.
fix: In Drupal open People, then Permissions, and check which roles can view unpublished content: Bypass content access control, or a permission from a contributed module such as View unpublished, especially for the Anonymous and Authenticated roles. Remove it from roles that should not have it, then clear the caches and check that a page cache or a CDN is not serving an old copy of the page.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: this check lists unpublished nodes with the credential you gave Gaugeline and asks the site for their pages as a visitor, so it runs only with --owner-consent (or gaugeline.consent.json) and a readUnpublished entry in gaugeline.adapters.json, and you should run it only on sites you own or have permission to test; per type named in the settings that is a node type, GETs of /jsonapi/node/BUNDLE with filter[status]=0, sort=id, page[limit] and page[offset] (up to 50 a page, the offset stepping by the page size asked, the next link read for the paging it states and never requested, and it must stay on the host and the path asked) and a sparse fieldset of status, drupal_internal__nid and path, with the credential in an Authorization header and nowhere else, never followed to a redirect and never sent over plain http; Drupal core reports no total, so the list is checked for a repeated id, a first page that differs when read again at the end, and a count when the site reports one (meta.count); a node listed with a status that is not false is could-not-check; at most 100 unpublished nodes are asked about per type (the rest are counted as not asked); then per node one GET of /node/NID on the Drupal address only, with no credential, no cookie and nothing the fetcher adds per address, redirects followed up to three times and only within the same host, at most 100 pages a run; an answer counts only when Drupal sent it (an X-Generator: Drupal header, or a Drupal generator meta tag), and when the final path is the node's path or its alias; a 403 or 404 that is Drupal's own is the node closed to a visitor; a 2xx that is Drupal's own is looked at once more with the credential (GET of the resource by its id, status only) and is the finding only when the node is still unpublished (a node published in between is could-not-check); anything else, a firewall's 403, a login page, a redirect elsewhere, a type that is not a node type, a list the credential cannot read, and a credential whose list is empty (its role may not view unpublished content), is could-not-check for that part, never a pass; a finding is a type, a node number and a status, never a title or a field
done: Every node you named that is not published answers a visitor with Drupal's own access denied.
estimateChanges: A few minutes when one node is open: check who may view unpublished content under Permissions, and whether a module or a custom access rule opens the node. Allow an hour when a module such as a content access or caching layer serves unpublished nodes to everyone.

title: A Payload collection marked private is readable by visitors with no key
what: gaugeline.adapters.json marks a collection private (privateCollections), and a plain GET of its list with no key is answered with documents.
why: Anyone who guesses the route can read the collection as data: orders, enquiries, customer notes, prices before they are announced. A search engine or scraper may already have it.
fix: In the collection's config, change access.read from a function that returns true to one that requires a signed-in user (it checks req.user), or narrow it with a query that returns only what is public. If the front end needs the data, read it on the server with the Local API. If the collection is meant to be public, take it out of privateCollections.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: this check asks Payload for collections you marked private, as a visitor with no key, so it runs only with --owner-consent (or gaugeline.consent.json), on sites you own or have permission to test; only for the collections named in the settings' privateCollections; per collection one GET of {PAYLOAD_URL}/{slug}?limit=1&page=1&depth=0&select[id]=true with no Authorization header, no cookie and nothing the fetcher adds per address, redirects not followed; a 200 whose body has a docs list with at least one document is the finding (its count is the reported totalDocs, or "at least 1" when none is reported); a 200 with no documents is could-not-check (a visitor may read it and there is nothing to count); a 403 is a closed collection only when its body is Payload's own refusal (errors[0].message is "You are not allowed to perform this action."), otherwise it is could-not-check (a firewall or CDN page answers 403 too, and a site in another language answers with a translated message); Payload looks a collection up before it looks at access, so a collection that does not exist is a 404 and is could-not-check with the spelling named, never closed; a pass means no public read of the list was seen, not that nothing is public (a collection can allow single documents by id, or other routes, and a closed list can still be open through GraphQL); any other answer is could-not-check; the answer is read as a count and nothing else, and a finding is a collection slug and a count, never a document
done: A visitor with no key cannot list a single document of any collection you marked private.
estimateChanges: Usually one change in the collection's config: replace a read rule that returns true with one that needs a signed-in user. Allow longer if the front end reads that collection with no key and needs a server-side read first.

title: A Kontent.ai item that is not published has a live page
what: An item is in Kontent.ai in a workflow step other than Published (a draft, in review, scheduled or archived) and has no published version, and the address its page should have answers on the live site.
why: Unpublished work is meant to be private: a price not announced yet, a closure notice, a page that was pulled. If the live site builds pages from the Preview API, anyone who guesses or is sent the address can read it, and search engines can find it.
fix: Make the live site read the Delivery API only: in the front end's data fetching use the Delivery API (with the secure access key if the project needs one) and keep the Preview API for a preview site behind a login. Then rebuild or revalidate the pages so the unpublished page is gone.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: this check asks the Kontent.ai Preview API for unpublished items with the Preview API key you gave Gaugeline, so it runs only with --owner-consent (or gaugeline.consent.json) and a readPreview entry in gaugeline.adapters.json, and you should run it only on sites you own or have permission to test; run only on sites you own or have permission to test; one list of GETs of {environment id}/items on deliver.kontent.ai with the secure access key if there is one (Authorization: Bearer, never in the address), then the same list on preview-deliver.kontent.ai with the Preview API key (Authorization: Bearer, sent to that host only), each in pages of 100 ordered by system.codename with includeTotalCount, skip stepping by the number of items that came back, asking only the slug element, redirects not followed; a list that ends with another number of items than its total_count, repeats an item, echoes another skip or counts a page wrongly is could-not-check; the ids of the Delivery list are held in a Set and the Preview list is filtered against it; a Preview list that lacks an item the Delivery list has is not the Preview list and is could-not-check; an item in the Preview list only whose workflow step is published, or is not a plain codename, is most likely published a moment ago and is never reported (it is counted and named as could-not-check); when something is left the Delivery list is read once more and a list that changed in between is could-not-check; HTTP 401 or 403 from the Preview API is the Preview key refused, which says nothing about unpublished items, so it is could-not-check, never a pass; an unpublished item's address comes from the urls pattern for its type and its slug (an item with no pattern or no slug, or with the same slug as a published item of its type, is could-not-check for that item), then one GET of that page on the checked site's own host only, redirects followed, at most 40 pages a run (the rest are could-not-check); a final 2xx answer is the finding, 404 or 410 is a pass for that item, a page reached through a redirect to another path, and any other answer, is could-not-check for that page; the Delivery API lists the default language, so an item published only in another language is not seen; the finding shows the type, the item's slug or id, its workflow step, the path and the status, never an element
done: Every Kontent.ai item that is not in the Published workflow step, in the types you gave an address for, has no page on the live site.
estimateChanges: A few minutes when it is one page: remove it from the front end, or find the route that builds pages from the Preview API. Allow an hour when the front end reads the Preview API everywhere and needs the Delivery API for the live build.

title: A page published in HubSpot answers 404 on the live domain
what: HubSpot says a site page, landing page or blog post is published on this domain, and the address it gives for it answers 404 or 410 on the live site.
why: Links, the sitemap, search results and the client's announcement point at a page that is not there, while the CMS shows it as live.
fix: In HubSpot, open the page and check its domain, its URL and that it is published to this domain and not only to a staging one; republish it if it was cloned or moved. If it should not be public, unpublish it.
tech: GET /cms/v3/pages/site-pages, /cms/v3/pages/landing-pages and /cms/v3/blogs/posts (each page of each list, stepped by the cursor the answer gives), keeping the pages whose state is PUBLISHED and whose own url is on the domain being checked (a page on another domain of the same portal is counted and not asked), then one anonymous GET of that address (redirects followed). A final 404 or 410 is the finding; any other answer that is not a 2xx is could-not-check for that page. A page with no usable https address is could-not-check. Ids, slugs and statuses only: no field is read for this.
done: Every page HubSpot says is published on this domain answers on the live site.
estimateChanges: A page that is gone for a whole list is a domain, a language or a URL setting in HubSpot. A single page is usually a slug that was changed after publishing or a page a redirect rule swallows. Pages HubSpot serves on another domain of the same account are not counted.

title: A page embeds a HubSpot form that has been deleted
what: A page on the live site embeds a HubSpot form by its id, and HubSpot answers that the form does not exist in this portal.
why: The form shows nothing or an error, so enquiries and orders sent through it are lost without anyone seeing a failure.
fix: Restore the form in HubSpot (Marketing, Forms, recently deleted), or edit the page or its template to embed a form that exists.
tech: The form ids and portal ids are read as text from the HTML of the published pages already asked for (data-form-id and portalId/formId in an hbspt.forms.create call; nothing is run); only forms of the portal the token belongs to (GET /account-info/v3/details) are asked about, one GET /marketing/v3/forms/{formId} for each different form (at most 50 a run); a 404, or a form marked archived, is the finding. A token without the forms scope, a page that names no portal or more than one, and a form of another portal are could-not-check or not counted, never a pass. Form ids and page paths only.
done: Every HubSpot form a page embeds still exists in the portal.
estimateChanges: Minutes to point the embed at the form that replaced the deleted one, or to restore it from HubSpot's recently deleted forms. Longer when the page's template holds the form id in several places.

title: A published page links to the editors' side of Adobe Experience Manager
what: The live page links to Adobe Experience Manager's author tier: an author host, or the editor, the CRX or the libraries path on the site itself.
why: Visitors land on a login screen or an error, and the link tells anyone where the editors' tier is and that the site runs Adobe Experience Manager. Editors who paste an address from their own browser into a page are the usual cause.
fix: Change each link to the page's public address on the publish host. In the page's component, use a link field that stores the content path and let the site's link rewriting build the public address, instead of pasting the editor's address.
tech: a[href] on the page whose host is author.{domain} or author-p{n}-e{n}.adobeaemcloud.com (any path), or whose path on the page's own host starts /editor.html, /crx/ or /libs/, or is /ui with a #/aem fragment (adapters/shared/aem-author.ts). Only the links the page already serves are read; nothing else is requested. Evidence shows host and path, never a query string.
done: No link on the page points at the author tier or an editors' path.
estimateChanges: One pasted link is one edit. Many means a component that stores the editor's address instead of a content path, which is one fix in the component and a re-publish of the pages that use it.

title: Your page signals to AI crawlers differ from what you said you want
what: You said what AI crawlers should be able to do (aiCrawlers in gaugeline.ai.json). The page sends a header or a meta tag that keeps a crawler you want away (noai, or noindex for one named crawler), or you want none of them and the site still publishes llms.txt, a guide written for AI assistants.
why: robots.txt is only one place to say it. A header from a CDN rule or a meta tag from a theme can quietly shut out the assistants you want to be found by, and a published llms.txt invites the ones you said to keep out.
fix: Remove the header or meta tag that blocks a crawler you want, or change aiCrawlers in gaugeline.ai.json if the signal is right and the intent changed. If you want no AI crawler on the site, remove llms.txt.
tech: Only with an aiCrawlers intent in gaugeline.ai.json. Reads the page's X-Robots-Tag header (read to 4,096 characters) and its meta tags named robots or for a known AI crawler (packages/core/src/data/ai-agents.json); a directive counts only from a fixed list. noai and noimageai count against the training crawlers (or the one named); noindex and none count against a crawler named in the header or in a crawler's own meta tag; a general noindex is the noindex check's. A signal that agrees with the intent is fine, and one that fails to block a crawler you want blocked is left to ai-crawlers-intent, which reads robots.txt. With the intent block, /llms.txt (read by the run, found with a 2xx plain-text answer) is a finding, once per site. noai and the Crawler: directive form are conventions from memory (uncited). No request is made; page text is never printed
done: The page's headers and meta tags, and llms.txt, say about AI crawlers what gaugeline.ai.json says you want.
estimateChanges: A header set by a CDN rule, a framework config or a plugin is found by looking at each; a meta tag from a theme is one template edit.

title: Your robots.txt does not do what you said you want for AI crawlers
what: You said what AI crawlers should be able to do (aiCrawlers in gaugeline.ai.json), and robots.txt does the opposite for one or more known crawlers. Gaugeline names them and says whether a rule names them or the rule for every crawler decides.
why: A rule copied from a staging site, or a plugin's default, can shut assistants out of a site that wants to be found by them, or let training crawlers in when you meant to keep them out.
fix: Edit robots.txt so each crawler listed gets the group you want, or change aiCrawlers in gaugeline.ai.json if the rules are right and the intent changed.
tech: for each known AI user-agent token (packages/core/src/data/ai-agents.json), isAllowed(robots.txt, token, /) differs from the aiCrawlers intent for its purpose; no robots.txt means every crawler is allowed
done: robots.txt does for each known AI crawler what gaugeline.ai.json says you want.
estimateChanges: A rule set in a firewall or a CDN rather than robots.txt is found by looking at those settings.

title: Visitors can type to an AI service and the page does not say so
what: What a visitor types into a form, a chat box or an assistant on this page goes to an AI service run by another company, and nothing on the page says that an AI or a bot is answering. Gaugeline names where the input goes and says it found no such words.
why: People type different things to a person and to a machine, and many will want to know who else sees it. Whether a notice is required where a business operates is a question for the client and their own counsel; Gaugeline does not say. Telling visitors is cheap and is what most of them would expect.
fix: Say it in plain words next to the box or in its placeholder, for example "Answers here come from an AI assistant and may be wrong", and check the privacy notice mentions that what visitors type is sent to the AI provider.
tech: Three kinds of flow, from the page's own HTML and scripts: a form whose action is the API host of a model provider (a fixed list of 15 hosts in packages/core/src/ai-disclosure/flows.ts); an AI assistant widget from the vendors table of ai-widget-inventory (those marked ai); and a script (inline, or one of up to 15 same-site script files) that writes a provider's host as an address while the page has a textarea or a text input. A disclosure is any of a fixed list of phrases (AI, artificial intelligence, chatbot, virtual or automated assistant, language model, generated by an AI, powered by a named model, bot) in the page's visible text, a placeholder, an aria-label, a title or an image alt; text in scripts, styles, templates and comments is not read. A page with a flow and none of the phrases is one medium finding naming the hosts and widgets, never page text, a field or a query. A flow built at run time from parts of an address, one on another page, or one inside a widget's own frame is not seen. The hosts are from memory (uncited). No request is made
done: Wherever a visitor can type to an AI, the page says in plain words that an AI answers, near the box or in its label.
estimateChanges: One sentence next to the box or in its placeholder. Deciding what it should say, and whether the privacy notice needs a line, is a conversation with the client and their own counsel.

title: A chat or AI widget loads on your page that you have not listed
what: A chat or AI assistant widget from another company loads on the page, and it is not on the allowed list in gaugeline.ai.json (or you have no list yet). Gaugeline names each one and where it loads from.
why: What a visitor types into a widget goes to its company, and many sites have a widget nobody remembers adding: a trial left on, a plugin's default, an assistant a salesperson turned on. The owner should know which ones are there.
fix: For each one, find who added it (a plugin, the tag manager, a theme setting). Remove the ones you do not want. Put the ones you do want in aiWidgets.allowed in gaugeline.ai.json, by name or by host, and the finding goes.
tech: Script and iframe addresses and inline scripts in the page's HTML (the first 16,384 characters of each inline script) matched against a fixed table of 23 vendors (packages/core/src/ai-widgets/vendors.ts), once per vendor; a host matches itself and its subdomains, never a look-alike; page text and comments are never read as a widget. With aiWidgets.allowed in gaugeline.ai.json, one medium finding lists the widgets not on it (an entry is a vendor id or a host or a parent of it; an empty list allows none); with no list, one low finding lists what loads. A widget a script adds after the page loads, and a widget loaded by a tag manager container, are not seen; vendor hosts are from memory (uncited). No request is made.
done: Every chat or AI widget on the page is one you chose, and each is in the aiWidgets list in gaugeline.ai.json.
estimateChanges: Finding who added a widget (a plugin, the tag manager, a theme setting) is the work; adding a name to the list takes a minute. A widget loaded by the tag manager has to be found there.

title: An Angular error is served as a normal page
what: A page of this Angular or Analog site answers 200 OK but its text contains an Angular error code, an injector error, a browser-only ReferenceError or a stack trace through @angular.
why: Search engines index a page that answers 200, error text included, and visitors see a broken page that no monitor flags. The stack trace also shows how the server is built.
fix: Find the server-side failure (code that uses window, document or localStorage must run only in the browser) and make the render error answer 500, or the 404 route answer 404, instead of returning the error as the page.
tech: Angular sites only, no extra request: when the final response is 200, the page's text outside script and style elements is searched for NG0xxx: messages, NullInjectorError or R3InjectorError, a ReferenceError for window, document, localStorage, sessionStorage or navigator, and indented stack frames through node_modules/@angular/
done: A failed render answers 500, and the page carries no error code or stack trace.
estimateChanges: The server-only failure needs finding first (browser-only code run on the server is the usual one); the status handling is a small change.

title: The iPhone app banner promotes a different app
what: The page's Smart App Banner (the apple-itunes-app meta tag) names a different app id than the page's App Store link.
why: Safari shows the banner at the top of the page on iPhone, so visitors install whichever app it names, which here is not the one the page links to.
fix: Set app-id in the apple-itunes-app meta tag to the same id as the App Store link.
tech: <meta name="apple-itunes-app" content="app-id=..."> differs from every apps.apple.com/.../id<digits> link on the page
done: The iPhone banner's app-id is the same as the id in the App Store link.
estimateChanges: The banner set in more than one template is one edit each.

title: A live page embeds a content entry marked as a draft
what: An island on this Astro page is handed data with a field named draft set to true: an entry the author marked as not ready.
why: Draft entries are meant to be hidden. When a page or island still receives one, its unfinished text is in the HTML for anyone to read.
fix: Filter drafts out where you read the collection (for example `getCollection('posts', ({ data }) => !data.draft)`), and build the island's props from that filtered list only.
tech: Astro sites only, no extra request: astro-island props in the HTML, a boolean field named draft or isDraft that is true; Astro has no built-in draft field, so this reads the common schema convention. The evidence gives the island and field name, never a value
done: No live page carries an entry whose draft flag is on.
estimateChanges: Filtering drafts in one shared helper fixes every page; filtering page by page takes longer.

title: Nothing on the page can be linked to buy
what: A page shows a price and a buy button, but no button is a link with an address or a submit button in a form with an action.
why: Nobody can share a link to the purchase, search engines see no offer, and if the script fails the page is a brochure.
fix: Make the buy button a link to your checkout or payment link, or a submit button in a form that posts to your cart, and let the script improve it from there.
tech: a price (a currency next to a number in the visible text, or an Offer price in the structured data) and at least one button or link whose text matches buy, add to cart, checkout, get it, purchase or download now; none is an a[href] with an address (not empty, #, javascript:, mailto: or tel:) or a submit button in a form with an action or its own formaction; a link to a hosted payment page (Stripe, Square, PayPal.me) anywhere on the page is a pass; the page is read as sent, so a button drawn by a script is not seen
done: The page has a real link or a form that posts to checkout, and the script only improves it.
estimateChanges: A buy button built entirely by a script means rebuilding that button, and each product page that uses it.

title: A promotion or notice on the page has a date that has already passed
what: Visible text such as "Happy hour through Oct 31", "Summer 2025 menu" or "Closed until Jan 3" names a date that is already in the past.
why: Guests plan around what the page says. A special that ended months ago, or a closure notice left up in spring, makes the business look unattended and sends people to something that is no longer there.
fix: Update or remove the text. For something that repeats each year, change the date; for a banner that should end on its own, give it an end date in the CMS.
tech: Visible text only (no script, style, noscript, template, hidden element, comment or attribute such as alt). A date is flagged when it is more than graceDays (1) before today in the venue's time zone and sits after an end word (through, until, ends, last day, hasta, jusqu'au and similar) or ends a range, or has a year and a promotional word within 40 characters (offer, special, menu, season, closed, holiday, hiring, sale, tickets...). A month and day with no year is read as the nearest occurrence, a season as the end of its last month. Never flagged: since, established or founded dates, pages whose structured data or og:type says article or news (or whose path is under historic in gaugeline.stale-dates.json), and a published or modified <time>. Words in packages/core/src/data/stale-dates.json; a page cut at the size limit is could not check
done: Every promotion, season and notice on the page is current, or has been taken down, and Gaugeline finds no date that has passed beside one.
estimateChanges: Text typed into a page is edited in minutes. Text spread over many pages, or in a theme or a template, takes longer, and a banner with an end date built in fixes itself.

title: A form sends fields the CRM doesn't have
what: A Web-to-Lead form on the page submits field names that are not fields on the Lead object in Salesforce.
why: Salesforce drops what it can't place. The visitor typed it, the form said thanks, and the CRM never got it.
fix: Add the field to Lead in Salesforce and use its name in the form, or remove the input from the form.
tech: The names of every input, select and textarea in each Web-to-Lead form in the HTML (hidden or visible; buttons and files excluded) against the field names and labels of Lead from Salesforce's read-only MCP server (getObjectSchema); Web-to-Lead's own names (first_name, zip, lead_source) are matched to their Lead fields; routing, anti-spam and utm_* names are skipped; custom fields sent by id (00N...) can't be compared and are counted; a form in an iframe or drawn by script is could-not-check
done: Every form field the CRM did not know now exists there, or the input is removed from the form.
estimateChanges: New fields in the CRM need someone with admin rights, and each form that sends them needs the same name.

title: Tracking starts after the form loads
what: The service's tracking code comes after its form in the page, or waits for the page to finish loading while the form is an iframe that loads first.
why: Salesforce documents that this can lose first-touch tracking, the referring site and UTM parameters.
fix: Load the tracking script directly in the page head, before the form, not from a window load handler.
tech: Position of the tracking script after the form in document order (counted over every form, iframe and script element), or inline tracking code started by addEventListener("load"), attachEvent("onload") or window.onload while the form is an iframe; no timing is measured, and code a tag manager moves at run time is not seen
done: The tracking script loads in the page head before the form.
estimateChanges: A tag manager that fires it late is a rule change, not a code change.

title: New leads are arriving without a source
what: Many of the leads created in your CRM since the last run have an empty lead source or campaign field.
why: A lead with no source can't be tied to the ad, email or search that brought it, so the campaign that worked looks the same as the one that didn't.
fix: Make the form send the source: add hidden utm_source and utm_campaign fields, map them to the CRM's lead source or campaign field, and fill the existing records that have none.
tech: Through Salesforce's read-only MCP server (soqlQuery on Lead, newest 200 created since the last run or windowDays ago): leads whose LeadSource, or each field named in sourceFields in gaugeline.crm.json, is null or blank; flagged at 2 or more leads and 10% or more of the sample; evidence is the counts, the field names and up to five record ids, never a name or an email
done: New leads arrive with a source and campaign, and the older records are filled in.
estimateChanges: Several forms each need the hidden fields. Filling in old records is a separate data job.

title: A form has nowhere to put campaign details
what: A form posts leads straight to Pardot, Web-to-Lead, HubSpot or Marketo with no hidden campaign fields.
why: Every lead arrives with its campaign, source and ad click blank.
fix: Add hidden utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign and gclid fields, fill them from the address, and map them in the form handler.
tech: A form element posting to Pardot, Web-to-Lead, HubSpot or Marketo with no hidden input named utm_*, gclid, a lead source or that service's default mapped field; a visible input does not count; an iframe is another document and is could-not-check
done: The form has hidden utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign and gclid fields, filled from the address and mapped in the handler.
estimateChanges: Several forms and a handler that needs a code change each add to it.

title: The page is behind the data it is built from
what: The source (your database or CMS) has newer data than the page shows, or a figure on the page differs from the same figure in the source.
why: The sync works but the visitor does not see it: a cache or a revalidation setting is serving an old copy, so fixing the sync would change nothing.
fix: Look at how the page is rebuilt after the data changes: its revalidate time, an on-demand revalidation that the sync should call, or a CDN that keeps the old copy. The evidence shows the Age header when a cache served it.
tech: for each rule with a source and maxLag in gaugeline.freshness.json, the newest time is read from the source (a one-row query or a Sanity field) and compared with the page's stamp: reported only when the page is older than the source by more than maxLag at every instant the stamp could mean; for each spot check (up to five per rule) the figure at the selector is compared with the source's figure for the page (a one-row query, or the row whose key column is the last part of the page's address) with exact decimal arithmetic and the tolerance given (an amount or a percentage of the source's figure); an unreadable source, stamp or figure is could not check; the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page
done: The page is rebuilt soon after its data changes.
estimateChanges: An on-demand revalidation call from the sync, a revalidate time and a CDN each need different work.

title: A PDF menu or price list and the site list different items
what: An item is on the site but not in the linked PDF, or the PDF still lists an item the site no longer has.
why: A dish removed from the site that is still on the printed menu is one you get asked for. A new one missing from the PDF is one nobody orders from it.
fix: Update the PDF or the site so both list the same items, or remove the PDF link until the PDF is current.
tech: same reading and matching as document-price-mismatch (normalised names, '&' and 'and' alike); items the site's structured sources name that the PDF does not, and PDF items found nowhere on the site; the second list is reported only when the two are shown to be the same menu (a structured source names one of the PDF's items, or the pages carry at least half of them), so a page listing a few dishes does not make every dish missing; both lists name at most five items and count the rest
done: The PDF and the site list the same items.
estimateChanges: Add or remove the items in the PDF or on the site so the two lists match.

title: Your domain has no DMARC policy
what: There is no DMARC record at _dmarc.<your domain>, so receiving servers have no instruction for mail that fails SPF or DKIM.
why: Mail pretending to be from you is delivered like any other, and large mail providers increasingly expect a DMARC record from anyone who sends.
fix: Add a TXT record at _dmarc.<your domain>: start with v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:<an address you read>, then move to quarantine once the reports look right.
tech: Public DNS only: no TXT record starting v=DMARC1 at _dmarc.<host without www.>. The host is read as given; a parent domain's policy is not looked up
done: A TXT record at _dmarc names a policy and an address you read.
estimateChanges: The address that receives reports has to exist and be watched, which is the ongoing cost.

title: Your domain has two SPF records, which cancels both
what: Two or more TXT records at the domain start with v=spf1.
why: Receiving mail servers treat more than one SPF record as an error and ignore all of them, so your mail is checked as if you had none.
fix: Merge them into one record: one v=spf1, every include from both, one -all or ~all at the end.
tech: Public DNS only: the domain has MX records (not a null MX) and two or more TXT records start with v=spf1 (RFC 7208 §4.5: a permerror)
done: The domain has one SPF record that holds every include from both.
estimateChanges: Each service in the two records has to be checked before the merge.

title: An event at your venue lists a different address
what: An event the page says is at the venue (by the venue's name or id) gives a different street address than the venue's own structured data.
why: Maps and search results send guests to the event's address, so a stale one sends them to the wrong door.
fix: Use the venue's own address in each event's location, ideally by referring to the venue's @id instead of repeating it.
tech: Event location names the LocalBusiness (same name or @id) and its address differs by house number or ZIP
done: Each event lists the venue's own address, ideally by the venue's @id.
estimateChanges: Events entered by hand are edited one by one. One venue record referenced by all of them needs a template change.

title: A click your tracking plan expects isn't reported
what: An element in gaugeline.events.json sends no event when clicked, sends it twice, or sends it without a parameter the plan requires.
why: Tracking breaks quietly when templates change: the report for that menu or button just goes empty, and before-and-after comparisons stop meaning anything.
fix: Restore the click handler or tag for that element, and fill every parameter the plan names (for a menu: link text, destination and parent menu).
tech: Each element a plan line selects (a CSS selector, or every link in nav, header, footer or main; at most 20) is clicked in the rendered page with analytics requests intercepted and never delivered, and dataLayer pushes are read for 1500 ms. One push with the event name and every listed parameter filled passes. Needs a rendered read (G39): until then it is could not check
done: The click handler or tag fires for that element with every parameter the plan names.
estimateChanges: The element may have been rebuilt, and the tag manager and the code both need checking.

title: A tracked link reports differently on a phone than on a desktop
what: A link your tracking plan lists sends its event at one screen width and not the other, sends a different event name, sends it twice, or fills a parameter at one width and leaves it empty at the other.
why: Many visitors are on a phone. When the phone menu is a separate template, its links often lose the handler or send another name, and the report counts only the desktop: a before-and-after comparison of a new menu then measures the wrong people.
fix: Make the phone menu send the same event as the desktop menu: the same handler or tag on both templates, with the same parameters filled.
tech: Each link the plan lists is clicked once at 1280 px and once at 375 px in the browser you installed (links only, analytics requests recorded and never delivered; the same observation as events-fire). For each link the plan's event is compared between the two widths: sent or not within 1500 ms, the event name another link-click event was sent under, how many times, whether each parameter the plan lists is filled (compared by kind: text, number, true or false, empty; never by exact text), and which other parameters one width sends and the other does not. A link silent at both widths is events-fire's. A link that could not be clicked at either width is could not check. Needs --renderer playwright: without it, or if the page cannot be loaded at 375 px, it is could not check
done: Every tracked link sends the same event, with the same parameters filled, on a phone as on a desktop.
estimateChanges: Usually one handler in the mobile menu component, or one tag condition that only matches on a wide screen.

title: A tracked link is hard to reach with the keyboard
what: A link your tracking plan lists is never reached when you press Tab, takes focus in a different place than it comes in the page, or carries a positive tabindex (1 or more), which moves it ahead of every link that has none.
why: Someone who cannot use a mouse moves through the page with the Tab key. A link they cannot reach cannot be used and cannot be tracked, and a link that jumps the queue makes the page's order surprising; a positive tabindex is the usual cause.
fix: Take the positive tabindex off (use no tabindex, or tabindex=0 to make a custom element focusable), keep the links in the order you want them read, and do not remove a link from the Tab order with tabindex=-1 unless something else gives the same action.
tech: The links the plan lists (at most 20) are read in two ways. First, a tabindex of 1 or more on a listed element, read from the HTML as sent (a tabindex a script adds later is not seen here). Second, in the browser you installed at 1280 px, the Tab key is pressed from the top of the page (at most 200 times; nothing else is typed) and the order the listed links take focus in is read: a link never reached is listed, and so is a link whose place in that order differs from its place in the page's HTML (only the links that moved, by the longest run of links that stay in order). The order of the page's HTML stands for the visual order; a layout that moves a link on the screen is not read. A link that could not be clicked at 1280 px, or a keyboard read that could not be made, is could not check. The second part needs --renderer playwright
done: Every tracked link can be reached with the Tab key, in the order it comes in the page, with no positive tabindex.
estimateChanges: Removing a tabindex or restoring a link's place in the page is a one-line edit in the menu component.

title: A page is missing a fact it should show
what: A fact you declared must appear on a page (mustAppearOn) is not in that page's HTML as it is sent.
why: The page visitors use to decide (the order page, the contact page) leaves out the thing they came for, or shows it only after JavaScript runs, which search engines and assistants may not.
fix: Put the fact in the page's server-rendered HTML. A fact in an image's description only is not visible text: write it out.
tech: for each mustAppearOn path among the pages checked, the fact's declared value is in the visible text, a link or JSON-LD of the HTML as sent (image descriptions don't count, and say so)
done: The fact appears as visible text in the page's server-rendered HTML.
estimateChanges: A fact that only lives in an image needs the text written out, one page at a time.

title: Two of your feeds serve the same posts
what: Two feeds the page advertises list exactly the same item links.
why: Subscribers to one feed get the other's posts (a news feed serving the blog, say), and readers who follow both see everything twice.
fix: Point each feed at its own collection, usually a query or category filter that was copied from the other.
tech: The advertised feeds read for feed-broken (at most 3), compared as Sets of normalised item links: equal and non-empty, in any order. Sharing most items is not a duplicate
done: Each feed serves its own collection.
estimateChanges: A filter copied between feeds is one edit each.

title: The feed this page advertises is not a feed
what: The advertised feed address answers, but with something that is not RSS or Atom, often an HTML page.
why: Feed readers cannot read it, so subscribers get nothing. A framework's catch-all route is the usual cause.
fix: Serve the feed's XML at that address, or point the link rel="alternate" tag at the address that does.
tech: the feed body does not start with an XML declaration, <rss> or <feed>
done: The feed address serves a feed, or the page's link points at the one that does.
estimateChanges: A feed made by a plugin that errors takes longer than correcting a link.

title: The feed this page advertises is too large
what: The feed response is larger than 2 MB.
why: Feed readers and aggregators time out or truncate large feeds, and frameworks such as Next.js do not cache responses over 2 MB, so every request rebuilds it.
fix: Limit the feed to recent items (20 to 50 is typical) and put a summary in each item instead of the full post.
tech: the feed response is larger than 2 MB (2,097,152 bytes)
done: The feed holds recent items only, with a summary in each.
estimateChanges: A feed generated by a plugin may expose no setting for this.

title: The page still shows a prediction for something that already happened
what: A page lists a prediction, a pick or a preview whose event date is already past, and it does not show the result.
why: A prediction for a finished game or a past night looks careless at best, and misleads at worst: visitors act on it and the page loses their trust the next time.
fix: Remove the item or switch it to the result when the event ends. Generate the list from the schedule so an event leaves it by itself, and rebuild or revalidate the page after the result is in.
tech: for each rule with a forecast in gaugeline.freshness.json that is active, each item matching forecast.item (up to 200 per page) has its date read from forecast.date inside it, its own datetime or named attribute, or a time element with a datetime inside it, or the page's Event structured data with the property named in forecast.jsonld; the event is past when it is past at every instant the date could mean (a date alone is over when the whole day is, in the site's time zone; a time is over after forecast.lasts, 3h by default); an item that contains forecast.settled already shows its result and is skipped; no items, a date that cannot be read or an item with no date is could not check; the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page
done: Items for events that already happened are gone from the list, or show their result.
estimateChanges: A list built by hand is edited by hand. One built from the schedule fixes itself but needs code, and a cache needs purging.

title: A form now posts to a different address
what: A form still uses the same service, but posts to a different host than last run.
why: A different host can mean a different account or region with the same service, so entries may land where nobody reads them.
fix: Confirm the new address belongs to your account with that service.
tech: With --since last only: the same form key and provider, with a different action host
done: The form posts to an address that belongs to your account with that service.
estimateChanges: If the change was not yours, finding who changed it comes first.

title: Anyone can read the schema of your WordPress GraphQL API
what: The GraphQL endpoint behind this headless WordPress site answers an introspection query with its schema to a visitor who is not logged in.
why: WPGraphQL turns public introspection off by default, so someone turned it on. The schema lists every post type, custom field and relation, including ones the site never shows, and tells a stranger exactly what to ask for.
fix: In WordPress, open GraphQL, then Settings, and turn off public introspection (leave it on for logged-in users and local development). If a build tool needs the schema, save a copy in the repository instead.
tech: Probing check: off unless --owner-consent or gaugeline.consent.json; run only on sites you own or have permission to test. Headless WordPress sites only (a front end with WPGraphQL state in its embedded data, or Next.js serving /wp-content/uploads/). One GET of /graphql on the site, and of the back end its images come from, with the query {__schema{queryType{name}}} in the address: the smallest query that says whether introspection is on. It is parsed with the GraphQL parser and refused unless it is one query; never a mutation, never a full schema, never a POST. An answer holding __schema.queryType.name is a finding (only the root type name is shown); an errors answer means introspection is off. An endpoint that answers a GET with an error status, or not in JSON, is could not check (a POST-only endpoint is). The setting's name and default are from the WPGraphQL security documentation, as quoted in a search result: its exact label was not confirmed (uncited)
done: The WordPress GraphQL endpoint refuses an introspection query from a visitor who is not logged in.
estimateChanges: One setting in WPGraphQL; a tool that reads the schema (a code generator) then needs a logged-in request or a copy of the schema.

title: A language version doesn't link back
what: This page's hreflang points at a version in another language, but that version's hreflang doesn't point back.
why: Search engines ignore hreflang pairs that aren't confirmed from both sides, so searchers may get the wrong language.
fix: Give every version the same full set of hreflang links, including one to itself.
tech: page A has <link rel=alternate hreflang> to B, and B (fetched) has none to A (a trailing slash is not a difference)
done: Every language version carries the same full set of hreflang links, including one to itself.
estimateChanges: The number of language versions and whether the links come from one component.

title: Most of this page's HTML is a data payload
what: More than half of the HTML, and over 300 KB, is inline data (JSON, __NEXT_DATA__ or a framework's streamed payload) rather than content.
why: Every visitor downloads data the page may never show, and it delays the first paint on phones.
fix: Send only the fields the page renders. In Next.js, trim what getServerSideProps or a server component passes to client components.
tech: inline data scripts are over 300 KB (307,200 bytes) and more than half the HTML; not reported when html-huge is
done: The page sends only the fields it renders.
estimateChanges: A framework data payload shared by many pages is trimmed in one place. Pages that pass whole records to the browser need one edit each.

title: Your calendar names a time zone it doesn't describe
what: Events in your .ics calendar use a TZID, but the file has no VTIMEZONE section for it.
why: The iCalendar standard requires the description. Some calendar apps fall back to UTC or the guest's zone without it, and show the wrong hour.
fix: Export the calendar with time zone definitions included, or add a VTIMEZONE for each TZID the events use.
tech: a DTSTART or DTEND TZID has no matching VTIMEZONE component (RFC 5545 §3.6.5)
done: The calendar carries a VTIMEZONE for each TZID its events use.
estimateChanges: Software with no export option for this needs a different export.

title: An image allowlist expression is not anchored
what: A Netlify remote_images expression in the settings you gave does not start with ^ and end with $, so it matches when the allowed address appears anywhere in the image address.
why: An address such as https://evil.example/?x=https://images.yourshop.example/ then passes the allowlist, and the Image CDN fetches it for anyone who asks.
fix: Anchor each expression and escape its dots: ^https://images\\.yourshop\\.example/.*$.
tech: Not a probing check: no request is made. Reads settingsFiles of gaugeline.images.json as text and reports each remote_images entry that lacks a leading ^ or a trailing $ (an entry that matches every address is image-optimizer-allowlist-wide). A statement about the file, not about the running site
done: Every remote_images expression in netlify.toml starts with a caret and ends with a dollar sign.
estimateChanges: One line per expression in netlify.toml.

title: Images are requested at an enormous width
what: An image is offered or requested 3840 pixels wide or more, wider than almost any screen shows it.
why: Phones and laptops may download a 4K-wide picture to show it a few hundred pixels across, which wastes data and slows the page.
fix: Cap the widths your image component generates (for Next.js, deviceSizes and imageSizes in next.config) and set the sizes attribute.
tech: a srcset candidate with a w descriptor, or a w= parameter, of 3840 or more
done: The image component generates widths up to a sensible cap and sets the sizes attribute.
estimateChanges: One shared image component is one edit. Hand-written srcsets are edited one by one.

title: None of the images on this page are described
what: The page has images, and not one has alt text that says what it shows.
why: Screen reader users hear nothing about any picture, and search engines have no words to index the images by.
fix: Give each meaningful image an alt that says what it shows. alt="" is right for decorative images, but a page where every image is decorative is rare.
tech: every img has a missing, empty or whitespace-only alt
done: Each meaningful image has an alt that says what it shows.
estimateChanges: Writing good descriptions takes time per image, and images inside CMS content are edited one by one.

title: Some images are very large files
what: An image on the page is over 500 KB.
why: Large images are the most common reason a page is slow on a phone, and a slow page loses visitors before it loads.
fix: Resize the image to the size it is shown at and export it as WebP or AVIF, or serve it through an image CDN or your framework's image component.
tech: a sampled image's Content-Length header is over 512,000 bytes; a server that sends no Content-Length gives no finding
done: The images are resized to the size they are shown at and served as WebP or AVIF.
estimateChanges: A site that serves originals needs an image component or CDN set up, then each image needs checking.

title: Images still load from an old WordPress site
what: Images on the page are served from /wp-content/uploads/, usually left over from a WordPress site the new site replaced.
why: When the old WordPress install or its host is switched off, every one of these images breaks at once.
fix: Move the images into the new site's own media library or asset folder and update the addresses.
tech: img src or srcset candidates under /wp-content/uploads/
done: The images live in the new site's own media library and no address points at the old site.
estimateChanges: The number of images, and links inside CMS content that still name the old address.

title: A language version of this page is missing
what: The page says (through hreflang, the sitemap or your language settings) that it has a version in another language, but that version returns an error or redirects to the homepage.
why: Visitors who switch language land on an error or on the homepage, and search engines drop the alternate from results.
fix: Publish the missing version, or remove it from the page's hreflang links and the sitemap. Pages meant to exist in one language only can be excluded in gaugeline.languages.json.
tech: an expected twin (hreflang, sitemap xhtml:link or the configured prefix, subdomain or parameter) answers 4xx or 5xx, or redirects to / or a language root; at most 5 versions are fetched
done: The missing language version is published, or removed from the hreflang links and the sitemap.
estimateChanges: Translating the page is the cost. Removing the link is minutes.

title: Some links go through a link shortener
what: Links leave the page through a shortener or redirector (bit.ly, t.co, lnkd.in, a /redirect?url= address) instead of linking directly.
why: Visitors can't see where the link goes before they click, the redirect adds a delay, and if the shortener expires or is blocked the link breaks.
fix: Link straight to the destination. Social icons in the footer are a common place for these.
tech: a[href] on bit.ly, t.co, lnkd.in, buff.ly, ow.ly, tinyurl.com, goo.gl, rebrand.ly, is.gd, cutt.ly, shorturl.at, tiny.cc (or a subdomain), or a /redirect, /out or /go path with a url= style parameter holding an http(s) address; footer links count too
done: Links go straight to their destination.
estimateChanges: Social icons in the footer are one edit. Wrapped links inside posts are one each.

title: A listing shows a different address
what: The street number or ZIP code on your Google, Yelp or Apple listing is not the one on your site.
why: Maps sends people to the address on the listing. After a move, or with a typo, guests arrive at the wrong door.
fix: Correct the address in the listing's own dashboard, or on the site if the listing is the right one.
tech: the house number and the 5-digit ZIP code are read from both addresses and each one both sides state must be equal; street names are not compared; the site's address is the text fact "address" in gaugeline.facts.json, else the LocalBusiness address in structured data
done: The listing and the site show the same address.
estimateChanges: Each listing is edited in its own dashboard, and an address change that needs verification can take days.

title: A listing doesn't know about a holiday closure
what: Your site announces a day you are closed, such as Thanksgiving or Christmas, and a listing still shows its normal hours for that day.
why: People check the listing on the day. If it says you open at 4 on a day you are shut, they come anyway.
fix: Add the closure to the listing's special hours in its own dashboard (Google Business Profile: Special hours; Yelp for Business: Holiday hours).
tech: closures on the site are dates in LocalBusiness openingHoursSpecification (validFrom and validThrough, opens and closes both 00:00) and dates or fixed US holidays within 40 characters of the word "closed" in the pages read, from today in the venue's time zone up to 60 days ahead; a listing is missing one when its special hours (Google Business Profile, Yelp) do not mark that date closed; sources that give no special hours (Google Maps, Apple) are reported as could not check
done: The holiday closure is in the listing's special hours.
estimateChanges: Each listing (Google, Yelp, Apple) is its own dashboard.

title: Your llms.txt sends assistants to pages that don't work
what: Links in /llms.txt return an error (4xx or 5xx) or redirect to a different site.
why: llms.txt is a short guide for AI assistants to your most useful pages. A dead or off-site link is the page they quote, or fail to.
fix: Update the links to the pages' current addresses, or remove the ones that no longer exist.
tech: links in /llms.txt answer 4xx or 5xx, or redirect off-site
done: Every link in llms.txt loads.
estimateChanges: A llms.txt generated by a plugin is fixed at the source.

title: Your llms.txt gives assistants an old phone number, address or hours
what: The phone number, street address or opening hours in /llms.txt disagree with the page's structured data.
why: Assistants quote llms.txt directly. An old number or old hours there is what someone hears when they ask if you're open tonight.
fix: Update llms.txt to match the structured data (or the other way round, whichever is wrong). Generate both from one source if you can.
tech: hours, telephone or address in /llms.txt differ from the page's LocalBusiness JSON-LD
done: llms.txt gives the same phone number, address and hours as the structured data.
estimateChanges: Generating both from one source removes the drift but needs a template change.

title: Some buttons open an email instead of a form
what: A contact button ("Talk to an expert", "Get a quote") opens one person's email program instead of a form.
why: The enquiry skips your CRM: it lands in one inbox with no campaign details, nobody else sees it, and visitors without an email program set up can't send it at all.
fix: Point the button at a form or a booking page that sends the enquiry to your CRM, and keep the email address as a plain fallback.
tech: a[href] starting mailto: with an address, whose text is a contact call to action (contact, talk, speak, get in touch, email us, book, quote, demo and similar) and not an address itself; one finding per page; the link's styling is not visible to Gaugeline
done: Each button opens a form or booking page whose enquiry reaches the CRM.
estimateChanges: A form and its CRM connection are built first if there is none, then each button is repointed.

title: A block that shows entries of a type is empty
what: A block on another page (an "insights" strip, a team row) is meant to show entries of a document type, shows none, and entries of that type are published.
why: Pages that embed a type break when it changes: a renamed field or a stricter filter empties the block, the page still loads, and it is a page nobody opened.
