fix: Compare the block's query with the type as it is now (renamed fields, a filter on a field older documents lack). If the block is meant to be empty for now, take it out of gaugeline.model.json.
tech: For each dependent in gaugeline.model.json: the page is read with GET and the entries are the selector's matches. With none, count(*[_type == T && (filter)]) over published documents (GET) says whether there is anything to show; a type with no published documents is not reported. With --since last and a block name, the evidence adds how many entries the saved run listed. A page that cannot be read is could not check
done: The block shows entries again, or is empty on purpose and listed as such.
estimateChanges: A renamed field in the query, a filter on a field older documents lack and a type that is now empty each fix differently.

title: Documents still hold a field the schema no longer has
what: Published documents have a value in a field that was removed from the schema: usually a leftover from before a rename, a merge or a clean-up.
why: The Studio no longer shows the field, so nobody can see or fix what is in it, but a query or a page may still read it, and the old value can be wrong or private.
fix: Decide for each field: if a page or query still needs it, put it back in the schema; if it moved to another field, copy the values across and then unset the old one with a one-off migration.
tech: GROQ cannot list the keys a document has without sending the document, which Gaugeline never does, so the fields looked for are named: the fields of the schema file in previousSchema that the current schema no longer has, and the fields under retired in gaugeline.model.json. For each, count(*[_type == T && defined(field)]) over published documents and the first three ids in id order (GET). A field the current schema still has is never reported. No value is requested or shown. Without a schema file, or with no field named, the check is could not check
done: Each field no longer in the schema is put back, copied across and removed, or left on purpose.
estimateChanges: The number of documents and fields. Unsetting values is a data migration that needs a backup first.

title: The menu changed since the last run
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, links in the header or footer menu were added, removed, moved to another parent, renamed or reordered.
why: A menu restructure changes many links at once and every page still loads, so nothing else reports the page that lost its only link.
fix: Check each change was meant. A removed link whose page now has no other link needs one, or a redirect if the page is gone.
tech: With --since last only. A link is its region, parent item and destination. Same destination under a new parent is moved; same identity with new text is renamed. A removed link whose destination has no inbound link from the pages read is high. On a first run (no saved menu yet): could not check
done: Each menu change since the last run was meant, and a page that lost its link has another or a redirect.
estimateChanges: The count of changes since the last run.

title: The footer isn't the same on every page
what: A page's footer links differ from the footer most of the pages read have, or a footer link gaugeline.nav.json marks as required (privacy, terms, contact) is missing.
why: A footer that differs on one template usually means that template was missed in a change; a missing privacy or terms link can be a legal problem.
fix: Use one footer for every template, and add any required link that is missing.
tech: With --since last or a gaugeline.nav.json (it reads the run's other pages). Footer destinations on the checked page and the run's other pages (4); the most common set is the reference. Required links match a footer link's text or path, case-insensitively
done: Every page shows the same footer with every required link.
estimateChanges: Templates that each carry their own footer are edited one by one.

title: Menu items go to the homepage
what: Links in the menu or header point at the homepage but are labelled as something else, such as Services or Contact.
why: Visitors who click Services land back on the homepage and think the page is missing. It usually means a menu item was added with no link.
fix: Point each menu item at its own page, or remove it until the page exists.
tech: a nav or header a[href] resolving to / whose text (or aria-label) is not Home or the site's name
done: Each menu item goes to its own page, or is removed until the page exists.
estimateChanges: Items whose pages are not built yet need those pages first.

title: Some menu links have no name
what: A link in the header or footer holds only an icon, an image with no alt text or nothing at all, and has no aria-label.
why: A screen reader reads it as just "link", so a visitor who cannot see the icon cannot tell the basket from the phone number, and voice control has no name to say.
fix: Add an aria-label that says where the link goes (aria-label="Basket"), or give its image alt text, or add text that only screen readers see.
tech: no request. a[href] inside the header (header, nav, [role=banner], or gaugeline.nav.json regions.header) or footer (footer, [role=contentinfo], or regions.footer) whose accessible name is empty after aria-labelledby, aria-label, the content (text, an image's alt, an svg title, a labelled descendant) and the title attribute; hidden and aria-hidden content adds nothing; whitespace, no-break space and zero-width characters are empty; CSS is not applied, so text hidden by a stylesheet counts as a name
done: Every link in the header and footer has text, an aria-label or an image with alt text that says where it goes.
estimateChanges: An icon link built from one shared component is one edit; links typed into a template are edited one by one.

title: Pages in the sitemap that no page links to
what: Addresses the sitemap lists that none of the pages read link to, in their menus, footers or text.
why: Visitors can only reach them from search or an old bookmark, and search engines treat a page nothing links to as unimportant.
fix: Link to each page from its section's menu or a related page, or take it out of the sitemap if it is gone.
tech: With --since last or a gaugeline.nav.json (it reads the run's other pages). Same-site sitemap addresses (one level of index) against every link on the checked page and the run's other pages (4); the checked page itself is excepted. A page linked only from a page not read is reported too: the evidence says how many were read
done: Each page in the sitemap has a link from its section or a related page, or is out of the sitemap.
estimateChanges: Many orphans from one section are one menu change.

title: The mobile menu is missing links the desktop menu has
what: The page has a separate mobile menu, and some destinations in the desktop header menu aren't in it.
why: Most visitors are on a phone: a page missing from the mobile menu is missing for them.
fix: Add the missing links to the mobile menu, or build both menus from one list.
tech: The separate mobile menu's destinations (gaugeline.nav.json regions.mobile, or a [data-mobile-menu], #mobile-menu or .mobile-menu element) against the header's. A menu toggle whose menu isn't in the HTML is could not check: it is built at a phone width, which needs a rendered read (not on yet)
done: The mobile menu has every link the desktop menu has.
estimateChanges: Two menus kept by hand are edited twice. One list feeding both needs a code change.

title: A menu link drops campaign tags
what: A link in the header or footer menu goes through a redirect that drops utm_source, utm_medium or utm_campaign.
why: A visit that arrives with campaign tags loses them at the redirect, so the report credits no campaign and the menu pages look like they bring nothing in.
fix: Make the redirect pass the query string on, or point the menu link at the address it ends at.
tech: header and footer a[href] of the checked page on the same site, each once (at most 40, header first; a longer menu is listed under could not check); one HEAD each (GET if HEAD answers 405 or 501) with utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign added after the link's own query, Gaugeline's own values and never a client's; the keys on the first address against the last, values compared after decoding, order ignored, the first redirect that drops a key named with its status. A final status of 4xx or 5xx is not judged here (broken-links does); 401, 403 and 429 are could-not-check; a script that rewrites the address is not seen
done: Every menu link arrives with the campaign tags it was asked with, or goes straight to the page.
estimateChanges: A redirect set in the host, a CDN and the app each need checking; a menu link that points at the final address needs no redirect at all.

title: The page still shows an old copy after an edit
what: With a content source connected, this Next.js page is still a cached copy made before its document last changed, more than 10 minutes after the change.
why: Editors publish a fix and visitors keep seeing the old version, so the fix looks broken.
fix: Revalidate the page when its document changes (an on-demand revalidation webhook from the CMS), or lower its revalidate time.
tech: Next.js sites with a content source (branch 30) only, otherwise unchecked: x-nextjs-cache or x-vercel-cache HIT or STALE with an Age header, the copy's age older than the document's last change, and the change more than 10 minutes ago. Without an Age header nothing is reported
done: An edit in the CMS shows on the live page without a redeploy.
estimateChanges: An on-demand revalidation webhook is set up in the CMS and the app. A revalidate time is one line but gives slower updates.

title: Pages that do not exist answer 200
what: An address that cannot exist on this site (made up from the site's own address) answers 200, or sends the visitor to another page that answers 200, instead of 404 or 410.
why: Google calls this a soft 404: every mistyped or deleted address looks like a real page, search engines spend visits on it and may index the empty result, and you never hear about dead links because nothing reports an error.
fix: Make the not-found route answer 404 (410 for pages removed on purpose). In Next.js use notFound() and a not-found page, in Nuxt createError with statusCode 404, in SvelteKit error(404), and on a host with a catch-all rewrite (a single-page app) add a 404 rule for unknown paths.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: one GET of /gaugeline-not-found-3f9c2a71 on the checked page's own origin, no cookie, no Authorization, no query, at most 4096 bytes of the answer read and never kept. A final status of 200 is a finding, also after a redirect (a redirect to the home page is the same soft 404); 404 and 410 pass; 401, 403, 429, 5xx and an unreachable site are could not check. The fetcher refuses private addresses unless --allow-private
done: The made-up address answers 404 or 410 and the page it shows says so.
estimateChanges: A framework's not-found route is one change. A host rewrite that sends every path to one file is a rule in the host's settings, and a single-page app may need a server answer for the first time.

title: A Nuxt data file is named as a page
what: The sitemap, the canonical address, og:url or an hreflang alternate of this Nuxt site names a framework file (a _payload.json, a /_nuxt/ build file or a /__nuxt_island/ component) as if it were a page.
why: Search engines then crawl and may index a JSON payload instead of the page, and the page's real address loses its signals.
fix: Keep payload and build addresses out of the sitemap (exclude _payload.json and /_nuxt/), and build the canonical from the page's route path, not from the address of the request that fetched its payload.
tech: Nuxt sites only: canonical, og:url, hreflang hrefs and sitemap entries whose path starts /_nuxt/, /__nuxt_island/ or /__nuxt_devtools__, or ends /_payload.json or /_payload.js. Read from the page and the sitemap already fetched; nothing extra is requested. Paths are compared as written, so a site under a base URL prefix is matched only on the suffix
done: The sitemap, the canonical and the language alternates name pages only, never a _payload.json or a /_nuxt/ file.
estimateChanges: A sitemap built by a module needs its exclude setting; a canonical built from the request path needs the payload suffix stripped.

title: A Nuxt page is cached in a way that will show old or other people's content
what: The HTML of this Nuxt page is told to be cached for a year or as immutable, or it sets a cookie while shared caches (a CDN) are allowed to keep it.
why: Edits to a page that caches for a year never reach visitors who already have it, and a CDN that keeps a response with a Set-Cookie hands one visitor's cookie to the next.
fix: In nuxt.config routeRules, give page routes a short time or swr/isr (for example '/**': { swr: 600 }) and keep long, immutable headers for /_nuxt/** files only. Do not set cookies on routes that are cached.
tech: Nuxt sites only, from the page's own response headers (nothing extra is requested): Cache-Control with immutable or a max-age or s-maxage of a year or more on an HTML page; or a Set-Cookie header together with public or s-maxage above 0 in Cache-Control and no Vary: Cookie, private or no-store. routeRules headers, swr and isr add these headers in Nuxt. Directives are held in a Map from name to number
done: A page's cache header says it may be kept briefly (or revalidated), and a page that sets a cookie is not kept by shared caches.
estimateChanges: A routeRules entry that applies to every route ('/**') is one change, but each route that needs a longer time then needs its own rule.

title: The share picture doesn't load
what: The og:image the page names answers with an error, or can't be reached.
why: When someone shares the page, the preview card shows no picture, or none at all, on the day you most want it to look right.
fix: Point og:image at an image that loads on the live domain (open the address in a browser to check), and use a full https:// address.
tech: One probe of the og:image address (HEAD, then GET on 405/501), counted in the images budget; 4xx, 5xx or no answer is a finding. No og:image is og-image-missing's to report
done: The og:image address loads on the live domain over https.
estimateChanges: One shared SEO component is one edit. Pages that set it by hand are edited one by one.

title: Shared links may show no picture
what: og:image is a relative address (like /previews/landing.webp), not a full https:// address.
why: Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack and iMessage need a full address. With a relative one, shares of the page show no picture.
fix: Write og:image as a full address, including https:// and the domain. Most frameworks have a site URL setting for this.
tech: og:image does not start with http:// or https:// (protocol-relative // addresses are flagged too)
done: og:image is a full address with https and the domain.
estimateChanges: One site URL setting in the framework usually fixes every page.

title: Shared links point at a different page than search engines see
what: The page's og:url (the address social apps use when it is shared) differs from its canonical tag.
why: Likes and shares are counted against one address while search engines rank another, and a share can open the wrong page.
fix: Set og:url to the same address as the canonical tag. Both usually come from one SEO component.
tech: og:url and <link rel="canonical"> differ by scheme, host, path or query (a trailing slash is not a difference)
done: og:url equals the canonical address.
estimateChanges: Both come from one SEO component on most sites.

title: This page is heavy to load
what: The HTML plus the images Gaugeline sampled add up to over 3 MB, and that is a floor: unsampled files come on top.
why: On a phone connection a page this heavy takes many seconds and costs visitors data.
fix: Start with the largest files in the evidence: resize and compress images, and trim the HTML's inline data.
tech: HTML bytes plus the Content-Length of sampled images (the files the run already requested) is over 3 MB (3,145,728 bytes); no extra requests are made
done: The page loads within the size budget, with the largest files resized or trimmed first.
estimateChanges: The number of large images and how much of the HTML is inline data.

title: A listing has fewer items than last run
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, a repeated list on a page (products, posts, people, events) has fewer items, with the ones that are gone where items carry links.
why: A shop page with 7 products instead of 12 still looks complete: items drop out when a feed, a filter or a category breaks, and nobody counts.
fix: Check the items that are gone were removed on purpose. If they weren't, look at what feeds the list. A listing meant to shrink goes under expectedChanges in gaugeline.pages.json.
tech: With --since last only. A list is a ul or ol with 3 or more items, or an element marked data-list, in the main content; it is named by its data-list value or the heading before it. For a paginated list only the first page is compared, and the evidence says so. On a first run: could not check
done: The missing items are back in the list, or the page is listed under expectedChanges.
estimateChanges: Finding what feeds the list, which may be a query, a filter or a deleted entry.

title: A page lost its structured data since the last run
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, a structured-data type that a page had (Product, Recipe, Event, Article) is no longer there.
why: Search results show rich listings (prices, ratings, dates) only from structured data; when a template or plugin change drops it, the page reads the same and the listing quietly goes plain.
fix: Put the markup back where the template lost it, or list the page under expectedChanges in gaugeline.pages.json when it was removed on purpose.
tech: With --since last only. Types are read from JSON-LD @type and microdata itemtype, with the schema.org prefix dropped. One finding per page, naming every type gone. On a first run: could not check
done: The structured data is back on the page, or the page is listed under expectedChanges.
estimateChanges: A template that lost it affects every page that uses the template.

title: The site shows two different handles for one payment service
what: With no payment details set, the pages checked show two or more different handles for the same service.
why: At most one of them is right. Customers can't tell which, and some pay the other one.
fix: Keep the right handle everywhere, and set it in gaugeline.payments.json so Gaugeline checks against it.
tech: Only without gaugeline.payments.json: a Zelle, Cash App, Venmo or PayPal handle with more than one distinct value (compared case-insensitively; Zelle phones by digits) across the pages checked
done: One handle is shown everywhere and is set in gaugeline.payments.json.
estimateChanges: Handles typed into several pages are one edit each.

title: The page's first large image is lazy, late or oversized
what: The first large content image of the page, which is usually the largest paint, is lazy-loaded, or is neither preloaded nor marked fetchpriority high, or is asked for at more than twice the width it is shown.
why: The largest paint is the number search engines and visitors judge a page's speed by. An image that the browser is told to wait for, that it finds late, or that is several times larger than needed delays it directly.
fix: Remove loading=lazy from the first large image, add fetchpriority="high" (or a preload link for it), and ask for it at about the width it is shown: a srcset and sizes, and a width parameter no larger than needed.
tech: The first img in the page's HTML outside a header, nav or footer, not named like a logo or icon and not under 300 by 100 pixels. Medium when it has loading=lazy, or when a width parameter or a Next.js image address asks for at least twice the width attribute and 1600 pixels (2560 when there is no width attribute); low when it is written 800 pixels wide or more and lacks both a preload link for its address and fetchpriority high (an image with no width attribute, or a narrower one, is not asked to be prioritised: most pages have one). This is a guess at which image the browser picks, which is why the finding says the first large image; it fetches no image and the same page gives the same finding
done: The page's first large image is not lazy-loaded, is preloaded or marked fetchpriority high, and is asked for at about the width it is shown.
estimateChanges: Minutes for one attribute on the hero image; an hour if the image component has to be changed to pass it.

title: A 3D scene starts as soon as the page loads
what: The page sets up a 3D (WebGL) scene, with a library such as three.js, Babylon.js or PlayCanvas or a WebGL call in its code, and nothing asks the visitor to click or tap to start it.
why: A 3D scene downloads a large library and models and keeps the graphics chip busy from the first second, on every phone, whether or not the visitor wants it. It delays the page's first paint and interaction and drains batteries, and a visitor on a slow connection or an old phone gets the cost and no benefit.
fix: Show a still picture first and start the scene when the visitor taps it or scrolls it into view, load the 3D library only then (a dynamic import), and skip it for visitors who ask for less data or motion.
tech: Plain rules over the page as sent and its own scripts. A 3D library by its script address (three, babylon, playcanvas, react-three, spline) beside a canvas element in the HTML, or a WebGL call in an inline script (a WebGLRenderer, a webgl or webgl2 context), counts as a scene set up at load; with --renderer playwright the canvas must be in the rendered page, whose size is reported. Words that ask for a click, tap or press to start, play or enter anywhere on the page make it a scene that waits for the visitor, and nothing is reported. Gaugeline gives the page no input, so a scene set up at load has started without any
done: The 3D scene starts only after a click, tap or scroll into view, or the page shows a still picture first; running Gaugeline again finds no scene that starts at load without a start step.
estimateChanges: A few hours to add a start step or a still poster and load the scene's library only when it is asked for; more when the scene is the whole front page.

title: The page shows placeholder images
what: Images on the page come from a placeholder service such as placehold.co, dummyimage.com or picsum.photos.
why: Visitors see grey boxes or random stock photos where the real product or team picture should be.
fix: Upload the real images and point the img tags at them.
tech: img src on placehold.co, placehold.it, placeholder.com, via.placeholder.com, dummyimage.com, picsum.photos, placekitten.com, placebear.com, loremflickr.com, fakeimg.pl, placeimg.com, lorempixel.com (or a subdomain)
done: The real images are uploaded and the img tags point at them.
estimateChanges: The number of images, and whether the real ones exist yet.

title: The page still has placeholder text
what: The page shows unfinished copy: lorem ipsum, TODO or TBD, a [bracketed placeholder], or a title or main heading such as Untitled, Staging or Test.
why: Visitors see an unfinished site, and search engines may show the placeholder in results.
fix: Replace the placeholder with the real copy. Search the CMS for "lorem", "TODO" and "[" before publishing.
tech: main content text matches "lorem ipsum", TODO/TBD/FIXME or [insert ...]-style brackets (code and pre ignored), or the whole title or h1 is one of "untitled", "untitled page", "untitled document", "new page", "page title", "title", "test", "test page", "testing", "staging", "staging site", "my site", "my website", "site title", "home page title" (English lists)
done: The placeholder is replaced with the real copy.
estimateChanges: Copy that has not been written is the real cost.

title: Your address takes several jumps to load
what: The address you entered redirects more than once before the page loads.
why: Each jump slows the first visit and can weaken how search engines credit the page.
fix: Point every redirect straight at the final address.
tech: more than one 3xx hop on the entered URL
done: Every redirect points straight at the final address.
estimateChanges: Rules in the host, a CDN and the app each need checking.

title: Alt text written in Sanity is not on the page
what: An editor wrote alt text for a picture in Sanity Studio, and the img on the page has no alt attribute or an empty one.
why: Screen readers skip an image with an empty alt and read the file name when there is none, so the description the editor took the time to write never reaches the visitor who needs it, and search engines never see it.
fix: Add the alt field to the query that loads the image and pass it to the img: alt={image.alt}. If the picture is only decoration, clear the alt text in Studio so the two agree.
tech: reads the Sanity dataset named by SANITY_PROJECT_ID and SANITY_DATASET with GET (published perspective, a Viewer token in a header): the published documents that refer to each upload on the page; an image value counts as having alt text when its alt field is text that is not blank; reported when every document using the upload has alt text and the img on the page has no alt attribute or alt=""; an upload used in several places where only some have alt text, or in no published document, is could not check; only a field named alt is read; the text itself is never kept or printed
done: Every Sanity image whose editor wrote alt text in Studio has that text in its alt attribute on the page.
estimateChanges: One line in the image component when the alt is never passed. Allow longer when the field has to be added to the query first.

title: A crop or hotspot set in Sanity Studio is not used by the page
what: An editor set a crop or a hotspot on a picture in Sanity Studio, and the address the page asks the image network for does not carry it, so the picture is shown uncropped or cut around the middle.
why: The editor drew the crop and the hotspot so the face, the dish or the shopfront stays in the frame. Without them a tall or wide slot cuts the heads off a team photo, and the editor has no way to see why.
fix: Build the address with the image value, not just its asset: urlFor(image).width(800).height(600).url() from @sanity/image-url writes the rect for the crop and cuts around the hotspot. If you write addresses by hand, pass the image's crop as rect and its hotspot as fp-x and fp-y with crop=focalpoint.
tech: reads the Sanity dataset named by SANITY_PROJECT_ID and SANITY_DATASET with GET (published perspective, a Viewer token in a header): the published documents that refer to each upload on the page, and on their image values the crop (an edge of 1 percent or more) and the hotspot (centre 2 percent or more off the middle); a crop is ignored when no address of the img has rect, fp-x, fp-y or crop; a hotspot is ignored when none has them, the address asks for both w and h with fit=crop, and the asked shape differs from the image's by more than 2 percent; an upload used with different crops in several places, or in no published document, is could not check; a size set only in CSS and object-position are not read, so a hotspot on an address with no w and h is could not check; only Studio values are read, none is printed
done: Every Sanity image on the page uses the crop and hotspot its editor set in Studio.
estimateChanges: One image helper when the page builds its addresses by hand; each call site when the front end writes them one by one. Allow longer if the editors have not set the hotspots yet.

title: Uploads the page uses are heavy in Sanity
what: Pictures the page uses are stored in Sanity at more than 500 KB, and some at more than 1 MB: a count, and the list, largest first.
why: The upload is what an unresized address delivers whole, what every new size is made from, and what the client's Sanity plan stores and serves. A 4 MB phone photo in a hero costs the visitor seconds on mobile data and the client bandwidth on every view.
fix: Re-export the largest files at the width the site needs (about 2000 px for a full-width banner) and re-upload them, and ask for a width and auto=format in every address so the visitor never downloads the upload as it was. Ask editors to resize before they upload.
tech: reads the Sanity dataset named by SANITY_PROJECT_ID and SANITY_DATASET with GET (published perspective, a Viewer token in a header): the size field, in whole bytes, of the asset document of each upload the page's image addresses name (at most 100 per run, in groups of 40); an upload is heavy when it is more than 512000 bytes (500 KB, 1024-based, the threshold images-heavy uses) and huge when it is more than 1048576 bytes (1 MB, 1024-based), so a file of exactly 512,000 bytes is not heavy; the list is sorted by size, largest first, then by asset id; it is the upload's size, not the size delivered, so a resized address is much smaller (the evidence says which uploads the page serves whole)
done: No Sanity upload the page uses is over 500 KB, or each one that is has been replaced by a smaller file.
estimateChanges: Re-exporting one photo is minutes; a whole media library uploaded at camera size is an afternoon, and the editors need a size rule so it does not come back. Allow longer if the originals are needed for print.

title: Sanity images are served at the size they were uploaded
what: An image from cdn.sanity.io is requested with no width or height, so the visitor gets the file as it was uploaded: often 3000 to 6000 pixels wide.
why: A phone photo from the shop owner is several megabytes. Shown a few hundred pixels across, it still downloads whole, and the page is slow on a phone for no visible gain.
fix: Ask for the size you show: add w (and h with fit=crop if the shape is fixed) and auto=format to the address, or build it with @sanity/image-url: urlFor(image).width(800).auto('format').url().
tech: an img src, srcset or picture source on cdn.sanity.io/images with none of w, h, max-w, max-h, min-w or min-h, whose upload is wider than 1200 px (the size is in the file name, so nothing is downloaded); other hosts, and addresses on a custom domain for Sanity's CDN, are not read; one finding per page; the page's own HTML only
done: Every Sanity image on the page asks for a width, and for auto format, in its address.
estimateChanges: Usually one image helper in the front end. Images written by hand into rich text are edited one by one.

title: Sanity images are delivered far larger than they are shown
what: An image from cdn.sanity.io is asked for at a width much greater than the width attribute on the page, and the page offers no smaller version.
why: The visitor downloads several times the pixels they can see. On a phone that is seconds of waiting and mobile data spent on detail the screen throws away.
fix: Ask Sanity for about twice the width the image is shown at (for a 400 px slot, w=800), or give the image a srcset with smaller widths and a sizes attribute so each screen picks one.
tech: an img with a width attribute whose smallest Sanity address (src, srcset or picture source) delivers more than 2 times that width and at least 200 px more; delivered is w times dpr, never above the upload, and the upload's own width when no w is given (read from the file name); an img with no width attribute is not judged; no rendering, so a width set only in CSS is not seen
done: No Sanity image is delivered at more than twice the width its slot shows.
estimateChanges: One width in the image helper, or the sizes list in a responsive image component.

title: A breadcrumb ends on a different page
what: The last item of a page's breadcrumb structured data points at an address other than the page's own canonical.
why: The trail should end where the visitor is. One that ends elsewhere usually means the breadcrumb was copied from another page.
fix: Make the last ListItem's item the page's canonical address, or leave the last item's URL out.
tech: the highest-position ListItem has a URL that differs from the canonical (or the page address) by scheme, host, path or query; needs a gaugeline.schema.json
done: The last ListItem of the breadcrumb is the page's canonical address.
estimateChanges: A shared breadcrumb component is one edit.

title: Structured data refers to something that isn't there
what: A structured data reference ({"@id": ...}) points at a node that is not defined on the page or on the other pages checked.
why: Search engines can't follow the reference, so whatever it stands for (the publisher, the author, the organization) is lost.
fix: Define the node the reference names (usually on the homepage), or correct the @id to the one you use.
tech: an object with only an @id resolves (after normalisation) to no @id defined on the sampled pages
done: The node the reference names is defined, or the @id is corrected.
estimateChanges: Structured data written by a plugin may not allow either change.

title: Pages redefine your organization instead of referring to it
what: Pages other than the homepage define the Organization or WebSite again, with its properties, instead of referring to the one node by its @id as your schema guide says.
why: Copies drift: one page gets an old logo or phone number, and search engines see several organizations where there should be one.
fix: On every other page, write {"@id": "<the configured id>"} where the Organization or WebSite is needed, and define it once on the homepage.
tech: an Organization or WebSite node with properties beyond @id and @type on a page other than / (needs organizationId or websiteId in gaugeline.schema.json)
done: Every other page refers to the Organization by @id and the homepage defines it once.
estimateChanges: Structured data written by several templates or plugins each need the change.

title: A page is missing structured data its template requires
what: A page that matches one of your schema guide's templates (for example /blog/*) lacks a type the guide requires there, such as Article or BreadcrumbList.
why: Rich results for that kind of page depend on the type, and one template that drifted usually means every page built from it did.
fix: Add the missing type to the template's structured data component.
tech: the most specific matching template's require list has a type missing from the page's JSON-LD (@type anywhere, @graph included); common subtypes count (an AboutPage is a WebPage, a BlogPosting an Article); needs templates in gaugeline.schema.json
done: The template's structured data includes the required type.
estimateChanges: Several templates that share the component are fixed once.

title: A third-party script is new, or lost its integrity attribute
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, the page loads a third-party script it did not load before, or one that had an integrity attribute no longer has it.
why: Any script on a checkout page can read what customers type. Knowing exactly which ones load, and noticing a new one, is what PCI DSS 11.6.1 asks of a payment page.
fix: Confirm the script was added on purpose and by whom. Remove it if not. For one you keep, add its integrity attribute so a changed file stops loading.
tech: With --since last only. Third-party means a host outside the page's registrable domain. A script is its host and path with no query string; the integrity attribute is present or not. Scripts that went away are not reported. On a first run: could not check
done: Each script that appeared since the last run is one you or the client added on purpose, and a script that lost its integrity attribute has it back.
estimateChanges: Finding out who added a script is the unknown. A tag manager can load many scripts that this page's code never names.

title: A security header sends less protection than before
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, one of these headers is gone or weaker: Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy, Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy.
why: These headers switch browser protections on. They vanish when a host, a CDN or a framework setting changes, and the site looks the same.
fix: Find what changed in the hosting or header settings and put the header back, or confirm the change was meant.
tech: With --since last only. The final response's headers. Reported: a header gone; Strict-Transport-Security with a smaller max-age or without includeSubDomains or preload; X-Content-Type-Options no longer nosniff; X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy and the Cross-Origin policies with a less strict value; a Permissions-Policy feature removed or given a new origin. On a first run: could not check
done: The header is sent as it was, or the change was meant.
estimateChanges: Usually one line in the host's or the framework's header settings. A CDN or proxy change can drop several at once.

title: Your sitemap lists pages on a different address
what: Every entry in the sitemap uses a different host than the site, for example a staging domain or the other of www and the bare domain.
why: Search engines ignore sitemap entries for a host the sitemap does not belong to, so the sitemap does nothing for this site.
fix: Generate the sitemap with the site's public address. In most frameworks this is a site URL or base URL setting.
tech: every sitemap entry's host differs from the page's host
done: The sitemap lists pages on the site's public address.
estimateChanges: A site URL setting is one line. A hand-written sitemap is edited by hand.

title: Search engines can't find a list of your pages
what: There is no sitemap at /sitemap.xml, and robots.txt does not say where one is.
why: Without a sitemap, search engines find pages only by following links, so new or deep pages take longer to appear.
fix: Publish a sitemap at /sitemap.xml (most site builders and frameworks can generate one) and add a Sitemap: line with its full address to robots.txt.
tech: /sitemap.xml is not a 200 sitemap and robots.txt has no Sitemap: line
done: A sitemap loads at /sitemap.xml and robots.txt names it.
estimateChanges: A framework or plugin that generates one is a setting. Without one it is built from the page list.

title: Your sitemap lists old addresses that redirect
what: Pages listed in the sitemap answer with a redirect (3xx) instead of the page.
why: A sitemap should list the final address of each page. Redirecting entries make search engines do extra work and can keep the old address in results.
fix: List each page at the address it redirects to. This often follows a move to https, to www, or to a new URL scheme.
tech: sampled sitemap entries return 3xx
done: Each sitemap entry is the address its page redirects to.
estimateChanges: A move to https, www or a new URL scheme changes every entry at once, and the sitemap is regenerated.

title: Your site publishes its source maps
what: A script or stylesheet this page loads names a source map, and the map can be fetched by anyone. A source map is the original, readable code the minified file was made from.
why: Anyone can read your site's original code, comments and file layout, which makes it easier to find a mistake, an internal address or a key left in the code.
fix: Turn production source maps off, or upload them to your error tracker and keep them out of the deploy. Vite: build.sourcemap false (the default) or 'hidden'. webpack: devtool false, or hidden-source-map. Next.js: leave productionBrowserSourceMaps off. Nuxt: sourcemap: { client: false }.
tech: GET of the map address a same-site file names, never a guessed one: the SourceMap (or X-SourceMap) response header or the last source map comment at the end of the file (a //# comment, /*# */ in CSS) of up to 15 script files and 5 stylesheets the page loads; at most 10 maps, same origin only, redirects not followed, a value that is not http(s) or not readable is not asked; a map counts only when its first 5 MB parse as a version 3 source map (so a page that answers 200 for every address does not); a map cut at the cap, a 401, 403, 429, 5xx and a network error are could not check; the evidence is file paths, counts of source files, whether the original code is included and a size class, never a name or a character from inside a map; an inline data: map is counted by size without decoding
done: The site's JavaScript and CSS name no source map a visitor can fetch, or the maps are kept on a private error-tracking service.
estimateChanges: One build setting. If the site reports errors to a tracker that needs the maps, upload them there at build time and delete them from the deploy.

title: An old version of the docs is open to search engines
what: This Docusaurus page says its version is no longer maintained (or unreleased), and search engines may list it as it is.
why: Search sends people to old instructions, prices or steps that no longer apply, and the old and new pages compete for the same searches.
fix: Set noIndex: true for the old version in the docs plugin's options, or give its pages a canonical address that points at the current version, and rebuild.
tech: Docusaurus pages only: the theme's theme-doc-version-banner with its no longer actively maintained or unreleased documentation text (@docusaurus/theme-classic and theme-translations 3.10.2), no noindex in the robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag, and a canonical that is missing or is the page itself. The version name is read from the docusaurus_version meta tag. VitePress has no versioning feature, so its version folders are not judged
done: Old documentation versions are marked noindex or point their canonical at the current page.
estimateChanges: Docusaurus sets noindex per version (noIndex: true in the docs plugin), and each old version needs it.

title: The same structured data is on this page twice
what: A schema.org type is described both in JSON-LD and as microdata (itemtype) on the same page.
why: Search engines see two descriptions of one thing, which can disagree, and may pick the wrong one or ignore both.
fix: Keep one: usually the JSON-LD, and remove the itemscope and itemtype attributes from the theme or plugin that adds microdata.
tech: a schema.org @type in JSON-LD is also a microdata itemtype
done: The page carries one copy of the structured data, usually the JSON-LD.
estimateChanges: A plugin or theme that adds microdata has to be configured or removed, which can change other pages.

title: The page is from an older build than the site
what: The build version written into this SvelteKit page differs from the one in the site's _app/version.json, so the page is a copy from an earlier deploy.
why: A prerendered or cached page from an old build points at script files that may be gone, and shows old content next to a new site: edits look unpublished.
fix: Purge the CDN's copy of the page on every deploy, or let it expire (a short s-maxage). A prerendered page is rebuilt on each build, so check the cache in front of it.
tech: SvelteKit sites only. The version: in the page's inline __sveltekit_ script against the version of one GET of <appDir>/version.json (the folder is read from the page's own module addresses; the file is public and fetched by every visitor's browser). A page whose version cannot be read, or a version file that is missing, is could not check. Pages sampled together are compared with the same file, asked for once per page
done: The page's build version matches the version file of the deployment that served it.
estimateChanges: A CDN purge on deploy is one setting; prerendered pages cached with no expiry may need each purged.

title: A page does not say what it should for the current switch
what: You said what a page must tell visitors while a feature is on or off ("order at the bar" while pre-orders are off), and the page does not say it.
why: A visitor who reaches the page learns nothing: no explanation, no other way to order. They are left guessing whether the site is broken.
fix: Show the message from the same switch that turns the feature off, so the two cannot disagree. If the evidence says a cache served the page, purge it after the switch changes.
tech: for each switch in gaugeline.switches.json, the page text for the current state (whenOff.pageSays while off, whenOn.pageSays while on) is read from the page as sent, without JavaScript, with hidden elements left out; the phrase is matched case-insensitively and ignoring accents, spacing and punctuation, in the page's own language when the phrase is given per language (a bilingual site's other-language pages are read through gaugeline.languages.json); a page that answers 404, a source or a page that cannot be read is could not check (the link checks report dead pages); the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page
done: The page shows the message from the same switch that turns the feature off.
estimateChanges: A cache needs purging, and each page that reads the switch needs the same source.

title: A tracking rule points at something that no longer exists
what: A Tag Manager trigger waits for a page address, link, form or element that no page on the site has, so its tags never fire.
why: Tag rules outlive the pages they were written for: a download or form trigger tied to a retired address goes quiet, and the report just shows fewer leads.
fix: Point the trigger at what the site uses now (the nearest match is in the evidence), or delete it and the tags that only it fires.
tech: The container export named in gaugeline.tags.json (no Tag Manager account is used). Page address conditions are compared with the pages read, their same-site links and the sitemap; click and form conditions (Click URL, ID, Classes, Text, Element; Form ID, Classes, Text, URL, Element) with the elements of the pages read. A trigger type, variable or comparison it doesn't read, a custom event, or a trigger limited to pages the run didn't read is listed under could not check
done: Each rule fires on something the site still has, or is deleted with its tags.
estimateChanges: The number of rules in the container, and who owns the tags that only they fire.

title: Two tags send the same event at the same moment
what: Two Tag Manager tags that aren't paused send the same event to the same place on the same trigger.
why: Every lead, download or sale is counted twice, so conversion numbers and the ad bidding built on them are wrong.
fix: Keep one of the tags and pause or delete the other (usually the copy).
tech: The container export named in gaugeline.tags.json, read without requests. GA4 event tags are the same when the event name and the measurement ID match; any other tag type when its type and every setting match. Paused tags are left out
done: One of the two tags is kept and the other is paused or deleted.
estimateChanges: Which copy is the real one has to be decided by someone who knows the account.

title: Some links are missing an attribute your tracking plan requires
what: A link or element that a line under attributes in gaugeline.events.json selects has no value for an attribute the plan requires, such as data-track on every nav link.
why: A tag that reads the attribute to name the click gets nothing for these links, so their clicks go unnamed or unreported and before-and-after comparisons of the menu stop meaning anything.
fix: Add the attribute, with a value, to those links, ideally in the one component or template that renders the menu.
tech: no request. Each attributes line of gaugeline.events.json: every a[href] in the region (nav, header, footer or main, as the click plan reads regions; javascript: links left out), or every element the CSS selector matches. An attribute with no value, or only spaces, is missing. One finding per line, with the count and the first three
done: Every element the plan selects carries each attribute the plan requires, with a value.
estimateChanges: Links built by one shared component are one edit; links typed into a template are edited one by one.

title: This page isn't set up for phone screens
what: The page has no viewport meta tag, so phones show it zoomed out as if on a desktop screen.
why: Visitors have to pinch and zoom to read anything, and Google treats the page as not mobile-friendly.
fix: Add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> to the page's head.
tech: no <meta name="viewport"> anywhere in the document
done: The page head has a viewport meta tag.
estimateChanges: A template shared by every page is one edit. Pages built with different templates are one each.

title: A title tag isn't what the plan says
what: The title tag the preview sends isn't the one the plan gives the page.
why: Someone edited the page, or the template overrode it, and the title the plan chose for search is gone.
fix: Set the page's title to the plan's, or update the plan if the change was deliberate.
tech: The page row's Title Tag against the HTML title, compared trimmed, case-folded, whitespace collapsed, quotes and dashes straightened; a brand suffix counts. No title in the HTML is reported with a hint that it may be set by JavaScript
done: Each page's title equals the plan's, or the plan is updated.
estimateChanges: Pages edited by several people need the change in one place.

title: An H1 isn't what the plan says
what: The page's first H1 isn't the one the plan gives it.
why: Usually a content change nobody recorded; the heading the plan chose for the keyword is gone.
fix: Set the H1 to the plan's, or update the plan.
tech: The page row's H1 against the first h1 in the HTML, compared like titles; a page with several H1s is noted
done: Each page's H1 equals the plan's, or the plan is updated.
estimateChanges: Deciding which side is right comes first.

title: A planned #section isn't on the page
what: A plan row with a #section points at an id that isn't on the page.
why: Links to the section land at the top of the page, and the plan's section was never built.
fix: Add the section with that id, or change the row to the id the page uses.
tech: The row's fragment against every element id in the HTML the preview sends
done: Each planned #section has an element with that id on the page.
estimateChanges: A section that was never built is the full cost of building it.

title: An old address takes more than one redirect
what: An old address takes two or more redirects to reach its page.
why: Each hop costs visitors time, and search engines follow only so many before giving up on passing signals.
fix: Redirect the old address straight to the final page. A server that adds a trailing slash first counts: redirect the old address's own form.
tech: More than one 3xx in the hop list the fetcher records; the trail is in the evidence
done: Each old address redirects once, straight to the final page.
estimateChanges: Rules in the host and in the app each need checking.

title: A menu item and its page are named differently
what: A menu item matches no page by name, and exactly one page shares a distinctive word with it.
why: The menu and the page plan disagree on the name, so the page's title, H1 and keyword may not be what visitors click.
fix: Use one name in both places, or record the difference on purpose.
tech: Distinctive words are five letters or more, not health, healthcare, medical, service(s) or management. Exactly one page name with one of them; the evidence gives both labels and both lines
done: The menu item and the page use one name.
estimateChanges: A name that is on purpose different is recorded rather than changed.

title: A menu item links to a page that still needs building
what: A menu item matches a page row whose Status says Need Page.
why: The menu will link to a page that hasn't been built: at launch it is a 404 in the navigation.
fix: Build the page before launch, or leave the item out of the menu until it exists.
tech: The matched row's Status cell against /need(s) page/i. Skipped, with a note, when the plan has no Status column
done: The page is built before launch, or the menu item is left out until it exists.
estimateChanges: A page that is not written yet is the real cost.

title: Two rows in the plan have the same title tag
what: Two or more rows of the plan plan the same title tag.
why: Search engines show the title in results; two pages with one title compete with each other and neither looks like the answer.
fix: Write a title that says what is different about each page.
tech: Title Tag cells compared trimmed, whitespace collapsed, lower case, with curly quotes and dashes straightened; a brand suffix is part of the title. Empty cells are left out
done: Each planned page has a title that says what is different about it.
estimateChanges: Writing good titles takes time per page.

title: Two rows in the plan have the same H1
what: Two or more rows of the plan plan the same H1.
why: The H1 tells visitors and search engines what the page is about; two pages with the same heading read as the same page.
fix: Give each page a heading that names its own topic.
tech: H1 cells compared the same way as titles. Empty cells are left out
done: Each planned page has a heading that names its own topic.
estimateChanges: Writing good headings takes time per page.

title: A slug misspells its own heading
what: A word in a page's address is one or two letters away from a word in the same row's page name or H1, such as credentialling for Credentialing.
why: The address is permanent once it is indexed and linked; fixing a typo later means a redirect, and until then the page looks careless in results.
fix: Use the heading's spelling in the slug (the corrected path is in the evidence) before the page is built.
tech: Words of 5+ letters in the last path segment, not in the row's page name or H1, within Damerau distance 1 of a heading word (2 for words of 8+ letters). Plural and tense endings (s, es, ed, ing) and listed British/American pairs are excused; accents are folded. One finding per row
done: The slug uses the heading's spelling.
estimateChanges: Easy before the page is built. After it is linked or indexed it also needs a redirect.

title: Two pages in the plan target the same primary keyword
what: Two or more pages of the plan have the same Primary Keyword, so they will compete for one search before a line of code is written.
why: Search engines show one page per query from a site; two pages chasing the same term split their links and usually both rank worse than one would.
fix: Give each page its own primary keyword, or merge the pages into one.
tech: Primary Keyword cells compared trimmed, lower case, spaces collapsed, quotes straightened and a trailing full stop removed; no stemming (singular and plural differ). Empty, n/a, none, tbd, - and bracketed placeholders are left out. A page and its anchor rows count once. Groups sorted by a Primary Volume column when there is one
done: Each page has its own primary keyword, or the competing pages are merged.
estimateChanges: Merging pages means content and redirect work.

title: Some old addresses in the plan's notes aren't settled
what: A notes column read with --legacy-from mentions a legacy page in words instead of by its address, or asks whether it should redirect, so no redirect can be checked for it.
why: Old addresses that rank keep their traffic only with a 301 to the right new page. A note nobody resolved is a redirect nobody will build.
fix: Put the old address in the note ("301 legacy /old-page here.") or decide and write it, then run the plan check again.
tech: Sentences in the --legacy-from columns containing "legacy": one that says 301 but names no path (no-path), or one with a path that starts with Confirm, contains whether or ends with a question mark (unconfirmed). One finding listing every line
done: Each old address in the notes is written as a path or decided, and the plan check passes.
estimateChanges: Someone who knows the old site has to say what each note means.

title: A printed link to a page now lands on the home page
what: A printed link to a page deeper than the home page now lands on the home page.
why: The classic lazy redirect after a restructure: the visitor who scanned for the menu has to find it again.
fix: Redirect the printed address to the page that replaced the one it was printed for, and add its expectedDestination to the register.
tech: No expectedDestination; the printed path isn't / and the trail ends on /
done: The printed address redirects to the page that replaced its original, and its expectedDestination is in the register.
estimateChanges: Several printed addresses each need their own redirect.

title: A printed address loses its tracking tags
what: A printed address's utm_ (or other configured) parameters are gone by the time it reaches its page.
why: Scans of that table tent or flyer can't be counted: the campaign looks like it did nothing.
fix: Pass the query string on in the redirect.
tech: Parameters on the printed URL whose names start with a tag prefix (utm_ by default) and are missing from the final address
done: The redirect passes the query string on, and the scan reaches the page with its tags.
estimateChanges: A short-link service may need its own setting.

title: The same product is in Printful more than once
what: Two or more Printful products have the same name, or the same external id.
why: An order for the product can be made from either copy, with different designs or prices, and the shop only knows one of them.
fix: Keep one product, delete the rest in Printful and point the website at the one you keep. Gaugeline does not choose which.
tech: Printful store products grouped by normaliseName, then by external id (trimmed, exact), each in one pass into a Map; a product in a name group and an external id group is listed once, in the name group; one finding per group with every copy's id, up to 10 and then a count; a blank external id or a name that normalises to nothing is never a group; runs only when Printful returned data
done: One product is kept in Printful and the website points at it.
estimateChanges: Orders attached to the copies need care before they are deleted.

title: The same product is on the website more than once
what: Two or more published Sanity products have the same name, or the same non-empty SKU.
why: The shop has the same product twice, so a price, a photo or a stock figure can be right on one copy and wrong on the other, and a link to checkout may be saved on only one of them.
fix: Keep one product, unpublish or delete the rest in Sanity and point the website at the one you keep. Gaugeline does not choose which.
tech: published Sanity products grouped by normaliseName, then by SKU (trimmed, lower-case), each in one pass into a Map; a product in a name group and a SKU group is listed once, in the name group; one finding per group with every copy's _id, up to 10 and then a count; an empty SKU or a name that normalises to nothing is never a group; runs only when Sanity returned data
done: One product is kept in the website's content and the others are unpublished or deleted.
estimateChanges: Links to the copies need a redirect.

title: The same product is in Stripe more than once
what: Two or more active Stripe products have the same name once case, spacing and punctuation are ignored.
why: Until one record is the real one, nothing can say what checkout should charge: the copies may carry different prices, and the website may point at any of them.
fix: Keep one, archive the rest in Stripe and point the website at the one you keep. Gaugeline does not choose which.
tech: active Stripe products grouped by normaliseName in one pass into a Map; one finding per group listing every copy with its id and default price, up to 10 and then a count; archived products are not counted as copies and are named in the finding when their group also has active ones; names that normalise to an empty string are never grouped; runs only when Stripe returned data
done: One product is kept active in Stripe and the others are archived.
estimateChanges: Payment links and subscriptions on the copies have to be moved first.

title: An email still has template variables in it
what: A rendered email still holds a variable that was never filled in, such as {{order_id}}, {% if paid %}, {name} or [object Object].
why: The customer reads "Order {{order_id}} is confirmed" or "Hi undefined", which looks broken and hides the one detail (which order, which booking) they opened the email for.
fix: Pass the missing value to the template, or delete the variable. For a preview that was exported before the data was merged, export the email from the real send path or with sample data.
tech: Handlebars and Mustache {{ }} and {{{ }}}, Liquid {% %}, ERB and EJS <% %>, JavaScript ${ }, JSX and message {name} and {props.name}, [object Object], Mailchimp *|MERGE|* tags, undefined and NaN as words, and null alone or after a greeting; read in the text a recipient sees and in attributes (style and script bodies and comments are left out, JSON-LD is not), and in the .txt beside it; one finding for each file, at the first line
done: The re-exported email has a real value wherever the template has a variable, and no placeholder is left in the HTML or the text version.
estimateChanges: A variable the email build never receives is one fix. A template that renders before its data arrives needs the render moved.

title: An image in an email will not load in an inbox
what: An image in a rendered email is on a relative path, on localhost or a private address, or on plain http://.
why: A relative or local image is a broken box in every inbox, and many mail apps block or warn about plain http images, so the logo or the product photo is missing exactly where the customer is looking.
fix: Serve the images from your live site over https and write their full addresses into the email (https://example.com/mail/logo.png), or attach them inline.
tech: img[src] in the rendered HTML with no scheme, with http:, or with an http(s) address on a local or private host (the list is the one email-relative-link uses); cid: and data: images are not read; the address is shown without its query; one finding for each email, at the first line
done: Every image in the email is an https:// address on a public host, or travels inside the message (cid:).
estimateChanges: Images served from one setting are a single change. Images pasted in by hand are edited one by one.

title: The domain's registration runs out soon
what: The domain's registration expires in under 30 days (fix soon) or under 7 (fix first), by the date the registry publishes.
why: When a domain lapses the site and every email address on it stop working, and a lapsed name can be bought by someone else. The first you hear of it is usually the owner on the phone.
fix: Renew it at the registrar the finding names, and turn on automatic renewal. If the client holds the account, send them the date and ask them to renew, or ask for access so it is not left to a card that may have expired.
tech: RDAP, the registries' public replacement for WHOIS: IANA's bootstrap file (data.iana.org/rdap/dns.json) names the registry's server for the TLD, then one GET of /domain/<name> there, no key. The date is the earliest "expiration" event; the registrar is the name in the registrar entity. Whole days from the run's clock in UTC. A registry with no RDAP service, a rate limit, an outage, a platform address (name.vercel.app) or a registry that hides its dates is could-not-check with the reason, never a guess; WHOIS is never read
done: The domain is renewed at the registrar, with a registration date a year or more ahead and automatic renewal on.
estimateChanges: Minutes when you hold the registrar login. Days when the client or a former agency does, because someone has to be reached to approve the renewal.

title: An access token expires soon
what: A GitHub or Vercel token you set up for Gaugeline reports an expiry date within 21 days (fix soon) or 7 (fix first), or in the past.
why: When a token lapses, whatever uses it stops with no warning: a deploy hook, a content sync, a scheduled job. It usually shows up as a site that quietly stops updating.
fix: Create a replacement with a later date, update everything that uses the old one, then revoke the old one. A token with no expiry is listed as "no expiry reported", not as a problem.
tech: Only tokens you put in GAUGELINE_GITHUB_TOKEN or GAUGELINE_VERCEL_TOKEN are asked. GitHub: one GET of /rate_limit, reading the GitHub-Authentication-Token-Expiration response header. Vercel: one GET of /v5/user/tokens/current, reading expiresAt. Only the date is kept, and the token is never printed, logged or put in a result. A token whose provider reports no date is could-not-check (no expiry reported); nothing is created or revoked
done: A new token is created with a date well ahead, the deploy or sync that uses it is updated, and the old one is revoked.
estimateChanges: Minutes for one token. Longer when it is copied into several places (a CI secret, a hosting setting, a teammate's machine) and nobody remembers where.

title: A Vercel project runs a Node.js version Vercel is retiring
what: A Vercel project you listed in gaugeline.renewals.json uses a Node.js version that Vercel has announced it will stop supporting (or already has).
why: Once Vercel retires a version, new deployments of the project can fail to build, and a site nobody touched for months stops being deployable the day someone needs to fix something.
fix: Set the project's Node.js version to a current one (Project Settings, then Node.js Version, and the engines field in package.json), deploy a preview and check the site before promoting it.
tech: GET /v9/projects/<name> on Vercel with GAUGELINE_VERCEL_TOKEN, reading only nodeVersion. The version's major is looked up in packages/core/src/data/vercel-node-runtimes.json: a dated list of the versions Vercel has announced for retirement, each with the page that says so. A version that is not in the list has no announced retirement and is not a finding. Under 7 days or past is high, under 90 days medium, further out low
done: The Vercel project builds and runs on a Node.js version Vercel supports, set in the project's settings and in package.json.
estimateChanges: Changing the setting takes a minute. Moving a project across two majors can turn up packages that no longer install or code that relied on old behaviour, so test it on a preview first.

title: The freelancer is the only owner or admin of a system the client depends on
what: A system has exactly one owner or admin that has accepted, and it is one of the freelancer's addresses (gaugeline.handoff.json). Two addresses listed together under sameAs count as one person.
why: One person is the single way in. If their login is lost, their account is closed or they are unreachable, nobody can add anyone, and the client has to wait for them.
fix: Make a second person an owner or admin: the client first, and ideally a teammate you trust as well. Then run the handoff again.
tech: Read as client-not-admin does. Owners and admins who have accepted, and who are not an API token, are counted by person: the addresses a person is listed under in sameAs share one key. Exactly one such person, whose address is in freelancerEmails, is the finding. A system whose members could not be read is could-not-check, never a pass
done: At least two different people can let others in or out of the system, and one of them is the client.
estimateChanges: Minutes in the provider's members page. It needs the client to accept an invitation, which can take as long as they take to open an email.

title: A system the site depends on lives in a personal account
what: The project that serves or feeds the site belongs to one person's account, not to a team or organisation.
why: A personal account is one person's login. It has no list of members to add the client to, it cannot outlive that person's access, and it often belongs to the freelancer who set the site up, so the client's site is tied to a login that is not theirs.
fix: Create a team or organisation owned by the client (or by both of you), move the project into it, and give the client's own address the owner role. Then run the handoff again.
tech: Vercel: the project's accountId. An id that begins with team_ is a team; any other is a personal account, whose one owner is the token's own user (GET /v2/user). Other systems report a personal account only when their API says so. A project whose owner cannot be told apart is could-not-check
done: The project lives in a team or organisation account that the client owns, and it has been moved there without a break in the site.
estimateChanges: Moving a project between accounts can change its address, its environment variables and its domain settings. Plan an hour for a small site, and check the site afterwards.

title: The page's HTML is different on every request
what: Visiting the page twice, a few seconds apart, gives different HTML even after nonces and CSRF values are ignored.
why: A page that is different on every visit cannot be cached, so the host builds it again for every visitor. On a Next.js site that is the usual cause of a hosting bill that grows faster than the traffic, and it makes the page slower as well.
fix: Find the first difference in the finding. If it is a time, a counter or a random id, print it in the browser instead of when the page is built, or move it behind a cache lifetime. If it comes from a CMS query, ask whether that part has to be fresh on every visit.
tech: Two GETs of the page about 3 seconds apart, the first being the one the check already made, both with no cookies (a variant a cookie would choose is the one a first-time visitor gets). Before comparing, volatile values are blanked by a fixed table: nonce attributes and 'nonce-' sources, the value of csrf-token meta tags and hidden CSRF fields, Cloudflare's scrambled emails; whitespace is collapsed. The finding quotes the first differing word in each body. A cookie whose name looks like an experiment (ab_test, variant, bucket) is named in the evidence. Pure string comparison: the same two bodies give the same answer. Only with --cost or gaugeline cost; pages listed under "pages" in gaugeline.cost.json are visited too
done: Two visits a few seconds apart give the same HTML, so the host can keep one copy and serve it, and the hosting bill stops growing with every visitor.
estimateChanges: Often an hour to find the value (a clock, a counter, a random id) and move it to the browser or behind a longer cache time. Longer when the page is built from a CMS query that includes it.

title: Hosting usage jumped
what: A usage figure the hosting provider reports for yesterday is more than a set multiple (2 by default) of its average over the 14 days before.
why: A site can quietly multiply its hosting bill when a page stops caching or a loop starts. The jump shows up in the usage figures days before the invoice, which is the time to fix it, and to tell the client before they find out.
fix: Open the provider's usage page for the metric named, and look for the day it started: a deploy, a page that began changing on every visit (see output-changes-every-request), a new image or API call. Fix the cause, then run again tomorrow.
tech: Read-only, one GET of the provider's usage with the token in the environment: Vercel's billing charges (GAUGELINE_VERCEL_TOKEN; Vercel has no read-only token type, so use one scoped to the team). Each service and unit is a metric, and the billed cost one more, summed by UTC day in thousandths (integers). The latest complete day before today by the injected clock is compared with the mean of the days before it (window and multiple in gaugeline.cost.json): flagged when more than the multiple, ignoring a day under one whole unit and a metric with no earlier usage. Sanity's usage has no documented read API, so it is could-not-check. Not applicable to a site on Wix, Squarespace, Webflow or Framer: a fixed plan. No token is could-not-check; the page checks still run
done: Yesterday's usage is back within the multiple of its recent average, or the jump is explained (a campaign, a launch) and the plan covers it.
estimateChanges: An hour to find the cause in the provider's usage page (a page that stopped caching, an image loop, a crawler). Longer if the fix is a plan change the client has to approve.

title: An unpublished or deleted item still has a live page
what: The site's sitemap lists a page that fits the address pattern of a content type, no published item has that address, and the page still answers 200.
why: The client took the item down, perhaps because it was wrong, out of date or private, and visitors and search engines can still read it.
fix: Purge or revalidate the page so it answers 404 or redirects, and check that the sitemap is rebuilt when an item is unpublished. If the page is meant to stay, publish the item again.
tech: Only with --published, and only when the run has a list of the whole site (the sitemap and feed adapter, which is the default) and an adapter with urls templates in gaugeline.adapters.json. Every address in the site's own sitemap that fits a template and that no published item resolves to is asked for with one GET, within the page budget; a 2xx answer is a finding. A list of everything published that is cut short (a rate limit, or more than 2000 items) means this is not looked for, and the reason is could-not-check
done: A page for an item that was unpublished or deleted is gone from the site or redirects, and the site's sitemap no longer lists it.
estimateChanges: Minutes to purge a page and fix its revalidation. An hour when the site never removes pages for deleted items.

title: The latest export is far smaller than the one before
what: The newest export file in a folder you named is under half the size of the one before it (or the percent you set).
why: A backup job that fails half way still writes a file. A database dump that suddenly shrinks is usually a table that was skipped or a job that ran out of space, and it is only found when someone tries to restore it.
fix: Compare what is inside the two exports (the list of tables or files). If the drop is wrong, fix the job and run it again; if it is real, note why.
tech: Only folders named under "exports" in gaugeline.backups.json. Files are listed, never opened: the size in bytes comes from the folder listing. Per day the biggest file stands for it (a second run does not hide a good export). The latest day's file is compared with the day before it in integers: flagged when its size times 100 is under the previous size times "shrinkPercent" (default 50), so a zero-byte latest file is always flagged. A previous export of zero bytes has nothing to shrink from. The day comes from the file name or, failing that, when it was last changed. Only with --backups or gaugeline backups
done: The latest export is about the size of the one before it, or the drop is explained (rows deleted on purpose) and the next export confirms it.
estimateChanges: Half an hour to open the two files' contents list and see what is missing: a table that failed, a bucket that was skipped, a job that ran out of disk.

title: A JavaScript library the site serves has a published advisory
what: Gaugeline reads the JavaScript files a page loads, finds the version of jQuery, jQuery UI, Lodash, Moment.js, Bootstrap or AngularJS in them, and lists the published advisories that name that version, with the version that fixes each.
why: Libraries in an old theme or plugin stay at the version they were installed at, and advisories are published about versions long after. This is a list of facts: which version is served and which advisories name it. Whether an advisory matters for this site depends on how the site uses the library, which Gaugeline cannot see, and it does not say.
fix: Look at where the file comes from: the theme, a plugin, a package in the project or a CDN address. Update it to a version past the fixes the finding lists, or take the library out when nothing uses it, then test the pages that use it. If it is bundled into code you cannot change, tell the client who maintains it.
tech: Only with --libraries. The script files the page's own HTML names (script src, same site or another, at most 20, each fetched once with GET, never any address the page does not name) are read as text and never run; at most 2 MiB of each is read and searched, and each script is reported once per run, on the first page that names it. The version comes from a banner comment, a version string in the code or the library's own file name (jquery-3.5.1.min.js, or jquery.min.js under a /jquery/1.12.4/ or lodash@4.17.21 folder; a query string and a folder with other files are never a version), the file's own text first, and only from a whole banner or code shape, never a sentence in a comment. It is compared with packages/core/src/data/library-advisories.json: for each advisory, the affected versions and the page that publishes it, with a verified flag that is false until someone has compared the entry with its page, and a finding says so while it is false. A finding shows the library, its version, the script's address (with no query), and each advisory with its id, a short description and the fixed-in version, never script text beyond the version. A library recognised by name with no version, a script that cannot be read or is longer than what is read, and minified files with no library name or version are could-not-check. A library bundled into one minified file with its banner removed is not seen. The same files give the same findings
done: The libraries the finding names are on versions past the fixes the advisories list, or the client has decided with the developer who knows the theme that they stay; running Gaugeline again shows the versions served.
estimateChanges: An hour for a library the theme loads from a file you can swap. A day or more when the library is bundled into an old theme or plugin and the code that uses it has to be tested on the newer version.

title: Text is too faint to read against its background
what: In the rendered page, some text has less contrast with the colour behind it than WCAG 2 asks for: under 4.5 to 1, or under 3 to 1 for large text (24 px, or 18.66 px and bold).
why: Faint text is hard to read for many people, in sunlight, on a cheap screen or with weaker eyesight, and it is the most common failure on the web. It also makes an accessibility complaint easy to win.
fix: Darken the text or lighten the background until the pair reaches the ratio. The finding gives the ratio and both colours; a contrast checker shows the nearest colour that passes. Fix it in the shared colour setting, not text by text.
tech: Only with --renderer playwright. The browser's own computed colours for up to 250 visible text elements (the text colour, and the background found by walking up through translucent layers to an opaque one, white at the top); WCAG 2 relative luminance and ratio, text colour laid over the background when translucent; 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text. Elements are grouped by colours and size, the three worst groups are named with up to three examples, and the ratio is cut down to hundredths (4.477 is 4.47 and fails).
