Text on an image or gradient, and text past the 250 sampled, is could-not-check, never a pass; disabled controls and aria-hidden text are left out. The same rendered page gives the same findings
done: Every piece of text sampled on the rendered page has at least the WCAG contrast with what is behind it: 4.5 to 1, or 3 to 1 for large text.
estimateChanges: Minutes per colour pair in a shared stylesheet or design token; more when the grey is set in many places or on top of photographs.

title: Keyboard focus does not follow the page
what: In the rendered page, an element has a positive tabindex (which makes it jump the queue), or pressing Tab moves back up the page two or more times.
why: People who use a keyboard or a switch move through a page with Tab, and expect it to follow what they see. A focus order that jumps around loses them, and a positive tabindex breaks the order for the whole page.
fix: Remove positive tabindex values (use 0 or none) and put the markup in the order it reads. Where the screen layout differs from the document order, change the document order rather than the tabindex.
tech: Only with --renderer playwright. The elements Tab reaches (links with an address, buttons, fields, summaries, iframes, editable elements and anything with a tabindex of 0 or more; disabled, hidden and tabindex -1 left out) are put in the order the browser visits them: positive tabindex first, ascending, then document order. A positive tabindex is medium. A move to a position more than 40 pixels higher than the one before counts as a jump back, and two or more are low, because one is usually a skip link or a sticky bar. Up to 300 elements are read. The same rendered page gives the same findings
done: No element has a positive tabindex, and keyboard focus moves down and across the page, not back up it.
estimateChanges: Minutes to remove a positive tabindex; an hour or more when the markup order itself has to follow the visual order.

title: The page's landmarks are missing or unclear
what: In the rendered page there is no main landmark, there is more than one, or several landmarks of one kind (two navs, two asides) have no names to tell them apart.
why: Screen reader users jump between landmarks to skip a menu and reach the content. A page with no main has no way to jump to its content, and two unnamed navs are announced the same.
fix: Put the page's content in one main element, and give each repeated nav, aside or region its own aria-label ('Main menu', 'Footer').
tech: Only with --renderer playwright. Visible elements with a landmark role, by tag or role attribute: main, nav (navigation), a header and footer outside an article, aside, main, nav or section (banner, contentinfo), aside (complementary), search, form and section with a name (form, region). No main is medium. More than one main, and two or more landmarks of one role with no names or the same name, are low. Up to 50 are read. The same rendered page gives the same findings
done: The rendered page has one main landmark, and landmarks of the same kind have names that tell them apart.
estimateChanges: Minutes: wrap the content in a main element, add an aria-label to each repeated nav.

title: A control has no name, or a widget cannot be reached
what: In the rendered page, a link, button or field the keyboard reaches has no accessible name, or an element with a role such as button or link cannot be reached with the keyboard.
why: A screen reader says what a control is called. A control with no name is announced as just 'button', and a div that acts as a button but cannot take focus cannot be used without a mouse at all.
fix: Give each control a visible label or text, or an aria-label for an icon. Use a real button or link element, which is reachable and named by default, instead of a div with a role.
tech: Only with --renderer playwright. For each element Tab reaches, the name is the aria-label, the aria-labelledby text, the label of a field, the value of a submit or button input, the text (or an image's alt or a graphic's aria-label) inside it, or its title, in that order; none is a finding. Elements with the role button, link, checkbox, switch, tab, menuitem or radio that are not natively focusable and have no tabindex of 0 or more are listed as not reachable. Up to 300 focusable and 50 unreachable elements are read. The same rendered page gives the same findings
done: Every control the keyboard reaches has an accessible name, and every element with a widget role can be reached with the keyboard.
estimateChanges: Minutes per control: an aria-label, a visible label or text in the button; a real button element instead of a div with a role.

title: The page animates and does not honour reduced motion
what: The rendered page has running animations and no prefers-reduced-motion rule in its stylesheets.
why: Moving content can cause dizziness, nausea or distraction for people with vestibular or attention conditions, who set 'reduce motion' on their device and expect sites to respect it. Animation that never stops is the hardest to avoid.
fix: Add a @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) rule that turns off or shortens animations and transitions, and do not start motion in script for visitors who ask for less.
tech: Only with --renderer playwright. The animations the browser reports on the page after it settled (CSS animations, transitions and the Web Animations API), and how many never end; and a prefers-reduced-motion media rule in any stylesheet the page's own script can read. Some animations and no rule is low, medium when one never ends. A stylesheet from another origin cannot be read, so with no rule seen and one of those present it is could-not-check, never a finding. A rule in script (matchMedia) is not seen. The same rendered page gives the same findings
done: Animation on the page is switched off or reduced for visitors who ask for it, with a prefers-reduced-motion rule in the page's own stylesheets.
estimateChanges: Minutes: one prefers-reduced-motion media query that turns animation and transition off.

title: Real visitors' Core Web Vitals are not all good on a page
what: Google's PageSpeed Insights reports, from real Chrome visitors, that fewer than 75% of loads of a page have a good Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint or Cumulative Layout Shift.
why: These are what visitors actually lived through, measured by their own browsers, and Google uses them as a ranking signal. A page that feels slow or jumps as it loads loses visitors before they read it, and the cost is greatest on phones and slow connections.
fix: Start with the vital that is poor. Largest Contentful Paint: make the biggest image or heading on the page small and load it first (the lab advice shows how long it takes). Interaction to Next Paint: break up long scripts and remove tags that run on every click. Cumulative Layout Shift: give images, embeds and ads a width and height so nothing jumps. Real-user figures move over weeks, so judge a fix after a few weeks of visits.
tech: Only with --pagespeed. One GET per page to pagespeedonline.googleapis.com (strategy MOBILE, category PERFORMANCE; no key and no other host or method) for the checked page and the first same-site pages of the run's sample, at most 5. The page's address without its query string, fragment, user name or path parameter is sent to Google, and only a public page's: nothing is sent with --allow-private, and a numeric address, a name with no dot or a reserved or private-use ending (a trailing dot dropped), a wildcard-DNS name, a name that resolves to any private, loopback, link-local or metadata address (or does not resolve) and a path that is not plain (the root, or at most 6 parts and 120 characters, each a number of up to 4 digits or a short lowercase slug of whole words with no mixed letter-and-digit word, no secret-looking word and nothing shaped like an email address) are never sent; no rule can see a person's name written as a slug, which is why the flag is opt-in and are could-not-check. The calls go one at a time. The Chrome UX Report's figures in the answer decide: a vital is good when at least 75% of loads (the raw share, not rounded) are in the good bucket (the 75th percentile is within web.dev's limit: 2.5 s, 200 ms, 0.1) and poor when more than 25% are in the poor bucket (over 4 s, 500 ms, 0.25); the answer's own percentile value is not used. Poor is medium, needs improvement is low. Lab scores never decide. A page with too few visitors uses the whole site's figures and says so; no real-user data, a vital that is missing or whose buckets are not those limits, a refusal (HTTP 429 when the shared keyless quota is used up) and an unreachable Google are could-not-check, never a pass. The same answers give the same findings
done: Real visitors' 75th-percentile Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift are all in web.dev's good range, as Google's PageSpeed Insights reports them for the page; running Gaugeline with --pagespeed again shows the shares.
estimateChanges: A day or two for one slow image, a late font or a layout shift from an ad or embed with no reserved space. A week or more when the cause is the framework, a tag manager full of tags or a plugin stack, and it has to be measured after each change.

title: WordPress, a plugin or a theme is older than its current release
what: Gaugeline reads the WordPress version a page shows (the generator tag, or the version on the files WordPress loads from wp-includes) and the version of each plugin and theme in the addresses of the files the page loads, and compares them with the current releases the public wordpress.org API lists.
why: Most WordPress updates fix something, and a site that falls behind keeps the problems the updates fixed. This states which versions are shown and which are current; it does not say a site can be attacked. A site that hides its versions is not reported as up to date: Gaugeline says it could not check.
fix: Take a backup, update on a staging copy if there is one, then update WordPress, the plugins and the theme the finding names, and look at the pages that use them. A premium plugin that is not in the wordpress.org directory is updated from its own vendor and is listed as could-not-check here.
tech: Only with --wordpress. The version of WordPress is the generator meta tag (WordPress 6.4.2), else the ?ver= on the core files under /wp-includes/ (the emoji and block-library files); a plugin's or theme's version is the ?ver= on its files under /wp-content/plugins/<slug>/ or /wp-content/themes/<slug>/, read as a release number written with dots (2.1.3, 5.8, 1.0.0-beta2) and never a date, a hash or a timestamp, which are cache-busters; a number that is WordPress's own (what WordPress writes when a plugin gives none) is not the plugin's, and neither is the number on a file the plugin bundles from another project (a vendor, lib or fonts folder, or a file such as font-awesome, bootstrap or swiper), which is that project's. What a page declares is only what its files say: a version newer than the directory's current release is could-not-check, not current. A plugin whose files carry more than one number, or none, is could-not-check. The current releases are one GET each to https://api.wordpress.org/core/version-check/1.7/ and https://api.wordpress.org/plugins/info/1.2/ (themes/info/1.2/ for a theme) with the slug the page shows, no key and nothing sent, at most 15 plugins and 15 themes for the whole run, shared by every page (the rest are listed as could-not-check with their number). A plugin or theme not in the directory (a premium or custom one) is could-not-check. A page the run reaches on a site that is not WordPress is skipped. Versions are compared as whole numbers in four parts (5.10 is after 5.8), and each component is reported once per run, on the first page that shows it.
done: WordPress, the plugins and the theme the finding names are on their current release (or the client has decided with the developer why one stays), and running Gaugeline again shows the new version numbers.
estimateChanges: An hour when the site has a staging copy and the updates are clean. A day or more when a plugin is years behind, the theme is customised, or nobody has tested updates on this site before.

title: The site's REST API lists its users to anyone
what: Gaugeline asks the site's REST API for its list of users the way a visitor's browser can, with no login, and reports when it answers with users.
why: The list gives each author's display name and the slug that is often also the login name, so anyone can learn who the accounts are before guessing passwords. It is on by default in WordPress, which is why it is common, and closing it costs a site very little. This is a fact about what is listed, not a sign of a break-in.
fix: Restrict the users route to logged-in users: most security plugins have the setting, or a short snippet in the theme's functions.php removes it for visitors. Check the author archive pages the theme shows, and that no plugin or app on the site needs the list public.
tech: Only with --wordpress. One GET of the REST root the page names in its api.w.org link (the same site only), /wp-json/wp/v2/users?per_page=100&_fields=id, with no key; if /wp-json/ answers 404, one GET of /?rest_route=/wp/v2/users (a site with plain permalinks). Only the id is asked for, so no name or slug is sent back, and only how many users were listed is kept and shown. A 401, 403 or 404 from both routes, or an empty list, is not exposed. Any other answer, an answer that is not a list, or a request that fails is could-not-check. The route is a documented, public REST route, so it is not a probing check under rule 14; it is still off unless --wordpress is given. Pages of a site that is not WordPress are skipped, and the site is asked once per run.
done: The REST API's list of users answers a visitor with no login with an error or an empty list, and running Gaugeline again finds no users listed.
estimateChanges: Minutes with a hardening plugin or a small snippet in the theme. A site whose app or booking plugin needs the list public takes longer, because it has to be given another way first.

title: Fulfillment lists a different price
what: A synced Printful variant's retail price is different from the price Stripe charges for the product.
why: Anything that reads Printful's price (a storefront sync, an invoice, a packing slip) shows customers a different number from the one they paid.
fix: Decide which price you mean, then change the other so the two agree, or have Printful's retail price follow checkout.
tech: each synced sync_variants.retail_price of the matched Printful product against the unit_amount of the matched Stripe product's default price, both whole minor units; compared only when the variant's currency is known and equal to Stripe's (a different currency is a notice, never converted); a variant with no retail price, or a Stripe default price with no fixed amount, is skipped with a notice; one finding per product listing up to three differing variants and both match rules
done: Fulfillment and checkout list the same price.
estimateChanges: Deciding which system owns the price comes first.

title: No default price in checkout
what: An active Stripe product that is matched to a product on your website has no default price.
why: Anything that asks Stripe for the product's price (a payment link, a checkout session, a price comparison) finds nothing, and the product cannot be bought or compared.
fix: In Stripe, open the product and set one of its prices as the default, or archive the product if it is no longer sold.
tech: a matched Stripe product with active true and default_price null, whether or not it has other prices; the evidence says how many prices it has; archived products and Stripe products with no Sanity partner are not reported
done: The product has a default price in Stripe, or is archived.
estimateChanges: Several products are one edit each.

title: A plan's free trial differs from checkout
what: The page promises a free trial that the matched Stripe price does not give, or Stripe gives a trial the page never mentions.
why: Someone who signs up for a free trial and is charged today, or who is surprised by a trial that hides when the first bill comes, files a dispute.
fix: Make the page and the Stripe price agree on the trial's length, or take the promise off the page.
tech: a trial of N days, weeks or months written next to the plan's name (7-day free trial, prueba gratis de 7 dias) against recurring.trial_period_days of the matched price (a month is 28 to 31 days); a trial set when checkout is created (subscription_data) is not visible on the price, so confirm there before changing the page
done: The page and the Stripe price agree on the trial length, or the promise is removed.
estimateChanges: A trial changed in Stripe affects customers who are already on it.

title: A query does not leave drafts out
what: The filter of a query in your code does not leave drafts out.
why: With the published perspective in the client that is safe. If anything runs the query with drafts included (preview mode, a token with the wrong perspective), unpublished content reaches a visitor.
fix: Add !(_id in path("drafts.**")) to the filter, or make sure the client always asks for the published perspective. Gaugeline cannot see the client, only the query.
tech: read from the repository with no request: the query's filter is parsed and does not require !(_id in path("drafts.**")) (or match "drafts.*") in an && chain
done: The query filters out drafts, or the client always asks for the published perspective.
estimateChanges: The same query pattern repeated in many files is one edit each.

title: Two documents share a title
what: Two or more published documents of one type are called the same thing, ignoring case and spaces around the title.
why: Different addresses, same name: usually content that was duplicated and not moved, which splits search results between two pages. It can also be two real pages that need different names.
fix: Open the documents named by their ids. If one is a copy, delete it and redirect its address; if both are real, rename one so a visitor can tell them apart.
tech: one GET of the query endpoint for each document type (perspective=published, so drafts are never read), projecting only _id, "slug": slug.current and title; one pass puts each id into a Map from the slug as it is, or from the trimmed and lower-cased title, to the ids that have it, and a bucket with more than one id is a group; documents with no slug or no title are left out of that key, a draft id is skipped, and types are grouped apart; a title shared by two or more ids of one type that do not all share one slug
done: Each document has its own title, or the copy is deleted with a redirect.
estimateChanges: A copy already linked from elsewhere needs a redirect.

title: A query fetches a field the code never reads
what: A query in your code asks for a field, and nothing that receives the result ever reads it.
why: Every field you ask for is data your visitors download and your server waits for, and nobody sees it. Over a few months a query collects fields from pages that changed, and the page gets slower for content it never shows.
fix: Open the file and line named and take the field out of the query, unless something Gaugeline cannot read (a script, another repository) uses it. A query listed as could not follow was left alone on purpose: its result goes somewhere Gaugeline cannot read, so none of its fields were reported.
tech: read from the repository with no request and no key: each groq template, defineQuery call and gql template is read into a tree of the fields it returns, named by alias ("slug": slug.current is slug), and the TypeScript compiler's symbols follow the result through variables, await, destructuring, props passed to components, map callbacks, returns and spreads into JSX props; a field counts as read when a property access or a destructuring reads its alias on a value that came from the query, held in a Map from query to the Set of aliases read, so unused is the aliases projected minus the aliases read; _id, _type, _key and _rev are never reported; a query whose result escapes (JSON.stringify, a function from a package, a field read by a name only known at run time) is listed as could not follow and none of its fields is reported
done: The field is out of the query, unless a script or another repository uses it.
estimateChanges: Gaugeline cannot see other repositories, so someone has to check before the field is dropped.

title: A write edits published content directly
what: A patch, createOrReplace or delete in your code has no drafts handling: its id is not a drafts. id.
why: It changes the published document directly. An editor who has unpublished changes in the Studio can lose them, or have them published by the next write.
fix: Patch the draft (the id with "drafts." in front) and let an editor publish, or leave it as it is if writing straight to the published document is what you want.
tech: read from the repository with no request at all: the TypeScript compiler reads client.patch(...).set(...), create, createOrReplace, createIfNotExists, delete, transaction chains and raw mutations arrays into a Map from each written field to the kind of its value (a plain string, an object with _ref, anything else), which is compared with the schema file given by --schema (the output of sanity schema extract); no mutation is sent, and the module cannot import an HTTP client; an id that does not start with drafts. and is not built by something named like a draft helper
done: The write patches the draft and an editor publishes, or writing to the published document is recorded as intended.
estimateChanges: Routes that write in several places each need the change, and editors need a publish step.

title: Two routes write the same field
what: Two or more routes in your code write the same field of the same document type.
why: Each route assumes it owns the field. When their rules differ, the last one to run wins, and the value drifts without anyone changing it on purpose.
fix: Decide which route owns the field and have the others call it, or accept it if they are meant to share it.
tech: read from the repository with no request at all: the TypeScript compiler reads client.patch(...).set(...), create, createOrReplace, createIfNotExists, delete, transaction chains and raw mutations arrays into a Map from each written field to the kind of its value (a plain string, an object with _ref, anything else), which is compared with the schema file given by --schema (the output of sanity schema extract); no mutation is sent, and the module cannot import an HTTP client; a Map from type.field to the routes that patch or replace it, and an entry with more than one route; a patch of a field that several types declare is not attributed to a type
done: One route owns the field and the others call it, or the sharing is recorded as intended.
estimateChanges: Deciding which route owns it comes first.

title: A webhook endpoint is switched off
what: A Stripe webhook endpoint has the status disabled.
why: Stripe sends a disabled endpoint nothing. If your site still depends on it, payments are made and the site is not told.
fix: If the endpoint is still needed, enable it in the Stripe dashboard (Stripe may have disabled it after days of failures, so read its last attempts first). If it is not, delete it so the list says what is live.
tech: GET /v1/webhook_endpoints; an endpoint whose status is disabled is a finding, whatever it takes; the evidence is the endpoint's host only
done: The endpoint is enabled in the Stripe dashboard, or deleted if it is no longer needed.
estimateChanges: Stripe disables an endpoint after days of failures, so the failures need reading first.

title: Supabase's security advisor reports a problem
what: Supabase's own security advisor reports a lint at ERROR or WARN level for the project.
why: The advisor is Supabase's own reading of the project's security settings. A lint left open is a known weakness in the database behind the site, found by the vendor and waiting for someone to act.
fix: Open Advisors, then Security Advisor, in the Supabase dashboard; each lint links to its remediation page. Fix the ERROR ones first.
tech: read through Supabase's hosted MCP server in read-only mode (get_advisors with type security); only each lint's code (a lower-case id), level and facing are kept, never its title, description or remediation text; lints are grouped by code and level, INFO is not reported, and rls_disabled_in_public is left to supabase-rls-off when the table list was read
done: Supabase's security advisor shows no ERROR or WARN lint for the project.
estimateChanges: Each lint names its own fix; some are one setting, some change how a function or a view is written.

title: The indexing switch accepts more than "true"
what: The environment variable that turns indexing on is accepted when it is `1`, `yes`, any non-empty text, or anything but one word, instead of only the exact text "true".
why: An environment variable is text, and people mistype it. If anything but `true` turns indexing on, an unset variable on a new preview, a typo or a value of `1` puts a site that should be hidden in front of search engines. Only an exact `true` should do that.
fix: Compare it with the exact text: `process.env.INDEXING === "true"`. Remove `!== "false"`, `Boolean(...)`, `!!...` and the bare `?` test, and set the variable to the word `true` on the host that should be indexed.
tech: static, reads the folder's code files as text and makes no request; a read of an environment variable belongs to the indexing switch when it is inside a robots value, a robots file or near an X-Robots-Tag header, or its name has INDEX, CRAWL, ROBOTS or SEO in it; === "true" (also after toLowerCase or trim) passes; another literal, !== a literal, Boolean(...), !!..., !..., a bare ?, && or || test, or the value passed on as it is, is a finding; a name that reads the other way round (NO_INDEX, BLOCK_CRAWLERS), !== "true", and a test that could not be read are not sure; the value is never printed, only the variable name, the file and the line
done: The setting that turns indexing on is tested against the exact text "true", and nothing else turns it on.
estimateChanges: One comparison per place the setting is read. If the variable is already set to 1 or yes on the host, it is changed there at the same time.

title: The noindex smoke test runs on previews but not on production
what: A CI workflow checks noindex (or X-Robots-Tag) on preview deployments, and no workflow does the same for production.
why: Production is where indexing matters. A test that only watches previews proves the preview is hidden; it says nothing about the live site, so a setting changed at launch (or one that never changed) goes unnoticed.
fix: Run the same test against the production deployment after each production deploy (a workflow on the main branch, or a deployment_status trigger for the Production environment). Expect the opposite there once the site is live: no noindex.
tech: static, reads .github/workflows files as text (comments are skipped) and makes no request; a workflow has the test when it mentions noindex or x-robots-tag; it targets previews when it says preview or runs on pull_request or deployment_status, and production when it says production or prod or runs on main or master; a finding when a workflow tests previews and no workflow with the test says anything about production; a workflow with the test and neither word, or a workflow file that could not be read, is not sure; no workflow files, or no test at all, passes (nothing is missing)
done: The CI workflows check the indexing setting on the production deployment as well as on previews.
estimateChanges: Usually one more step or trigger beside the preview test. If production is deployed outside CI, the check has to be run by whatever deploys it.

title: The webhook signature is compared with a plain comparison
what: The code that receives a Sanity publish webhook compares the signature (or a shared secret) with ===, !==, == or !=, instead of a constant-time comparison.
why: A plain comparison stops at the first character that differs, so how long it takes can tell a caller how much of a guess was right. A constant-time comparison takes the same time whatever the input. The official @sanity/webhook helper, read in its source at 4.0.4, itself compares with a plain `!==`, so using it is reported as advice, not as a failure.
fix: Compare with crypto.timingSafeEqual on two Buffers, after checking their lengths are equal (timingSafeEqual throws when they differ, so return a 401 first).
tech: reads the code files of the folder named, never runs them; a receiver is a file that imports @sanity/webhook or next-sanity/webhook, reads the sanity-webhook-signature header, or is a route that revalidates behind a secret; a finding is a ===, !==, == or != with a signature, hmac, digest, hash, secret or token on one side and something that is not a literal, a length, a type test or a yes-or-no on the other; timingSafeEqual in the file passes; the official helper alone is an advice finding (worth knowing) and not a failure; a receiver with none of these is could-not-check; the finding names the file and the line, never the values
done: The receiver compares the signature with crypto.timingSafeEqual on two buffers of the same length.
estimateChanges: A few lines in one route file; larger if the receiver is copied into several routes.

title: The webhook's signed timestamp has no age limit
what: The code that receives a Sanity publish webhook reads the signed timestamp but does not reject one that is old, or one that is in the future.
why: The signature covers the timestamp and the body, but a request that was captured once stays valid for as long as nothing compares the timestamp with the time now. Anyone who can capture a delivery can send it again. The official @sanity/webhook helper, read in its source at 4.0.4, makes no age check, so a receiver that only uses it has none, and is reported as advice.
fix: Read t from the signature header, and reject the request with a 401 when Math.abs(Date.now() - t) is more than a few minutes (five is common). Check the signature first, so the rejection does not leak which part was wrong.
tech: reads the code files of the folder named, never runs them; a receiver is a file that imports @sanity/webhook or next-sanity/webhook, reads the sanity-webhook-signature header, or is a route that revalidates behind a secret; a file that reads the timestamp (a t= pattern, or a name such as timestamp or signedAt) and never compares it with Date.now() is a finding; Math.abs of the distance passes; an age test without a future test, or the other way round, is a finding; a file that only uses the official helper is an advice finding (worth knowing); a comparison Gaugeline cannot read, or a receiver with no timestamp and no helper, is could-not-check; the finding names the file and the line, never the values
done: The receiver rejects a signed timestamp that is more than a few minutes old, and one that is in the future.
estimateChanges: A few lines in one route file, once the timestamp is read from the header; larger if the receiver only uses the official helper, which hides it.

title: The webhook body is parsed before its signature is checked, or read with no size limit
what: The code that receives a Sanity publish webhook parses the body (req.json(), or Next's parsed req.body) before the signature is checked over the raw body, or reads the whole body with no size limit.
why: The signature is over the raw bytes the sender sent, and the helper's documentation says to pass it the payload straight from the request, not a re-encoded JSON string. Parsing first and signing the re-encoded value can make a valid delivery fail, or hide a difference between what was signed and what is used. A body read in full with no size limit can be made to use a lot of memory by anyone who sends one, before the signature is looked at.
fix: Check the Content-Length header against a limit (64 KB is plenty for a publish), read the body once as text with req.text(), check the signature over that text, and only then JSON.parse it. In a pages/api route, export config with api.bodyParser set to false.
tech: reads the code files of the folder named, never runs them; a receiver is a file that imports @sanity/webhook or next-sanity/webhook, reads the sanity-webhook-signature header, or is a route that revalidates behind a secret; req.json() with no raw read, or JSON.parse before the first signature step, or req.body in a pages/api route without bodyParser false, is a finding; a raw read or the helper's parseBody with no content-length check, stream reader or limit option is a finding; a receiver with neither a body read nor the helper is could-not-check; the finding names the file and the line, never the body
done: The receiver checks the size, reads the raw body, checks the signature over it, and only then parses it.
estimateChanges: A few lines in one route file; larger if the receiver is a pages/api route that must turn the body parser off.

title: The webhook receiver writes the body, an id or a secret to its logs
what: The code that receives a Sanity publish webhook writes the request body, a document id, the signature or the secret to a log.
why: Logs are kept, copied to other tools and read by more people than the content or the secret was meant for. A publish body holds the document's content (a clinic's notice, a customer's name in a booking), and a secret in a log is a secret that has leaked.
fix: Log what happened, not what was received: the document type, the status you answered with, a count. If you need to trace one delivery, log a short random id you made up, not Sanity's document id.
tech: reads the code files of the folder named, never runs them; a receiver is a file that imports @sanity/webhook or next-sanity/webhook, reads the sanity-webhook-signature header, or is a route that revalidates behind a secret; the arguments of every console, logger or log call (log, info, warn, error, debug, trace) are read, strings blanked; a name for the body (body, rawBody, payload, req.body), a document id (_id, documentId), the signature, or the secret read from process.env, is a finding that names the kind, the file and the line, never the value; nothing else in the call is printed
done: The receiver's log lines hold the document type, the status and what happened, and never the body, an id, the signature or the secret.
estimateChanges: One or two log lines in one route file; larger if a shared logger prints whole requests.

title: A read is cached for a time and by a tag
what: One read sets both a revalidate time and tags, or a file sets a revalidate time for a page whose reads use tags.
why: With tags, the content changes when an editor publishes and your webhook clears the tag. With a revalidate time as well, the same read is also refreshed on a timer, so the page can change with no publish, and a missed webhook is hidden until the timer runs out. Both are documented Next.js options for different jobs; together, it is hard to say from the code when a page will change.
fix: Pick one per read. If a publish clears the tag, drop the revalidate time. If you want a timer (for a feed with no webhook), drop the tags.
tech: reads the code files of the folder named, never runs them; a revalidate that is a number above zero, in an object that also has a tags option (a fetch's next option, or unstable_cache's options), or as a file's own `revalidate` setting in a file whose fetches use tags, is a finding naming the file and the line; revalidate false or 0 is not a timer; a revalidate that is not a number or false, in an object with tags, is could-not-check; the finding never prints the tags or the time
done: Each read is cached either for a time or by a tag, not both.
estimateChanges: One option per read; larger if the time was chosen because publishing does not clear the tag yet.

title: A query asks for a reference without following it
what: A GROQ query lists a reference field (an author, a category, a linked page) and does not follow it with ->, so the result holds a reference and not the document.
why: A page built from that result has an id where the author's name, the category's title or the linked page's address should be: a link that goes nowhere, a name that is missing, or the text [object Object] on the page.
fix: Follow the reference and say what you want from it: author->{ name, 'photo': image.asset->url }. For a list of references, author[]->{ name }.
tech: reads the folder's code files (.env files never): the names of the schema fields declared with type reference (also as the members of an array of references), and the GROQ queries written as string or template literals that start with *[; a projection item that is exactly such a name, or an alias of it, and is not followed by -> is a finding (the file, the line and the field's name); a name used elsewhere in the schema for a non-reference field is a false positive; no query is run; no schema in the folder, or no query written in the source, is could-not-check
done: Every reference a query asks for is followed with -> and the fields wanted, so the page gets the name or image and not an id.
estimateChanges: Adding -> and a projection is a line per query. A query shared by many pages means checking each page's use of the result.

title: An image field can be published with no alt text
what: A Sanity schema has an image field with no alt-text field, or an alt-text field an editor is not required to fill in.
why: Alt text is what a screen reader says and what shows when a picture does not load. If the editor can leave it empty, some pictures will go live without it, and nobody sees the gap until someone who cannot see the picture visits.
fix: Add a field to the image: defineField({ name: 'alt', type: 'string', title: 'Alternative text', validation: (Rule) => Rule.required() }). For a picture that is only decoration, give editors an explicit choice rather than an empty field.
tech: reads the folder's code files (.env files never); in the files that define a Sanity schema, an object with type image whose fields list has no field named alt, altText or alt_text, or whose alt field has no validation calling required(, is a finding (the file, the line and the field's name); an image type defined once and reused is read where it is defined; no Sanity schema in the folder is could-not-check; the page-side half (an image block with no asset) is not read here
done: Every image field has an alt-text field that an editor must fill in before publishing.
estimateChanges: Adding the field and the rule is a few lines per image field. Writing alt text for pictures already published is the real work, and it is the client's or yours to schedule.

title: A page section and its component do not match
what: A section the schema lets editors add has no component in the page renderer, or the renderer has a component that no schema section matches.
why: A section with no component renders nothing: an editor adds a gallery to the page, publishes, and the page looks the same. A component with no schema is code nobody can reach, and it tends to be copied around until someone changes the wrong one.
fix: For each section the schema lists, add its component to the renderer's map (or its case). For a component with no section, either add the section to the schema's list or delete the component.
tech: reads the folder's code files (.env files never); the type names listed as members of an array field named sections, blocks, pageBuilder, content or modules in the files that define a schema, against the renderer: the files outside the schema that mention _type; a section name that appears quoted in no renderer file is a finding (the schema file and line); a renderer object with two or more name: Component entries, one of whose keys matches no name in the schema, is a finding (the renderer file and line); no section array in the schema, or no renderer file, is could-not-check
done: Every section type an editor can add has a component, and every component has a section type.
estimateChanges: Adding a missing component is the real work, and depends on its design. Deleting a dead one is minutes.

title: Sanity's hidden editing text is not cleaned where it must be
what: The project turns on Sanity's click-to-edit encoding, and a file that fetches content compares it, builds a link or attribute from it, or uses it in metadata without stegaClean.
why: Click-to-edit works by hiding invisible characters inside the text a query returns. Where that text is compared with a word, used as a link, or put in a page title, the hidden characters make the comparison false, the link wrong or the title carry junk, and it only happens in preview, so it is hard to see.
fix: Wrap the value in stegaClean (from @sanity/client/stega) before you compare it, use it in a URL or attribute, or put it in metadata. Leave visible text as it comes, so click-to-edit keeps working.
tech: reads the folder's code files (.env files never); looks first for the setup (stega: true or an object, defineLive, VisualEditing, studioUrl): none found means nothing is encoded and the check passes; then, in each file that fetches Sanity content (.fetch(, sanityFetch(, urlFor() and does not mention stegaClean, a metadata title or description built from a property, a property compared with a string literal (fields starting with an underscore are left alone), or an href, src, id, target or rel built from a property, is a finding (the file, the line and what it is); over-cleaned visible text needs a rendered page and is not read; no source file read, or some left out, is could-not-check
done: Wherever fetched text is compared, used in a link or attribute, or put in metadata, it goes through stegaClean first.
estimateChanges: Wrapping each use in stegaClean is a small change per file. Finding every place the text travels in a larger site is the real work.

title: A form endpoint accepts posts with no origin check, honeypot or token
what: A route handler or API route takes a form submission and has no check of where it came from, no honeypot field and no signed or captcha token.
why: Anyone, or any script, can post to the address. The kitchen channel and the inbox fill with spam, a booking list fills with fake dates, and another site can make a visitor's browser post to yours.
fix: Check the Origin header against your own site, add a hidden honeypot field that a person never fills in, and add a captcha or a signed token if spam continues. Or move the form to a Server Action, where Next compares the Origin with the site's host for you.
tech: reads the folder's code files (.env files never); a route.ts handler that exports POST, or a pages/api route, that reads the submitted body and has none of: the Origin or Referer header, a honeypot, a captcha or signed token (Turnstile, reCAPTCHA, hCaptcha, CSRF, nonce, HMAC, signature), a session check, is a finding; paths named webhook, hooks, stripe, cron, auth, callback, revalidate, trpc or graphql are not forms and are left alone; Server Actions are not looked at; when a middleware or proxy file mentions an origin or token check the result is could-not-check; the finding is the file and the line of POST; no source file read, or some left out, is could-not-check
done: Every public form endpoint checks the Origin header, a honeypot field or a signed token before it acts on a submission.
estimateChanges: A honeypot field and an Origin check are a few lines. A captcha such as Turnstile also needs a key and a change to the form. Moving the endpoint to a Server Action avoids the Origin check by hand.

title: A module needs the content token just to be imported
what: A module throws, at the top level, when a content-system token (Sanity, Contentful and others) is not set.
why: Everything that imports the module, even for a page that never reads a draft, now fails without the secret: every build, every test run, every preview and every CI job. A freelancer ends up putting a fake token in each of them, and a missing token breaks the whole site instead of the one page that needed it.
fix: Read the token inside the function that needs it (the draft preview, the write), and throw there. Public published reads need no token at all.
tech: reads the folder's code files (.env files never); at the top level of a module (not inside a function or block), an if whose condition reads a variable named like a content-system token (a content system's name and TOKEN, SECRET or KEY) or a constant set from it and whose body throws, an invariant or assert call of it, or the variable followed by ?? or || and a throw, is a finding; the finding is the file, the line and the variable's name; NEXT_PUBLIC_ names, scripts, seed, migrations and bin folders, *.config.* files and sanity.cli files are left alone; no source file read, or some left out, is could-not-check
done: Importing a module never needs the content token: it is read inside the function that uses it, on the draft or write path only.
estimateChanges: Wrapping the read in a function is minutes. A token read in many modules at the top level means going through each import.

title: A 'use server' file exports something that is not an async function
what: A file that starts with 'use server' exports a constant, a plain function, a class or an enum next to its server functions.
why: A 'use server' file is a file of server functions that client components import and call, and the examples in Next.js's documentation export only async functions there. A constant or helper exported from it is not a server function and does not belong in it. Putting the value in a module of its own keeps the file's exports honest.
fix: Move the constant, helper or class to another module and import it where needed. If it must stay on the server, start that module with import 'server-only', so a client import fails the build.
tech: reads the folder's code files (.env files never); in a file whose first statement is 'use server', a top-level export of a const, let or var whose value is plainly not async (a literal, object, array, new, class, function, non-async arrow), a non-async function, a class or an enum is a finding; type-only exports are ignored; an export whose kind the text cannot settle (a wrapped call, an imported name, export *) is could-not-check; the finding is the file, the line and the exported name; no source file read, or some left out, is could-not-check
done: Every export of a 'use server' file is an async function; constants, helpers and classes live in a module of their own.
estimateChanges: Moving a constant or helper to its own file is minutes. A helper imported by many client components means updating each import.

title: An accessibility test passes when the page has violations
what: A test that scans a page with axe asserts that violations exist (greater than 0, not equal to an empty list) instead of asserting that there are none.
why: The test is green while the page is inaccessible, and turns red on the day the page is fixed. Everyone who sees a green accessibility test believes the page was checked and found clean. For a bar's booking page or a clinic's contact form, that is a person who cannot book.
fix: Assert that there are none: expect(results.violations).toEqual([]), as Playwright's accessibility guide does. If a test deliberately scans a broken page to prove the scanner works, keep it, name the page and the test so that is clear, and add the same scan of the real page with the assertion above.
tech: static, reads the test files of the folder (a .test or .spec file, or a code file in a tests, test, e2e or __tests__ folder) as text, never runs them, and makes no request; a test is an accessibility test when it mentions an axe package (@axe-core/playwright, axe-core, jest-axe, vitest-axe, cypress-axe), AxeBuilder or checkA11y; in one, an expect of something named violations compared with toBeGreaterThan(0), toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1), toBeTruthy(), not.toEqual([]) or not.toBe(0), or expect(violations > 0).toBe(true), is a finding that names the file and line; a test file that was not read, with nothing found, is not sure; only the file and line are printed
done: The accessibility tests assert that the scan finds no violations.
estimateChanges: One assertion per test; larger if the page has real violations that the test was written around and now need fixing.

title: The licence notice of a starter project is not in the folder
what: The folder says its code is MIT or ISC licensed, or says it was made from a starter or template, and no file in it holds the MIT or ISC licence text.
why: The MIT and ISC licences let anyone use the code on one condition: the copyright and permission notice must stay with copies of it. Starting a client's site from a public starter and deleting its LICENSE file breaks that condition, and it is the kind of thing a client's lawyer or an acquirer finds in the first hour. Gaugeline cannot see where the code came from: it can only say that a notice is missing and what made that matter. It does not say that anything was copied.
fix: Copy the starter's LICENSE file into the project (or its text into a NOTICE or THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES file), keeping the copyright line. If nothing from a starter is in the project, say so in the README, or change the license field in package.json.
tech: static, reads the folder's text files (including a LICENSE, LICENCE, COPYING or NOTICE file with no extension) and makes no request; a notice is the permission sentence of the MIT or ISC licence found in any file; a finding when no file holds one and package.json declares MIT or ISC, or the README says the project is based on, forked or cloned from, or built from a starter, template or boilerplate, naming the file and line and never printing text; a licence file that holds some other text, or a folder the reader did not finish, is not sure; no notice and nothing that says where the code came from is not sure, never a pass; a notice found anywhere passes
done: The folder holds the MIT or ISC licence text of the starter the project was made from, with its copyright line.
estimateChanges: Copy the licence file from the starter's repository; larger if more than one starter was used or nobody remembers which.

title: The certificate no longer covers a name it did
what: The https certificate after cutover lacks a name the one before covered (www, a subdomain), or there is no certificate where there was one.
why: Visitors on the name that dropped off see a security warning instead of the site.
fix: Add the missing name to the new host's certificate (most hosts add www as a separate domain).
tech: Names from subjectAltName, a wildcard covering one label. A new issuer or a renewed date alone is not a change
done: The new certificate covers every name the old one did.
estimateChanges: Most hosts add www as a separate domain, and each extra name is one more.

title: The domain's DNS records changed at cutover
what: Against the snapshot taken before cutover, the domain's DMARC record, a DKIM key (for the selectors in gaugeline.cutover.json) or its address records (A, AAAA) are different.
why: A lost DKIM key or DMARC record breaks mail authentication quietly; new address records are the cutover itself, worth confirming they point where the new host says.
fix: Check each value against what the new host and your mail provider publish. List a change that was meant under expectedChanges in gaugeline.cutover.json.
tech: TXT at _dmarc.<domain> (v=DMARC1), TXT at <selector>._domainkey.<domain>, A and AAAA at the domain; sets compared. A lookup that failed in either run is could not check
done: Each changed record matches what the new host and the mail provider publish, or is listed under expectedChanges.
estimateChanges: The number of records, and records edited at both a registrar and a host.

title: An old address takes more than one redirect to reach its page
what: An address from the old site reaches its page on the new site only after two or more redirects, or never settles because the redirects loop.
why: Every extra redirect is another round trip for the visitor, and search engines pass less on through each one and may stop following a long chain.
fix: Point the old address straight at the page's final address with a single 301, and make the slash, www and https rules agree with it.
tech: The redirects of the GET to each path on the new site are counted from the fetcher's record of every hop. One redirect is accepted; two or more, or a loop, is the finding. A trail that ends in 404 is migration-page-missing instead.
done: Each old address that moved reaches its new address in a single redirect.
estimateChanges: Usually one rule changed in the host's redirect settings. A chain made of a framework's trailing-slash rule plus a manual redirect needs the manual one pointed at the final address.

title: A page's title changed in the move
what: The title the old site gave a page (its name in the list, and the old page's <title>) does not match the new page's <title>, og:title or first heading.
why: The title is what a search result shows. A title that changed by accident, because a CMS field was not mapped, can cost clicks and rankings the page had earned.
fix: Put the old title back in the new page's title field, or leave the new one if you changed it on purpose.
tech: Both titles are lower-cased with accents, punctuation and spacing removed; they match when equal or when one holds the other as whole words, so adding or dropping the site's name is not a change. The list's title is compared with the new <title>, og:title and first <h1>; the old page's <title> with the new <title> and og:title. With neither an old title nor an old page, the page is could-not-check.
done: Each page that moved has the title it had, or a change you made on purpose.
estimateChanges: One field per page in the CMS. A title built from a template that was mapped wrongly changes them all at once.

title: A page's canonical address changed in the move
what: The old page named an address as its canonical, and the new page names a different one (or none), and neither is the address the page now lives at.
why: The canonical tells search engines which address to keep. One that points at the blog index, the home page or an address that redirects asks them to drop the page.
fix: Make the new page's canonical the address it is served at. If it moved, that is its new address; the old address should redirect to it.
tech: Paths are compared (the host is left out, since a preview and the live site differ), ignoring a trailing slash and case. The new canonical must equal the old canonical's path or the path the redirects ended on. Needs the old page: with --old, the old site's own address; a page with no old canonical is skipped.
done: Each page's canonical is the address it had, or the address the page now lives at.
estimateChanges: One setting in the framework or the SEO plugin's replacement, then a rebuild. A canonical built from the wrong base address changes every page.

title: A page lost a structured data type in the move
what: The old page had structured data of a type (Article, FAQPage, Event, Product, Recipe, LocalBusiness, BreadcrumbList) that the new page no longer has.
why: Structured data is what earns a page its rich result in search: the FAQ dropdown, the event date, the star rating. Without it the page appears as a plain link.
fix: Add the missing JSON-LD to the new page's template, filled from the page's own content, and test it with a rich results tester.
tech: The @type of every JSON-LD node (an @graph read through) and every microdata itemtype, on the old and the new page. Types that describe the whole site (WebSite, WebPage, Organization, Person, ImageObject, SearchAction) are left out. A type the old page had and the new one lacks is the finding; a new type is not. Needs the old page: with --old, the old site's own address.
done: Each page still carries the structured data types it had (Article, FAQPage, Event, Product and so on).
estimateChanges: A type the new build never wrote means adding the JSON-LD to the page template and filling its fields from the CMS. One template covers every page of its kind.

title: Work saved in the Webflow CMS is not on the live site
what: A collection item was saved as ready (not a draft) and has never been published, or it was changed after it was last published, so the live site still shows the old version or none.
why: The client believes the change is out. Customers see the old price, the old opening hours, or no page for the event they were told about.
fix: In Webflow, review the staged items and publish the site. If an item should not go out yet, set it back to draft so it is not mistaken for finished work.
tech: GET /v2/collections/{id}/items (the staged list) for each collection: isDraft false, isArchived false, and lastPublished absent (staged) or more than 2 seconds earlier than lastUpdated (changed). Drafts and archived items are never reported. Ids, slugs and dates only: no field is used for this.
done: Every item the client saved is published, or is a draft on purpose, and a run of Gaugeline lists none that is staged.
estimateChanges: Publishing is one click in Webflow, but it publishes the whole site, so check what else is waiting before you do. Allow longer where the client has to approve the wording first.

title: A Shopify theme preview link on the live site can be indexed
what: The live site links to a theme preview address (a preview_theme_id address, or a shopifypreview.com host), and that page has no noindex and no canonical pointing at the public page.
why: A preview shows an unfinished theme, can hold test content, and can compete with the real page in search.
fix: Remove the preview link from the page, menu or template that holds it. Share previews by sending the link directly, not by publishing it.
tech: One GET of the home page, then one GET of each linked address that carries preview_theme_id or is on the store's own shopifypreview.com host (at most 5, only addresses the site itself links to, and only on the site's own host, the store's own myshopify.com host or its own shopifypreview.com host: a link to another store's Shopify host is could-not-check and is not asked for; none is guessed). The address in a finding keeps only the preview_theme_id parameter. Indexable means a 2xx answer with no noindex in the robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag and no canonical to a different address.
done: No link on the live site leads to a theme preview that search engines may list.
estimateChanges: Removing a preview link from the theme or a page is a minute. A preview theme shared in a menu or a newsletter template needs the link found first.

title: A Squarespace product page and its stock disagree
what: A product page offers the product as in stock while the Squarespace Inventory API says every variant is out of stock, or says it is out of stock while the API says a variant can be bought.
why: Shoppers order what cannot be shipped, or leave a product that could have sold. Search results show the page's availability.
fix: Open the product in Squarespace and check each variant's stock. If the page is out of date, publish it again or clear a cache in front of the site.
tech: GET /1.0/commerce/products and GET /1.0/commerce/inventory (cursor pages; a key without the Inventory permission, or a plan that does not offer it, makes this check could-not-check and leaves the price check as it is), then one GET of each visible product's page. The API side: "in" when any variant has a row that is unlimited or has a quantity above 0, "out" when every variant has a row and none can be bought, otherwise unknown (a variant with no row is never read as out of stock). The page side: the Product offers' availability in its JSON-LD (InStock, OutOfStock, SoldOut ...), or the page's one add-to-cart button saying sold out when the product data names no availability (no other button counts); mixed or missing words are unknown. Only "in" against "out", either way round, is a finding; unknown on either side is could-not-check. Findings carry a word and a name, never a quantity or a page's text
done: No product page offers something the Squarespace Inventory API says is sold out, or says sold out for something the API says is in stock.
estimateChanges: Usually one product: a stock count changed after the page was cached, or a variant was marked unlimited by mistake. Many products at once mean a cache in front of the site.

title: The Sitecore preview endpoint answers on the public site
what: gaugeline.adapters.json says the preview endpoint should not be reachable from the public site (expectPrivate: true), and a plain GET of its path on the public host, with no key, is answered by a GraphQL server.
why: The preview endpoint reads from the content management back end, so it can return content that has not been published. It is meant to be protected by its own API key, and its being on the public host means a visitor can reach it and the key is the only thing between them and draft content.
fix: Keep the preview endpoint off the public host: put the content management host on its own address that is not linked from the site, or block the path on the public host at the CDN or the web server, and send the preview key from the server only. If the endpoint is meant to be public, remove expectPrivate from gaugeline.adapters.json.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: this check asks the preview endpoint's path on the public site's own host, so it runs only with --owner-consent (or gaugeline.consent.json), on sites you own or have permission to test; only when the settings say expectPrivate: true; one GET of {site origin}/sitecore/api/graph/edge with no sc_apikey header, no cookie and no redirect followed, reading at most 8 KiB; a 200 or 400 whose body is a JSON object with a data or errors key is the finding (a GraphQL server answered a visitor with no key; no content is requested and none is read); 401 or 403 is a protected endpoint and 404 or 410 is a path that is not there, both with no finding; a 200 or 400 that is not a GraphQL answer (a page that answers every path) and any other status, redirects included, are could-not-check
done: The preview endpoint's path does not answer on the public site's host, because gaugeline.adapters.json says it should not (expectPrivate).
estimateChanges: Usually one rule on the host or the CDN in front of it: block the path /sitecore/api/graph/edge on the public host, or point the front end at the Delivery endpoint only. Allow longer if the public front end calls the preview endpoint from the browser and that call has to move to the server.

title: The Prismic cache is serving an older master ref than the origin
what: The repository's root on the public cache host (cdn.prismic.io) names a different master ref than the origin host (prismic.io) did on three reads six seconds apart, and the origin's ref shows a document published after the newest one the cache's ref shows.
why: A site built or rendered against the cache's ref keeps showing the older content, so what the client just published does not appear, and nothing on the site says so.
fix: Wait a minute and run again. If it stays, find what holds the old ref: a front end that stores the master ref at build time (ask for it again on each request, or rebuild from Prismic's publish webhook), or a proxy or hosting cache in front of the Prismic API. Prismic's own client keeps the ref for five seconds.
tech: GET /api/v2 on <repository>.cdn.prismic.io and on <repository>.prismic.io (the origin), no token unless the repository refuses without it (then an Authorization: Token header, never the address), reading the one ref with isMasterRef true from each; the same master ref is a pass; different refs are read again after 6 seconds, twice, and only the same two different refs on all three reads are compared by the newest document each shows (GET /api/v2/documents/search with that ref, pageSize=1, orderings=[document.last_publication_date desc], lang=*); a finding only when the origin's newest publication is later than the cache's; two different refs that show no such difference, or refs that keep changing across three reads (a publication in flight), are could-not-check; the finding quotes two times and one document id, never a field
done: The public cache of your Prismic repository serves the same master ref as the origin, so visitors see what you last published.
estimateChanges: Usually nothing to change: a stale ref clears when the cache refreshes. If it stays, a few minutes to look at what sits in front of Prismic (a proxy, a build that stored the ref, or a hosting cache) and to make the front end ask for the master ref on each request or after each publish webhook.

title: A Prismic release lists a document older than the copy that is live
what: A release's own list shows a document whose copy was last published before the copy that is live now.
why: If the release holds that older copy, publishing it may put it back over the newer live one, and the change someone published since would disappear from the site. Prismic does not say which documents a release holds, so this is a reason to look, not proof.
fix: In Prismic open the release, and for each document named remove it from the release or refresh it from the live version. If the older copy is what you want live, publish it as a new version and leave it in the release.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent and checkReleases: true: this check reads the repository's releases, which hold content that is not published, with the access token you gave Gaugeline, so it runs only with --owner-consent (or gaugeline.consent.json) and checkReleases: true in gaugeline.adapters.json, on sites you own or have permission to test; GET /api/v2 with the token in an Authorization: Token header (never the address) for the refs, then for the master ref and for each release ref (at most 10 releases, ordered by id) GET /api/v2/documents/search with that ref, lang=*, an explicit orderings, page and pageSize, read as ids, types and publication times only; each list is a snapshot at its ref and is checked page by page (the page asked for, the same total, no document twice, the count read equal to the total); a document in a release whose last publication time is earlier than the same document's at the master ref is the finding (its id and type, never a field), but only when the release's list shows at least one document that differs from the live list (missing from it, or with another publication time), otherwise the release is could-not-check ("cannot tell what the release holds"), never a pass, because Prismic does not say which documents a release holds and the premise that a release ref differs from the master's is unconfirmed; the refs are read again afterwards and a change in the master ref or a release's ref starts the reading over once, a second change is could-not-check; a release that cannot be listed, more than the release limit, a repository that lists no release and a token the repository does not accept are could-not-check for that part; what a release read returns for a document is Prismic's own and this comparison is not described on its documentation page, which the docs page says
done: No release in your Prismic repository holds an older copy of a document than the one that is already live.
estimateChanges: A few minutes in Prismic per release: open the release, remove the documents that are already live in a newer version, or update them from the live version, before the release is published.

title: A HubDB row differs from the page that shows it
what: A published row of a HubDB table has a value in a column you named in gaugeline.adapters.json, and the dynamic page for that row does not show it.
why: Visitors see a price, a time or a name that is not the one the client keeps in the table, so what is sold or announced is not what the table says.
fix: Open the dynamic page's template and check the column it prints, then publish the table again (a table change shows on the page only once the table is published). If the template formats the value differently, name another column or accept the difference.
tech: GET /cms/v3/hubdb/tables for the published tables, GET /cms/v3/hubdb/tables/{table}/rows for the published rows (stepped by the cursor), and the dynamic page that uses the table (a published page whose dynamicPageHubDbTableId is the table's id); for each row with a path, one anonymous GET of the page's address plus the row's path. Only the columns named under `fingerprint` for `hubdb.<table>` are used: each value is looked for in the words of the page (scripts, styles and tags removed, entities decoded, case ignored; a number as written, with two decimals and with a thousands comma, as a whole number). The values are held only for that comparison; a finding names the table, the row id, the page and the column, never a value. A table with no dynamic page, a row with no path, a row with nothing that can be looked for and a page that was not read are could-not-check.
done: Every column you named for a HubDB table shows the table's value on the page that displays the row.
estimateChanges: Usually a page template that reads a different column, or a table published after the page was cached. Allow longer when the template formats the value (a price with a currency sign is looked for as written and with two decimals).

title: Some AI assistants can't read your site
what: robots.txt stops one or more known AI crawlers from reading the home page. Gaugeline says which, and whether the block names them or comes from a rule for every crawler.
why: People ask assistants about a business before they open its site. Blocking AI crawlers is a fair choice; blocking them by accident means assistants answer from old or second-hand information.
fix: If the block is on purpose, there is nothing to do. If it comes from a Disallow: / meant for a staging site, remove it, or add groups for the assistants you want to allow.
tech: known AI user-agent tokens (packages/core/src/data/ai-agents.json) are disallowed / by robots.txt
done: The assistants you want can read the site, or the block is recorded as on purpose.
estimateChanges: A block set in a firewall or a CDN rather than robots.txt is found by looking at those settings.

title: This Analog page calls public endpoints that need a second look
what: A page of this Analog site names a server function (/_analog/fn/<id>) or a page endpoint (/api/_analog/pages/<path>). Both are addresses anyone can request, not only your page.
why: A server function runs for any visitor who calls it, signed in or not, and a page endpoint answers any GET with the page's server data. Treating them as part of the page, instead of as public endpoints, is how booking and patient-list handlers end up open.
fix: Check each server function and page loader: validate the input, check the session inside it, and return only fields the page shows.
tech: Analog sites only, no extra request (Gaugeline never calls a server function, which can be a POST): the names come from /_analog/fn/<id> and /api/_analog/pages/<path> in the page's HTML. They also show the site runs on the server, not as a static build
done: Each server function and page endpoint checks who is asking and returns only what any visitor may see.
estimateChanges: Endpoints that already check a session and validate input need nothing; each one without takes its own fix.

title: The store lists the app under a different name
what: The name the App Store or Google Play shows for a linked app differs from the name you expect.
why: A renamed or replaced app can mean the link points at an old listing, or at someone else's app.
fix: Check the link points at the right listing. If the app was renamed on purpose, update the expected name.
tech: the store's app name differs from the expected app name (case, punctuation and a leading "The" ignored); only runs when an expected name is set
done: The link points at the right store listing, or the expected name is updated.
estimateChanges: Renaming the app in the store is a review by the store, which takes days.

title: A downloadable file is on a public asset address
what: A page links to a file (pdf, zip, epub, mp3, mp4, docx or xlsx) on a public asset store and shows no price, or the link is a terms, privacy or policy page.
why: That is fine for a brochure or a menu. It becomes a problem the day the file is something a customer bought, because anyone with the address can open it.
fix: If the file is free, nothing to do. If it will ever be sold, serve it from a download route that checks the purchase and hands back a short-lived signed link.
tech: a[href] to a file with a sold file type on a public asset store host, on a page with no price, or whose link text is terms, privacy or policy; one finding per page; the file is never requested; the query string is not printed; a signed address with an expiry is a pass
done: The file is served from a route that checks the purchase and hands back a short-lived link, or is left public on purpose.
estimateChanges: A free file needs nothing. A file that will be sold means building the route and moving the file.

title: This Astro page calls public endpoints that need a second look
what: A page of this Astro site calls Astro Actions (/_actions/<name>) or loads server islands (/_server-islands/<name>). Both are addresses anyone can request, not only your page.
why: An action runs for any visitor who posts to it, signed in or not, and a server island answers any GET. Treating them as part of the page, instead of as public endpoints, is how booking and contact handlers end up open.
fix: Check each action handler: validate the input (an Astro Action takes a Zod schema), check the session inside it, and rate-limit it. For a server island, confirm it renders only what any visitor may see.
tech: Astro sites only, no extra request (Gaugeline never calls an action, which is a POST): the names come from /_actions/<name> and ?_action=<name> in the page's HTML and /_server-islands/<name> in its scripts. They also show the site runs on the server (an adapter), not as a static build
done: Each action validates its input and checks who is asking, and each server island shows nothing it should not.
estimateChanges: Actions that already check a session and validate with a schema need nothing; each one without takes its own fix.

title: The site wouldn't let Gaugeline read the page
what: The page answered with a refusal (401, 403, 429, 503 with Retry-After) or a bot-challenge page instead of its content.
why: A firewall or bot protection is in front of the site. That isn't a broken site, but it can also stop search engines' and AI assistants' crawlers, and nothing else could be checked.
fix: If the site should be readable by crawlers, allow them in the firewall or bot-protection settings. Gaugeline never retries or disguises itself to get through.
tech: The final answer for the page is 401, 403, 429, 503 with a Retry-After header, or a 200 under 60 words with a known challenge marker (Just a moment, Attention Required, cf-chl, a captcha form). Every check that needs the page is then listed as could not check; only robots.txt and DNS checks run
done: The site lets crawlers read the page, or the block is accepted as on purpose.
estimateChanges: A firewall or bot-protection setting on a host you do not control is a support request.

title: The page doesn't say which address is the real one
what: There's no canonical tag.
why: Copies of the page with tracking parameters can be treated as separate pages.
fix: Add a self-referencing canonical tag.
tech: no <link rel="canonical">
done: Each page has a canonical tag that names its own address.
estimateChanges: One shared SEO component is a single edit.

title: The footer copyright year is out of date
what: The copyright notice in the page's footer names a year before the current one.
why: A year that never changes tells visitors, and anyone judging the site, that nobody has touched it in a while.
fix: Set the footer to the current year, or print it from the date in the template so it updates itself.
tech: the footer element or role=contentinfo (the whole page when it has none) is searched for a (c), © or "copyright" notice with a year or range of years; the latest year in the page's notices is used, and it is stale when it is before the current year in the venue's time zone, with graceDays (1) after 1 January before last year's counts; one finding for the page checked, not one per page
done: The footer shows the current year, or builds it from the date so it never goes out of date.
estimateChanges: One footer in a theme or layout is a one-line change; a footer repeated by hand on many pages is slower.

title: A page of changing numbers does not say when they were updated
what: A page under one of your freshness rules shows no update time at all, in the place you named or in its structured data.
why: Without a stamp nobody can tell fresh numbers from stale ones, and neither can Gaugeline: a sync can stop and the page gives no sign.
fix: Print the time the data was last updated on the page, from the same record the numbers come from (a time element with a datetime attribute, or dateModified in the structured data), then point the rule at it.
tech: for each rule with a stamp in gaugeline.freshness.json that is active (in the months of activeWhen, in the site's time zone), the page as sent without JavaScript has no element matching the selector with a datetime, content, named attribute or text, and no property of that name in its structured data; a stamp that is there but cannot be read is not reported here (data-stale lists it as could not check); a rule that is not active is listed as could not check, not passed
done: The page prints when its numbers were last updated, from the same record.
estimateChanges: Several pages with changing numbers each need the stamp.

title: Your Sanity content can be read by anyone
what: The Sanity dataset your images come from answers queries without a token.
why: That is fine for a blog, and a risk the day someone adds a form or an order type to it: everything in it is readable by anyone who looks.
fix: If nothing in it is private, nothing to do. Otherwise make the dataset private in sanity.io/manage and give the site a read token.
tech: Project and dataset read from cdn.sanity.io image addresses; one GET to <project>.api.sanity.io with the query {"count": count(*), "types": array::unique(*[]._type)} and no token, at most 2 datasets; never document contents
done: The dataset is private with a token for the site, or left public on purpose.
estimateChanges: A site that reads the dataset from the browser needs those queries moved to the server.

title: A PDF could not be read, so it was not compared with the site
what: A PDF linked from your site has no text Gaugeline can read (a scan or a picture of a page, an encrypted file, or fonts that do not say which letters they are).
why: Nothing in it was compared with your site, so a wrong price in it would go unseen. Search engines and screen readers cannot read a scan either.
