fix: Export the PDF from the original menu or price list as text, not from a scan, and leave it unencrypted. Gaugeline never reads images (no OCR): a guessed price would be a false finding.
tech: the linked PDF is read by the optional @gaugeline/documents package, text layer only, no OCR; a file with no text operators, an encrypted file, fonts without a ToUnicode map and streams of an unsupported kind are reported here (low severity) with the reason; a file that is too big, cut short, refused or not a PDF is could-not-check instead; limits: 10 MB per file (config documents.maxMegabytes up to 25), 200 pages, 4 MiB inflated per stream, 48 MiB in all
done: Every PDF menu or price list linked from the site has a text layer Gaugeline can read.
estimateChanges: Re-export the PDF as text (not a scan) if you want it checked, or ignore this note.

title: Your DMARC policy only watches
what: The domain's DMARC record has p=none: receiving servers report mail that fails, and deliver it anyway.
why: That is the right first step, and it doesn't stop anyone sending mail as you. Left at none, it never will.
fix: Read the DMARC reports for a few weeks, fix any service of yours that fails, then change p=none to p=quarantine (and later p=reject).
tech: Public DNS only: the TXT record at _dmarc.<host> starting v=DMARC1 has p=none; sp (the subdomain policy) does not change this
done: The DMARC policy moves from none to quarantine, then reject, after the reports look clean.
estimateChanges: The weeks spent reading reports and fixing each sender that fails.

title: Some events are missing details search engines need
what: An event in the page's structured data has no start date, no location or no event status.
why: Google needs these to show the event in results, and the status is how a cancelled or moved night is shown as such.
fix: Give every Event a startDate, a location and an eventStatus (for example https://schema.org/EventScheduled).
tech: Event JSON-LD without startDate, location or eventStatus (one finding listing each event and what it lacks)
done: Every Event has a startDate, a location and an eventStatus.
estimateChanges: Events entered by hand are edited one by one.

title: Two menu links report the same click
what: Two links to the same page, under different parent menus, send identical event values, so the report can't tell which one was clicked.
why: A comparison of a new menu is only real if every link reports where it sits: identical values merge the two links into one row.
fix: Add the parent menu (or another value that tells them apart) to the event both links send.
tech: Links that passed events-fire, grouped by destination: two with different parent menus whose events carry the same values for the plan's parameters. Needs a rendered read (G39): until then it is could not check
done: The two menu links report different events, told apart by the parent menu.
estimateChanges: One shared menu component is one edit.

title: A click sends an event your tracking plan does not list
what: Clicking an element the plan selects makes the page push an event to dataLayer whose name no line of gaugeline.events.json (or the CSV spec) lists.
why: An event nobody planned is usually a tag someone added or a second install: the numbers it feeds are not the ones the plan describes, and a before-and-after comparison cannot tell the two apart.
fix: Add the event to the plan if it is wanted, or remove the tag or handler that sends it.
tech: Each element a plan line selects is clicked in the rendered page with analytics requests intercepted and never delivered (the same read as events-fire, at most 20 elements), and the dataLayer pushes within 1500 ms are read. A pushed event name that no events line names is listed; the tag manager's own gtm.* events and pushes with no event name are left out; the same event on several links is one finding. The spec's events that never fire are events-fire's. Needs a rendered read (G39): until then it is could not check
done: Every event a click sends is one the tracking plan lists, or the plan is updated to list it.
estimateChanges: Often one tag in the tag manager; an event that was added on purpose is a row in the plan.

title: Several form services on one page
what: Forms or form scripts from more than one service (for example HubSpot and Typeform) are on the same page.
why: Leads from one page end up in different places, and each service needs its own tracking, consent and follow-up.
fix: Check that each form is meant to be there, and move the page to one service if you can.
tech: Sightings of more than one of Pardot, Web-to-Lead, HubSpot, Formstack, Marketo and Typeform on one page (form action, iframe src, embed script); the tracking code alone is not a sighting
done: Each form on the page is meant to be there, or the page uses one service.
estimateChanges: Moving forms to one service means rebuilding each of them.

title: The data sent with a Gatsby page has text the page does not show
what: This Gatsby page's page-data file, or a static query it lists, has text fields whose text is nowhere on the page a visitor reads.
why: Everything a page query returns is written to a public JSON file. A field the page does not show is either unused (so it can go) or used by a script (so it is worth a look): either way it is public.
fix: Select only the fields the page needs in its query, or move the rest to a source that checks who is asking.
tech: Gatsby sites only. The page's own /page-data/<path>/page-data.json and the /page-data/sq/d/<hash>.json files it lists (the files the framework's client fetches on every visit; one GET each, at most eleven, walked to depth 8, capped). Text fields of 4 or more characters whose first 40 characters are not in the page's visible text (tags taken out of html fields); addresses, ids, dates and image plumbing are left out; names only, never values. Fields named like something private are left to gatsby-private-fields. A file or page text that cannot be read in full is could not check. Fields used by scripts or other pages are shown too, so read the list as a prompt (uncited)
done: The page's data files hold only fields the page shows, or the rest is deliberate.
estimateChanges: Each unused field is dropped from the query that returns it; fields used only by scripts or by other pages may be deliberate.

title: A hidden section is past its launch date
what: Today is after the launch date set for a hidden section, and gaugeline.hidden.json still lists it as hidden.
why: Either the launch slipped and nobody updated the plan, or it launched and the hidden checks are now guarding the wrong thing.
fix: Move the until date, or remove the section from gaugeline.hidden.json now that it's live.
tech: A hidden section's until date (YYYY-MM-DD, the whole day in UTC) is before the run's clock; no request is made
done: The until date is moved, or the section is removed from gaugeline.hidden.json.
estimateChanges: One entry in one file.

title: A page breaks your written house rules
what: The page does not follow a rule you wrote down: its headings are in the wrong case, it uses a character or a word you ruled out, a button says something other than your label, or a phone number is written in another shape. Each finding names the rule, the page and the element.
why: A style guide only works if every page follows it, and nobody reads every page. A word or a button label that is off is the kind of thing a visitor notices as the site looking careless, and the kind of thing that creeps back each time someone edits a page.
fix: Change the text on the page to follow the rule, or, if the rule is out of date, change it in gaugeline.rules.json. A button label or a phone number that is set in one shared component is fixed once, there.
tech: Only with a gaugeline.rules.json (headings.case, forbidChars, forbidTerms, buttonLabel, phoneFormat; a draft from gaugeline house-rules is never read until it is renamed). Reads the page already fetched, with no request: the title, the h1 to h3 headings (at most 200), the buttons and links (at most 500) and the visible text (the first 100,000 characters, scripts, styles and hidden elements left out), each cut to 2,000 characters except the page text. Nothing in the file is a pattern: a heading is judged by its words' capitals (a name, an acronym or a word with a capital inside is left alone; sentence case is broken only when at least three other words are all in capitals, and title case when a word outside a short list of small words is in lower case), a character is one of em dash, en dash, exclamation mark or ellipsis (the character or three dots), a banned word is a whole word or phrase compared as a list of lower-case words, a button counts when it says the label in other capitals or punctuation or with more words (a link only in other capitals or punctuation) and a phone number counts when it has the mask's digits in another shape. One finding per rule, naming at most three elements with a snippet of at most 48 characters; a phone number is shown as its shape (###), never its digits. A rule that cannot be read (no text, text cut at the limit with nothing found, a heading with no upper or lower case) is could-not-check, never a pass. Which button a label is meant for is not known: a button that says something else entirely is not recognised. Proper names look like title case, and the heading rule says so. No request is made; page text is never printed beyond the snippet
done: The page's headings, characters, words, button labels and phone numbers follow the rules in gaugeline.rules.json.
estimateChanges: One copy edit per finding, or one change to a shared component such as a button or a footer. A rule that is wrong for the site is a one-line edit to gaugeline.rules.json.

title: Some language codes are not valid
what: hreflang uses a code that isn't a valid language tag (such as "sp" or "es_US"), or a page with three or more languages has no x-default.
why: Search engines ignore an hreflang with an invalid code, and without x-default they guess which version to show everyone else.
fix: Use BCP 47 codes such as es, es-US or es-419 (a hyphen, not an underscore), and add hreflang="x-default" for the version to show when no language matches.
tech: an hreflang value is not a BCP 47 tag (two-letter languages must be ISO 639-1), or 3+ distinct languages have no x-default
done: Every hreflang value is a valid code such as es-US, with an x-default.
estimateChanges: A plugin that writes the codes may need a setting changed.

title: Some images have no alt attribute
what: Some images have no alt attribute at all, not even an empty one.
why: Without alt, screen readers read the file name aloud. An empty alt="" tells them to skip a decorative image; a missing one does not.
fix: Add alt to every img: a short description, or alt="" for decorative images.
tech: img elements with no alt attribute (one finding with a count and the first three)
done: Every img has an alt attribute: a description, or alt="" for decoration.
estimateChanges: Images inside CMS content are edited one by one.

title: Images use older, heavier file formats
what: Images are served as JPEG, PNG or GIF with no WebP or AVIF version offered.
why: WebP and AVIF are usually a quarter to a half smaller for the same picture, so the page loads faster.
fix: Offer WebP or AVIF with a <picture> element or srcset, or let your image CDN or framework image component pick the format.
tech: a sampled image's Content-Type is image/jpeg, image/png or image/gif and it has no WebP or AVIF candidate (SVG is never reported)
done: Images are offered as WebP or AVIF through a picture element, srcset or the image component.
estimateChanges: A site with no image pipeline needs one set up first.

title: A language version declares the wrong language
what: A version's <html lang> names a different language than the version is (for example the Spanish page still says lang="en").
why: Screen readers read the page with the wrong voice and pronunciation, and browsers offer to translate it into its own language.
fix: Set <html lang> per version from the page's language, usually in the layout component.
tech: <html lang>'s primary subtag differs from the version's language (from hreflang or the configured scheme)
done: Each version's html lang matches the language of its content.
estimateChanges: One layout component usually sets it for every version.

title: Some text wasn't translated
what: Strings you listed as default-language text (button labels, headings) appear on another language version.
why: A Spanish page with an English "Add to cart" button looks unfinished, and some visitors won't know what it does.
fix: Translate the strings in the components that render them; they are usually hard-coded in a shared button or heading.
tech: a string from untranslated in gaugeline.languages.json appears in another version's main text or link names (case ignored); needs the list
done: The strings that were left in the other language are translated.
estimateChanges: Strings hard-coded in shared components are found and moved to the translations, then translated by someone who knows the language.

title: Some links don't say where they go
what: Links whose whole text is "read more", "click here", "learn more" or "here".
why: Screen reader users often browse a page by its links, and hear a list of identical "read more"s. Search engines also read link text to understand the destination.
fix: Make the link text name the destination, such as "Read more about pricing", or add an aria-label that does.
tech: a link's accessible name (aria-label, else its text) is exactly "read more", "click here", "learn more", "here" (English list)
done: Each link's text names its destination, or carries an aria-label that does.
estimateChanges: A shared button component used everywhere is one edit.

title: Links on this page go through a redirect
what: Links to other pages on the site answer with a redirect (3xx) before reaching the page.
why: Each redirect adds a round trip for visitors, and search engines pass a little less on through every hop.
fix: Change the link to the address it ends up at. This usually follows a move to new URLs, https or www.
tech: a sampled same-site a[href] answers 3xx first and ends in 200
done: Each link goes to the address it ends up at.
estimateChanges: A move to new URLs changes every link at once, in the content as well as the templates.

title: Your llms.txt is not in the format assistants expect
what: /llms.txt exists but has no # title, no ## section with a list of links, or is so large it is no longer a short guide.
why: llms.txt is meant to be a short Markdown guide to your most useful pages. A file an assistant cannot parse into a title and links is ignored or misread.
fix: Start with one # line naming the business, optionally a > summary, then ## sections of - [Page](https://...): note lines. Put long text in llms-full.txt.
tech: /llms.txt (2xx, not HTML) has no H1, or no H2 section with a Markdown link list item, or is over 200000 characters; an HTML 200 counts as missing
done: llms.txt has a title, at least one section of links, and stays a short guide.
estimateChanges: A llms.txt generated by a plugin is fixed in the plugin's settings.

title: One page has two names in your menus
what: The same link appears in the menu, header or footer with two different labels.
why: Visitors wonder whether the two labels are two pages, and the site reads as unfinished.
fix: Use one label for each page everywhere. Menus kept in two places (a header and a footer component) drift apart first.
tech: one href (a #fragment makes a different destination) has more than one distinct label across nav, header and footer (case and trailing arrows ignored)
done: Each page has one name in every menu.
estimateChanges: Menus kept in two components are edited twice.

title: Shared links have no picture
what: The page has no og:image tag.
why: When the page is shared in a chat or a social post, it shows as a plain link with no picture, which fewer people click.
fix: Add <meta property="og:image" content="https://..."> with a 1200 by 630 picture for the page.
tech: no og:image (or og:image:url) meta property
done: The page has an og:image with a full address, about 1200 by 630 pixels.
estimateChanges: Making the pictures is the cost if none exist.

title: An animation makes the browser lay the page out on every frame
what: The page's own styles animate layout properties (position, size, margin, padding, font size) or transition all, or one of its scripts has an animation loop that reads a layout value and then sets a style.
why: Layout is the most expensive thing a browser does each frame. Animating it, or reading it right after changing it (a forced reflow), makes the page stutter and keeps the main thread busy, which delays everything a visitor taps.
fix: Animate transform and opacity instead of top, left, width and height, name the properties a transition changes instead of all, and in an animation loop read layout values first and write styles after, once per frame.
tech: Plain rules over the page's inline styles and its own script files (each fetched once for the key check and shared, never a request of this check's own). Layout properties in a keyframes rule or a transition (top, left, width, height, margins, paddings, font-size, line-height, all) are low. A script text with a requestAnimationFrame call within 500 characters of both a layout read (offsetWidth, clientHeight, scrollTop, getBoundingClientRect, getComputedStyle) and a style write is medium and counted once per script. Stylesheets in separate files and scripts from other sites are not read; a script that cannot be read is could-not-check
done: Animations move transform and opacity only, and no animation loop reads a layout value after setting a style in the same frame.
estimateChanges: An hour per animation to move it to transform or opacity; a loop that reads and writes layout has to be restructured to read first and write after.

title: A heavy page has no Save-Data or low-end-device fallback
what: The page loads a 3D scene, an autoplaying video or an animation library, and nothing in its own scripts or styles reads the visitor's data saver, device memory, core count or connection type.
why: The visitors who most need a lighter page are on small phones and slow or capped connections, and they get exactly the same heavy load as someone on a desktop. A page that looks at the hints the browser already offers can send them a still picture instead.
fix: Read navigator.connection.saveData, navigator.deviceMemory, navigator.hardwareConcurrency or the prefers-reduced-data media query before starting the heavy part, and show a still picture or a lighter version when they say the visitor is low on data or power.
tech: Plain rules. Heavy means a 3D library or WebGL call, a video tag with autoplay, or a script named gsap, lottie, anime or framer-motion. The page's own inline scripts and styles and its own script files (already fetched once for the key check, never a new request) are searched for saveData, Save-Data, prefers-reduced-data, deviceMemory, hardwareConcurrency and effectiveType. None found is low. Scripts from other sites and separate stylesheet files are not read, so a fallback only there is not seen; a script that cannot be read, or was cut, makes the check could-not-check
done: The heavy parts (3D, autoplaying video, an animation library) are skipped or lightened for a visitor whose browser asks to save data or reports little memory, few cores or a slow connection.
estimateChanges: Half a day to read the data saver and device hints and swap the heavy part for a still picture; more if the page is built around the heavy part.

title: A price changed since the last run
what: A product's price in the page's structured data is different from the last run's.
why: Sometimes that is the plan. When it isn't (a sync from the shop, an edit to the wrong product), customers and search results see the wrong price.
fix: If the change wasn't meant, correct the price at its source (the shop or CMS) and rebuild; if it was, nothing to do.
tech: With --since last only: the JSON-LD Offer price (integer minor units; anything but 48 or 48.00 is unread) for a product key (sku or name plus currency) present in both runs
done: The price is corrected at its source and the site rebuilt, or the change is accepted as meant.
estimateChanges: A price kept in several places is edited in each.

title: Your phone number or address is in structured data but not written on the page
what: The page's LocalBusiness structured data has a phone number or street address that appears in no visible text on the pages Gaugeline read (as sent, without JavaScript).
why: An assistant answering 'what's their number?' quotes text it can read. A fact that is only in markup, in an image or built by scripts is often missed or second-guessed.
fix: Write the phone number and street address as plain text on the home or contact page (the footer is fine), not only in an image or a script.
tech: the JSON-LD telephone digits and streetAddress are not found in the visible text (scripts, styles and templates removed) of the checked page or the other pages sampled
done: The phone number and street address in your structured data are also written as text on a page.
estimateChanges: A fact that only lives in an image needs the text written out.

title: This page calls server functions that anyone can address
what: The markup of this Qwik or SolidStart page names a server-function address: Qwik's ?qfunc= (a server$ call) or ?qaction= (a routeAction$ form) or SolidStart's /_server (a "use server" function).
why: A server function is a public address: anyone can call it with their own input, whether or not your page has a button for it. It is worth knowing which ones exist and what each one lets a stranger do.
fix: For each server$ or "use server" function, check the caller (session, role) and validate the input before it reads or writes anything, and return only what the page shows. Gaugeline does not call these addresses.
tech: Qwik and SolidStart pages only, from the page already read, no extra request and never a call: counts occurrences of qfunc= and qaction= (Qwik) or /_server (SolidStart) in the page's markup. Whether a function is safe is not something a read can tell, so this is a heads-up, not a verdict; ?qfunc=, ?qaction= and /_server are from the package source (request-handler runServerFunction; server-runtime.js)
done: Every server function checks who is calling and what it may do, and none returns more than the page needs.
estimateChanges: Each server function is read once; most only need an input check and a session check.

title: One Sanity image is processed and downloaded more than once
what: The same uploaded image is requested with different parameters by different images on the page, such as one width in the header and another in a card.
why: Each variant is a separate file for Sanity's CDN to make and for the visitor to download, and none of them is in the browser's cache for the others.
fix: Use one address for the image and let CSS size it, or give it one srcset the browser chooses from. If a card needs a different crop, that is a different picture: upload it as its own image.
tech: the same asset id (the hash in the file name; the same bytes are the same asset) in two or more img elements with different parameter sets; an img's own srcset and picture sources are one image and are not compared with each other; parameter order is ignored; the page's own HTML only
done: Each Sanity asset on a page is requested with one set of parameters, and differing sizes come from one srcset.
estimateChanges: Usually one shared image helper used by every component that shows the image.

title: Breadcrumbs don't start where your guide says
what: The first item of a page's breadcrumb structured data is not the Home name and address your schema guide sets.
why: Search results show the breadcrumb trail; one that starts somewhere else on some pages looks inconsistent and can point at the wrong page.
fix: Start every BreadcrumbList with the configured first item, for example Home at /.
tech: the lowest-position ListItem's name or URL differs from breadcrumbs.firstName / breadcrumbs.firstUrl in gaugeline.schema.json (name case ignored, URL resolved)
done: Every BreadcrumbList starts with the configured first item.
estimateChanges: A shared breadcrumb component is one edit.

title: The editor studio can be cached
what: A studio route you listed answers 200 with no no-store in its Cache-Control header (no header at all, or one with other directives).
why: A response that may be stored can be shown again from a browser or a shared cache after the studio has changed, so an editor can be handed an old page of it. no-store is the directive that says a response must not be stored in any cache. (Gaugeline has not confirmed from Sanity's documentation how a studio is cached.)
fix: Send Cache-Control: no-store for the studio's route: a headers() entry in next.config for an embedded studio, or a rule in the settings of the host that serves it.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent and a gaugeline.studio.json that names the studio's route (studioRoutes, at most 4): one GET of each, no cookie or Authorization, at most 4096 bytes of each answer read and never kept, once per run; Gaugeline never picks a route such as /studio itself. A 2xx answer, after redirects, whose Cache-Control has no no-store directive is a finding; 401 and 403 are not; a route that answers 404, 410, 429, a 5xx or nothing is could-not-check; the finding names the route and the status, never a header value
done: Every studio route you listed answers with no-store in its Cache-Control header.
estimateChanges: One headers() entry in the framework's config for an embedded studio. A studio served from another host is set in that host's settings, and a hosting platform's default cache rules may need a rule of their own.

title: The page's data has text the page does not show
what: This SvelteKit page's __data.json has text fields whose text is nowhere on the page a visitor reads.
why: Everything load returns is sent to every visitor. A field the page does not show is either unused (so it can go) or used by a script (so it is worth a look): either way it is public.
fix: Return only what the page needs from load, or move the rest to a route that checks who is asking.
tech: SvelteKit sites only. One GET of <page>/__data.json (the page's own data, fetched by the framework's client on every navigation; devalue payload walked to depth 6, capped). Text fields of 4 or more characters whose text is not in the page's visible text; names only, never values. Fields named like something private are left to sveltekit-private-fields. A payload or page text that cannot be read in full is could not check. Fields used by scripts or other pages are shown too, so read the list as a prompt (uncited)
done: The page's __data.json holds only fields the page shows, or the rest is deliberate.
estimateChanges: Each unused field is dropped in its load function; fields used only by scripts or by other pages may be deliberate.

title: A phone link may not dial correctly
what: A tel: link has spaces or brackets in the number.
why: Some phones and click-to-call tools dial the wrong number, or nothing, when the link has spaces or brackets.
fix: Write the link as digits with a leading + and country code, for example href="tel:+14155550100". Keep the spaced format in the visible text only.
tech: an a[href^="tel:"] contains a space, ( or ); "-" and "." pass. One finding per distinct number
done: Each tel: link is digits with a leading + and country code.
estimateChanges: Links typed into content are one edit each.

title: A temporary address doesn't name the real one
what: The page is served from a hosting provider's temporary address and has no canonical tag.
why: If a search engine finds the temporary address, nothing tells it the real page is on your domain, and the preview can show up in results.
fix: Add <link rel="canonical" href="https://yourdomain/..."> to every page, so each preview points at the real address.
tech: The final address's host ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev and the HTML has no link rel=canonical
done: Every page on the temporary host has a canonical pointing at the real domain.
estimateChanges: A shared layout is one edit.

title: An agent discovery file on your site is broken
what: The site serves one of the standard /.well-known/ files AI agents look for (an agent card, an OAuth resource description or a legacy plugin manifest), and it is not valid JSON.
why: Agents read these files to learn what the site offers and how to sign in. A file that does not parse is skipped, or breaks the agent's setup.
fix: Fix the JSON, or remove the file if it is no longer used. A site with none of these files has nothing to fix: they are optional.
tech: GET of each path in packages/core/src/data/well-known.json answers 2xx with a non-HTML body that does not parse as a JSON object; 404, HTML and 5xx answers mean no file
done: Every agent discovery file the site serves is a valid JSON object.
estimateChanges: A file generated by a plugin is fixed at the source.

title: Invisible characters sit inside words on the page
what: Zero-width characters are inside words in the page's visible text.
why: A word with a hidden character in it no longer matches itself: search can't find it, and copy-pasted or tampered text can carry marks nobody meant to publish.
fix: Remove them from the source text: retype the word, or paste it as plain text.
tech: U+200B to U+200D, U+2060 to U+2064, U+180E or U+FEFF between two Latin, Cyrillic, Greek or digit characters in visible text; emoji joiners, Persian non-joiners and zero-width marks at the end of a text (content source maps) are not counted
done: The invisible characters are removed from the words they sit inside.
estimateChanges: The number of fields they came from. Text pasted from a word processor often repeats the problem.

title: A redirect drops the old address's query string
what: An old address with a query string redirects to an address without it.
why: Campaign tags and filters on old links are lost, so their visits can't be told apart.
fix: Pass the query string on in the redirect rule.
tech: The legacy address has a query; the trail's final address has none
done: The redirect passes the query string on.
estimateChanges: One rule is one edit. Several rules each need it.

title: Addresses in the rank export are neither live nor planned
what: Pages in the --rank export (Search Console or a rank tracker) are neither in the --live list nor in the plan.
why: Usually the export is of another site or property, or of pages already gone: the numbers on the uncovered list may not be the site's.
fix: Check the export is of this site's property and recent, or add the pages to --live if they still exist.
tech: Export paths (the --live key: lower case, no trailing slash, no query or host) not in the set of live paths or row paths. One finding with the count and three examples
done: The rank export is of this site and recent, or the missing pages are added to --live.
estimateChanges: Getting a fresh export from the search tool.

title: One page's primary keyword is another page's secondary
what: A page's Primary Keyword is also listed as a Secondary Keyword of other pages.
why: Often deliberate, supporting pages in a cluster; worth a look, because a strong supporting page can outrank the page meant to win the term.
fix: Check the supporting pages link to the primary page, and that none of them is built to rank for the term itself.
tech: Each Secondary Keyword cell is split on commas, semicolons and line breaks and compared like primaries. Reported from the primary's side, only when one page has the term as its primary
done: The supporting pages link to the primary page and none is built to rank for its term.
estimateChanges: Content edits on each supporting page.

title: A printed address takes more than two redirects
what: A printed address takes more than two redirects to land.
why: Every hop is a wait on a phone, often on a weak signal, and one broken hop breaks the code.
fix: Redirect the printed address straight to its page.
tech: More than two 3xx in the trail; the trail is in the evidence
done: The printed address redirects once, straight to its page.
estimateChanges: Rules in a short-link service, the host and the app each need checking.

title: An email has no plain-text version
what: An .html email has no .txt file with the same name beside it, and gaugeline.emails.json says every email should have one.
why: A message with only an HTML part is more likely to be treated as bulk mail, and anyone whose mail client shows text only, or reads aloud, gets nothing.
fix: Export or write the plain-text version (order.html and order.txt), and send both as one multipart message.
tech: only when gaugeline.emails.json sets "textVersion": true; an .html or .htm email with no .txt of the same name in the same folder (order.es.html wants order.es.txt); without that setting the check says it could not run and passes nothing
done: Each .html email has a .txt with the same name beside it, and the export writes both.
estimateChanges: Most email tools export a plain-text version with one option. A hand-written template needs the text written.

title: A page marked static is never served from the CDN's cache
what: A page you marked static in gaugeline.cost.json was a cache miss on both of two visits a few seconds apart.
why: A page that is meant to be the same for everyone should be built once and served from the CDN. When every visit is a miss, the host does the work every time, which costs money and makes the page slower.
fix: Look for what opts the page out of the cache: a Cache-Control of no-store or private, a cookie or header the page reads, a fetch with cache: no-store, or a dynamic function. On Next.js, make the route static or give it a revalidate time.
tech: Only pages marked static ("static" in gaugeline.cost.json: a path or a "/folder/*"). Two GETs about 3 seconds apart, no cookies. The cache state is read from x-vercel-cache (HIT, STALE, PRERENDER, REVALIDATED are hits; MISS, BYPASS misses), cf-cache-status (HIT, STALE, UPDATING, REVALIDATED; MISS, EXPIRED, BYPASS, DYNAMIC) and a positive Age; a hit on either visit passes. A response with none of those is could-not-check, not a guess. When a lifetime of a second or more explains the misses, revalidate-too-often is reported instead
done: The page's second visit is served from the CDN's cache (a hit), so the host does not build it for every visitor.
estimateChanges: Usually a cache header or a revalidate setting, an hour. More when something the page reads (a cookie, a header, a no-store fetch) opts it out of the cache.

title: A page marked static is rebuilt too often
what: A page you marked static sends a cache lifetime shorter than the minimum you set (60 seconds unless you changed it).
why: A lifetime of a second or two means the host rebuilds the page about as often as it is visited. A page that changes once a day does not need that, and every rebuild is billed.
fix: Raise the lifetime to what the content needs: an hour for a menu, a day for an about page. On Next.js that is the revalidate setting; on any host it is the s-maxage in Cache-Control.
tech: Only pages marked static ("static" in gaugeline.cost.json). The lifetime is s-maxage when Cache-Control has one, else max-age; no-store, no-cache and private count as zero. A max-age with no s-maxage is the browser's lifetime: when the CDN answered a hit (Vercel and Cloudflare keep such a page until the next deploy or purge) it is fine. Compared with "minimumSeconds" (default 60). A page with no Cache-Control header is could-not-check. A zero lifetime on a page that never hit the cache is reported as never-cached instead
done: The page's cache lifetime is at least the minimum in gaugeline.cost.json (60 seconds by default), so the host keeps a copy instead of rebuilding it.
estimateChanges: Minutes: a number in a revalidate setting or a header. Decide with the client how stale a page may be.

title: Trackers load on a page with a form or a listed path
what: Gaugeline lists the advertising pixels, analytics, session replay tools and tag managers that load on a page with a form, an embedded form service or a path you listed as sensitive, with the id each one carries.
why: A form or a page about a health condition, a booking or an intake is where visitors share details, and anything that loads there can receive information about the visit. Clients are often surprised to find what the site loads. This is a list of facts: whether any of it is allowed is for the client and their own counsel to decide, and Gaugeline does not say.
fix: Show the client the list. For each tracker, ask who set it up and what it is for; where it is not needed on this page, move it out of the page template or restrict it in the tag manager. For the question of whether a tracker is allowed here, the client should ask their own counsel.
tech: Only with --trackers. A page counts when it has a form that collects details (a search box, a GET form whose visible fields are named like a search, does not count), an embedded form service, or a path listed under "sensitivePaths" in gaugeline.trackers.json. Trackers are read from the script addresses and inline scripts in the HTML (and the noscript fallback tags) by a fixed table of patterns: Meta pixel, TikTok pixel, LinkedIn Insight Tag, Google Analytics 4, Google Tag Manager, five session replay tools (Hotjar, Microsoft Clarity, FullStory, LogRocket, Mouseflow) and the tracking code of HubSpot, Pardot and Marketo. Each finding shows the kind and the id the page's own code carries, never page content or a form field. A tag a script adds after the page loads is not seen (a run that fires scripts is a later branch); the same page gives the same findings
done: The client has seen the list of trackers on this page, with their ids, and has decided with their own counsel which stay; running Gaugeline again shows the list they chose.
estimateChanges: An hour to go through the list with the client. More when a tag manager adds trackers that have to be taken out one by one, or the form service's own tracking cannot be turned off.

title: A Tag Manager container on a page with a form or a listed path holds trackers
what: A Google Tag Manager container loads on a page with a form, an embedded form service or a path you listed as sensitive, and its public file contains tracker ids (Meta, TikTok, LinkedIn, session replay, Google Analytics 4).
why: A tag manager hides what the page loads: the page's own code shows one container id, and the trackers are inside it. They are the same kind of fact as the ones in the page's code, and the same question for the client and their own counsel. Gaugeline lists them and does not say whether any is allowed.
fix: Open the container in Tag Manager and look at the tags the finding names and their triggers. Where a tracker is not needed on this page, change its trigger so it does not fire here, or remove it. For the question of whether a tracker is allowed here, the client should ask their own counsel.
tech: Only with --trackers, on the pages the first check counts. The container's public file (GET www.googletagmanager.com/gtm.js?id=GTM-XXXX, the file every visitor receives) is read as text, once per container, at most three per page, and never run; its escaped characters are decoded and the same table of patterns is applied, with Google Analytics 4's measurement id read from a tag's settings. What the file holds is what the container could load: whether a tag fires on this page depends on its triggers, which Gaugeline does not run, and the finding says so. A tag built from a template that keeps its id out of the file is not seen. A container that cannot be read, or is longer than the size cap, is could-not-check with the reason
done: The client has seen what each Tag Manager container on this page holds and has decided with their own counsel which tags stay; running Gaugeline again shows the list they chose.
estimateChanges: An hour in the Tag Manager workspace per container, with the client. More when tags are built from templates and the triggers are long.

title: Which change moves the page's blocking time or Largest Contentful Paint (advice)
what: The page is loaded in a browser on this computer as it is (twice, to see how much two identical loads differ) and again with reduced motion forced, with JavaScript off and with scripts from other sites blocked. A change that moves total blocking time or Largest Contentful Paint by more than the page's own spread, 10% and a floor is listed with how much it moved.
why: Knowing that a speed problem goes away when third-party scripts are blocked, or that a page waits for an intro animation a visitor who asked for less motion would never see, says where to look first. It is a lab measure from one computer, unthrottled: it says which change matters, not what visitors experienced.
fix: Look at what the change removed. Blocking time that disappears without third-party scripts points at a tag, widget or chat script: load it later or drop it. A paint that gets sooner with reduced motion points at an animation or intro the page waits for: do not hold content back for it. A paint that gets sooner without JavaScript means the page waits for a script to show its main content: render that content on the server.
tech: Only with --attribution and --renderer playwright. The checked page is rendered five times, one after the other, in the browser you installed: twice as it is, then with prefers-reduced-motion forced, with JavaScript off, and with scripts from another site (another registrable domain, judged on the address and on every redirect hop) refused, which counts towards the request cap and is never requested. Largest Contentful Paint is the browser's last candidate, measured in milliseconds from just before the load was started, through the DevTools timeline; total blocking time is the time every long task spent over 50 ms from the start, never more than the load took, collected by an observer our script creates before the page's own scripts run, and not measured with JavaScript off (no script runs, so it is could-not-check for that change, never 0). A change is reported when it is larger than the two plain loads' spread, than 200 ms (100 ms for blocking time) and than 10% of their mean, as low-severity advice, in the order reduced motion, JavaScript, third-party. A page that shows under half its text without JavaScript is not compared for that change. Speed Index is not measured: it needs a video of the load. A load that fails, a missing timing or no browser is could-not-check. The five loads count towards the run's cap of 10 rendered pages, and the numbers are this computer's and unthrottled. A hostile page can call the measurement function itself and lie to its own measurement: reports that cannot be real (too many, under 50 ms, longer than the load, more in all than the load took) make the page's blocking time could-not-check, but a page that invents plausible tasks, or holds the thread unseen, is not caught. This is advice for the owner of a site who runs it on their own site, not a security boundary, and a finding says what the browser saw
done: Running Gaugeline again with --attribution shows no change (reduced motion, no JavaScript, no scripts from other sites) that moves total blocking time or Largest Contentful Paint by more than the page's own spread, or the owner has decided with the developer that the ones listed are acceptable.
estimateChanges: An hour to read the numbers and find the one script, tag or intro animation behind them; the fix is the usual one for that cause (delay or remove a third-party tag, shorten the long script, skip the intro for visitors who asked for less motion).

title: A simulated phone load of a page scores under 90 (advice, not a verdict)
what: Lighthouse, run by Google's PageSpeed Insights on a simulated mid-range phone with a throttled connection, scores a page's performance under 90 out of 100. This is a lab test of one load, kept apart from what real visitors measured.
why: A lab run is repeatable, so it shows where time goes (largest contentful paint, total blocking time, layout shift, speed index) and whether a change helped. It is not what visitors experienced: a page can score badly in the lab and be fine for real people, or the reverse, so it never decides pass or fail.
fix: Use it to find the cause once real visitors' figures say there is a problem: the largest element, the long scripts behind total blocking time, and what moves the layout. Do not chase the score on its own.
tech: Only with --pagespeed, from the same one GET per page as pagespeed-field-vitals (Lighthouse, mobile, performance category, run on Google's servers; Gaugeline runs no browser for it). A score under 90 is one low-severity finding with the score, largest contentful paint, total blocking time, layout shift and speed index as Lighthouse reports them. It is advice and never a pass or a fail; an answer with no Lighthouse run is could-not-check. A failed read is reported once, by pagespeed-field-vitals
done: Lighthouse's simulated-phone performance score for the page is 90 or more, or the owner has decided with the developer that the lower score is acceptable because real visitors' figures are good.
estimateChanges: An hour to read the numbers and find the one script or image behind them. The fixes are the same as for real visitors' figures.

title: On the website, not in fulfillment
what: A product on your website has no matching product in Printful.
why: For something you print, nobody will make the order. For a ticket, a download or a service, that is expected and nothing needs fixing.
fix: If the product should be printed, create it in Printful or save its Printful id on the website product. Otherwise leave it.
tech: a published Sanity product that matchProducts paired with no Printful product; runs only when both Sanity and Printful returned data; low because most shops sell some products that are not printed; one finding per product with its name and id
done: The product exists in Printful and is linked by id, or is left as website-only on purpose.
estimateChanges: Setting up artwork and variants in Printful if the product is new there.

title: In fulfillment, not on the website
what: A Printful product is not linked to any product on your website.
why: It is probably a sample, a draft or a product that was taken off the website. It can still be ordered through Printful's own store.
fix: Delete it in Printful if it is a leftover, or save its id on the website product it belongs to.
tech: a Printful product in matchProducts' unmatchedPrintful; runs only when both Sanity and Printful returned data; one finding per product with its name and id
done: The leftover is deleted in Printful, or its id is saved on the website product it belongs to.
estimateChanges: Checking nothing still sells from it.

title: In checkout, not on the website
what: An active Stripe product is not linked to any product on your website.
why: It may be a payment link or an invoice item on purpose. If it is a leftover, it clutters reports and someone may sell it by mistake.
fix: If it is meant to exist, leave it. If not, archive it in Stripe, or save its id on the website product it belongs to.
tech: an active Stripe product in matchProducts' unmatchedStripe; archived ones are skipped; runs only when both Sanity and Stripe returned data, because with no website products read every Stripe product would be unmatched; one finding per product with its name and id
done: The product is left as meant, archived, or linked by id to its website product.
estimateChanges: Subscriptions on it need care before it is archived.

title: A price is stored in two systems
what: The same price is saved on the Sanity product and on the matched Stripe product, and the two agree today.
why: Two copies that agree today are the cause of next month's mismatch: the next price change has to be made twice, and one of them will be forgotten.
fix: Decide which system owns each price, usually checkout, and have the other read it instead of storing its own copy.
tech: a Sanity product with a price whose matched Stripe product has a default price with a fixed amount, in a known currency, equal to it; one finding per run listing the count and the first five products; products whose prices differ are price-mismatch, not this
done: One system owns each price and the other reads it.
estimateChanges: The number of products, and code on both sides that has to change to read instead of store.

title: A subscription price in checkout has no plan on the page
what: A Stripe product you listed as a plan has an active subscription price that no plan on the page stands for.
why: A price that is live in Stripe but never shown is either a plan you forgot to put on the site, or an old price that can still be bought from an old link.
fix: Add the plan to the page, or archive the price in Stripe if it should no longer be sold.
tech: for each Stripe product in gaugeline.plans.json products (active), its prices with active true and a recurring object that no plan on the page was matched to; one finding per product listing up to three prices; a product that is archived, or not among the products that were read, says nothing here
done: The plan is on the page, or its price is archived in Stripe.
estimateChanges: Page design for the plan if it is shown for the first time.

title: A field your query asks for is missing on some documents
what: A query asks for a field that some published documents of the type have and others do not.
why: Fine when the field is optional. When the page assumes it is there (a link built from it, an image with no fallback), the documents without it break or show a gap.
fix: If the field is optional, make the template cope with it missing. If it is not, fill it in on the documents listed by their count, or mark it required in the schema.
tech: one GET of the query endpoint for each document type (perspective=published, so drafts are never counted), asking for count(*[_type == T]) and count(*[_type == T && defined(path)]) for each distinct field path, held in a Map from type to a Map from path to an integer; a reference or an array of objects is counted at the field itself (topic, not topic->title); the answer is integers, so no document and no field value is read; a path whose count is above 0 and below the type's total
done: The template copes with the field being missing, or every document has it, or the field is marked required.
estimateChanges: Filling in many documents is a data job. A template change is one edit.

title: A document has no stated total
what: A document of the type has no stated total at the field the rule names, so there is nothing to compare its parts with.
why: Either the pipeline skipped the field or the field was renamed. It is not a mismatch, because nothing was promised, but a page that prints the total prints a blank.
fix: Open the document by its id and fill the stated field in, or check the field name in the rule against your schema.
tech: one GET of the query endpoint for each rule (perspective=published, so drafts are never read); the filter does the comparing, so only ids and whole numbers come back, never a stated number, a part or any other field: the type's document count, the _id of the documents that have no stated number, and the _id of those where stated != coalesce(math::sum(parts), 0); a part that does not dereference is null and math::sum skips it; exact equality on the numbers, and the stated field or a part that is not a number on some document is exit 2 and nothing is reported; !defined(stated)
done: The stated field is filled in on each document named, or the rule's field name is corrected.
estimateChanges: Many documents are filled in one by one unless a migration sets them.

title: tsconfig targets es5 on a modern Next.js app
what: The tsconfig.json of a Next.js 13 or later app sets compilerOptions.target to es5, directly or through a tsconfig it extends.
why: es5 is the language level of browsers from over a decade ago. A modern Next.js app is built for current browsers, so the setting asks tools that read it to treat modern language features as missing and to write them out the long way, which can make the code bigger and slower for no visitor's benefit. Gaugeline has not confirmed what Next.js itself does with it.
fix: Set target to es2017 or later (create-next-app's own tsconfig is a good reference), and check that the project still compiles. If an old library needs the setting, keep it in that library's own tsconfig.
tech: static, reads tsconfig.json files and package.json as text and makes no request; only a tsconfig whose nearest package.json declares next 13 or later is read; comments and trailing commas are tolerated; extends is followed through relative files inside the folder (the last entry of an array wins); compilerOptions.target compared without case is es5: a finding that names the file and line that sets it; an extends that is a package, a file not in the folder, a file that was not read or that cannot be parsed, with no target of its own, is not sure; no target set, or es2017 or later, passes; the value of no other option is printed
done: tsconfig.json sets a target of es2017 or later, or none.
estimateChanges: One line in tsconfig.json; larger if an old library in the project relies on the old setting.

title: Draft mode code uses an API that next-sanity 13 removed
what: The code imports a draft mode hook, or sets an option or a prop, that next-sanity 12 had and next-sanity 13 removed, and the installed version is 13 or later.
why: Code copied from a site built on next-sanity 12 compiles in places and fails in others, and the failure is in preview: the editors' draft mode breaks or quietly stops refreshing while the published site looks fine, so it is noticed when a client first tries to preview a change.
fix: Follow next-sanity's v12 to v13 migration guide for each name listed: useDraftModePerspective becomes the resolvePerspectiveFromCookies helper in a server component, useIsLivePreview and useDraftModeEnvironment are replaced by useIsPresentationTool and useVisualEditingEnvironment, and the removed SanityLive props and defineLive options are dropped or replaced as the guide describes.
tech: static, reads the code files and package.json as text and makes no request; the installed version comes from the lockfile; it applies only when it is 13 or later; a finding for each import of useDraftModePerspective, useIsLivePreview or useDraftModeEnvironment from next-sanity or next-sanity/hooks, each of refreshOnFocus, refreshOnReconnect, refreshOnMount, intervalOnGoAway or tag written directly on a <SanityLive> tag, and each of stega or fetchOptions written directly in the options of defineLive, naming the file, line and name; a version below 13 is not a finding; a version that cannot be read, or no next-sanity in any package.json, with one of these names in the code, is not sure; no such name passes; no other text of a file is printed
done: The draft mode and visual editing code uses only what the installed next-sanity version provides.
estimateChanges: A hook swap is a few lines; the removed SanityLive props can each need a small component, as the migration guide shows.

title: A publish webhook clears the cache for draft ids too
what: The code that receives a Sanity publish webhook reads the document id and clears the cache, and nothing in it skips an id that starts with drafts. or versions.
why: Sanity keeps a draft under an id that starts with drafts. (and a content release version under versions.). If the webhook is also sent for those, every saved draft clears the cache: the site refetches content no visitor can see, and an editor typing for an afternoon keeps the cache cold. (Gaugeline has not confirmed from Sanity's documentation which documents a webhook is sent for.)
fix: Return early, before the cache is cleared, when the id starts with drafts. or versions.; or set the webhook in Sanity to send published documents only. Either is enough.
tech: reads the code files of the folder named, never runs them; a receiver is a file that imports @sanity/webhook or next-sanity/webhook, reads the sanity-webhook-signature header, or is a route that revalidates behind a secret; a call to revalidateTag, revalidatePath or updateTag in a receiver that reads the document id (_id, documentId, docId, ids) and has no mention of drafts. or versions., and no getPublishedId, isDraftId, isVersionId or isPublishedId call, is a finding at the first such call; a receiver that clears the cache and never reads an id is could-not-check, because the webhook's own settings in Sanity may already exclude drafts; the finding names the file and the line, never an id, a tag or the secret
done: The receiver returns before it clears the cache for an id that starts with drafts. or versions., or the webhook is set to send published documents only.
estimateChanges: One early return in one route file; a few minutes more if the receiver is copied into several routes or the webhook's trigger is changed in Sanity.

title: A content client is created when the framework's config file loads
what: A framework's config file (next.config, nuxt.config, astro.config and similar) makes a client for a content system such as Sanity or Contentful at the top level, or imports a module that does.
why: Every build, every test run and every tool that reads the config now runs the client's setup and needs its settings, so a fake project id ends up in each of them, and the setup runs at build time whether or not a page needs it.
fix: Keep the config file free of clients. Make the client in the function that reads content, and keep the few values the config needs (a redirect list, an image host) as plain data, or generate them in a script that runs before the build.
tech: reads the code files of the folder named, never runs them; looks at next.config, nuxt.config, astro.config, svelte.config, remix.config, vite.config, react-router.config and gatsby-config files (.js, .mjs, .cjs, .ts); a file that imports a content-system package (@sanity/client, next-sanity, contentful, @prismicio/client, @directus/sdk, DatoCMS, Storyblok, Contentstack, Kontent, Ghost, Strapi) and calls createClient, createDirectus, createDeliveryClient, createManagementClient, createPrismicClient or new <Name>Client outside a function is a finding at that line; so is a config that imports a local module that does; a call inside a function or a dynamic import is not; no source file read, or some left out, is could-not-check; the finding names the file and the line, never a setting
done: The framework's config file makes no content client: it is made in a function, in a module the config does not import.
estimateChanges: Minutes if the client is only used for one list: move it into the function that needs it. More if the config's values come from the content system and need a build step.

title: A form loads its validation library into the browser only to read field names
what: A client component imports a schema (zod, yup, valibot and similar) or defines one, and the only thing it does with it is read its field names (.shape, .keyof()).
why: Everything a client component imports is sent to the visitor's browser. The validation library, and the whole schema with its rules, are downloaded on every page with the form, so that the page can list a few field names a plain array would hold.
fix: Export the field names as a plain list, or derive them in a server component and pass them in. Keep the schema where the submission is validated, on the server.
tech: reads the code files of the folder named, never runs them; a file that starts with "use client" and imports, from a local module that loads zod, yup, valibot, joi, superstruct or arktype, a schema declared as const x = <lib>.object(...), or declares one itself after importing the library, and whose every use of it is .shape, .keyof(), .entries or .fields (a use only in a type does not count) is a finding at the import; a parse, safeParse, validate or resolver call means the browser validates and is left alone; a use Gaugeline cannot read (assigned, passed on, exported) is could-not-check; no source file read, or some left out, is could-not-check; the finding names the files and the library, never a field name
done: A client component gets its field names from a plain list, and the validation library is imported only where a schema validates a submission.
estimateChanges: Minutes: export the field names as an array next to the schema, or derive them in the server component and pass them down. More if the same schema also validates in the browser.

title: Visual editing is set up with no route mapped to a document
what: The Presentation tool is configured with no resolve.mainDocuments (no resolve option, a resolve with only locations, or an empty list), so no route of the site is mapped to the document it shows.
why: Presentation can open the document behind a page only when it is told which route shows which document. Without that mapping an editor looking at a page in the preview cannot jump to the document to edit it. (Gaugeline has not confirmed from Sanity's documentation the message the editor sees.)
fix: Add resolve.mainDocuments to presentationTool, with defineDocuments: for each kind of page, its route (/menu/:slug) and the type or GROQ filter of the document it shows. Add locations as well if editors should see where a document is used.
tech: reads the code files of the folder named, never runs them; a call of presentationTool in a file that imports it from sanity/presentation or @sanity/presentation, with its options written in the call, and no resolve option, a resolve object with no mainDocuments, or an empty mainDocuments list, is a finding at the call; options that are not written in the call, a spread, or a resolve that is not an object written in the call is could-not-check; the routes are not compared with the site's pages; no source file read, or some left out, is could-not-check; the finding names the file and the line, never a route or a project id
done: The Presentation tool's resolve option lists mainDocuments: each route of the site that shows a document maps to it.
estimateChanges: A few lines per kind of page with defineDocuments: a route and a type or a filter. More if the site has many kinds of page.
